answer.text:
What you have is a common-gate (CG) NMOS voltage-amplifier stage.  
The gate of M1 is fixed at a dc bias voltage Vb, the small-signal input is injected
into the source through the coupling capacitor C1, and the output is taken at the
drain through the load resistor RD.

────────────────────────────────
1. DC (bias-point) analysis
────────────────────────────────
For dc the capacitor is open-circuited, so VS = 0 and

    VGS(Q) = Vb
    ID ≃ ½ kn (Vb – VTH)²(1 + λVDS)               (saturation model)

The quiescent output voltage is

    VOUT(Q) = VDD – ID RD.

To keep M1 in saturation

    VDS(Q) = VOUT(Q) > VGS(Q) – VTH = Vb – VTH.

Hence Vb is chosen so that the required ID is obtained while the above inequality
is satisfied and VOUT(Q) stays comfortably inside the rails (often ≈ VDD/2).

────────────────────────────────
2. Small-signal (ac) model
────────────────────────────────
At signal frequencies C1 is a short, so the small-signal source node voltage is

    vS = vIN.           (gate is ac-ground because Vb is dc)

Small-signal drain current

    iD = gm(vG – vS) + gds(vD – vS)
       = –gm vIN + gds(vOUT – vIN)                    (vg = 0).

The same current must flow through RD (top of RD is ac ground):

    iD = –vOUT / RD.

Solve for the voltage gain Av = vOUT / vIN:

      –vOUT / RD = –gm vIN + gds(vOUT – vIN)

⇒  vOUT(1/ro + 1/RD) – vIN(gm + 1/ro) = 0

⇒  Av  =  vOUT / vIN  =  (gm + 1/ro) / (1/ro + 1/RD)
        = (gm ro + 1) / (1 + ro / RD).

Useful limiting case (ro ≫ RD, gm ro ≫ 1):

      Av ≈ gm RD        (positive, i.e. no phase inversion).

────────────────────────────────
3. Input and output impedances
────────────────────────────────
Input current (into the source):

    iIN = gm vIN + gds(vIN – vOUT)
         = vIN[gm + gds(1 – Av)].

With Av given above and gm ro ≫ 1 the second term is negligible, so

    RIN = |vIN / iIN| ≃ 1 / gm      (very low – typical of CG stages).

Output resistance looking into the drain:

    ROUT ≃ RD || ro.

────────────────────────────────
4. Frequency response (role of C1)
────────────────────────────────
C1 merely removes the dc path from the signal source to the transistor.
Together with the Thevenin resistance of the source (RSIG) and RIN it forms a
high-pass network whose lower –3 dB pole is

    fL ≈ 1 / [2π C1 (RSIG + RIN)].

The upper bandwidth of the stage is set by the transistor’s parasitic Cgd, Cdb,
the load, and any circuitry that follows.

────────────────────────────────
5. Salient features of the stage
────────────────────────────────
• Configuration: common gate, non-inverting.  
• Voltage gain: ≈ gm RD (tens of V/V easily).  
• Input impedance: low (≈ 1/gm), useful for current-source or RF matching.  
• Output impedance: high (≈ RD), good for driving high-impedance loads or
  for use as the first device in a cascode stack.  
• C1 allows the input node to sit at ground while the gate is biased at the
  optimum Vb; at signal frequencies it is effectively a short.

Hence the circuit is a single-transistor common-gate amplifier that provides
a substantial, non-inverting voltage gain with low input and high output
resistance, widely used in RF front ends and as the “cascode” device in many
analog integrated-circuit blocks.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Identifies the common-gate topology but misses that the source node is directly shorted to ground, so the input is shorted and the ideal gain is zero. The claimed gain of approximately gmRD is therefore incorrect.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
Only two circuit nodes are able to accumulate charge and therefore store energy dynamically:

1. Gate node (the node between RS and the MOS gate).  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CGS to ground, and CGD to the drain node.

2. Drain/output node.  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CDB to ground, and the other plate of CGD to the gate node.  
   • RD returns the node to AC ground (VDD is an AC short).

The source and body are tied to ground, so CSB does not create an independent energy-storage node, and VDD is AC ground as well.

Because there are only two independent energy-storage nodes, the small-signal transfer function Vin → Vout is second-order; i.e., the amplifier exhibits

2 poles.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two poles and accounts for the capacitors, including that CSB has both terminals grounded and contributes no dynamic state.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
In small-signal (ac) analysis every pole is produced by an independent node whose voltage has to change the charge on at least one capacitor.  

1. Source, bulk and the supply node VDD are ac grounds, so any capacitor that is tied only to those nodes (e.g. CSB, part of CGS, part of CDB) does not introduce an independent state variable.  
2. The remaining high-impedance nodes are  
   • the gate node (behind RS) – it sees CGS to ground and C GD to the drain,  
   • the drain/output node – it sees RD (to ac ground), CDB to ground and C GD to the gate.  

Thus there are exactly two independent energy-storage nodes → the transfer function is second-order and the stage exhibits two poles (plus whatever zeros the C GD feed-forward path creates).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two poles and accounts for the capacitor network: CSB is inactive with source and bulk grounded, while CGS, CGD, and CDB load the two active nodes. The wording about parts of CGS and CDB is imprecise, but does not change the correct conclusion.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
Look at how many independent signal nodes can store energy.

1. Gate node (Ng) – it is not fixed; it is reached through the source resistance RS.  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CGS (to ground) and CGD (to the drain node).

2. Drain / output node (Nd) – its voltage is set by RD, ro, etc., not by an ideal voltage source.  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CDB (to ground) and CGD (to the gate node).

The source and body are hard-wired to ground, so CSB is strapped across ground and does not create a state variable.  
Because only two independent node voltages (vg and vd) can vary, the small-signal model yields two first-order differential equations. Hence the transfer function denominator is second-order:

Number of poles = number of independent energy-storage nodes = 2.

(If the driving source had zero impedance, i.e. RS = 0, the gate node would be forced, leaving only one pole at the output.)

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
1.  What the circuit is  
   • M1 is an n-channel MOS transistor used in common–source mode (gate = Vin , drain = Vout , source = VF).  
   • RD is the load in the drain.  
   • R1–R2 form a resistive feedback network that ties the source node (VF) to the output node (Vout).  
   • Because the feedback is taken from the output and returned to the source, the device operates the way an op-amp with “series–shunt” (voltage-series) feedback would: the MOSFET contributes a large open-loop gain, while the divider forces a precise closed-loop gain that is almost independent of gm once the loop gain is high.

2.  Large-signal (dc) bias equations  
   Id  = (1/2)k′(W/L)(Vin – VF – VTH)²        (M1 in saturation)        (1)  
   Vout = VDD – Id RD                                                       (2)  
   KCL at VF :      Id  = (Vout – VF)/R1 + VF/R2                           (3)  

   Solving (1)-(3) simultaneously gives the dc operating point {Id , Vout , VF }.  
   To keep the device in saturation we must also have                             
        Vout – VF  ≥  Vin – VF – VTH.

3.  Small-signal model  
   Substitute the small-signal quantities (lower-case) into the MOS π-model (ro may be added but is neglected here for clarity).

   id  =  gm (vin – vs)                               (4)  
   vout = – id RD                                    (5)  
   KCL at the source node vs :  
        id  = vs/R2  + (vs – vout)/R1                (6)

   Solve (4)-(6) for the closed-loop gain Av  =  vout / vin :

        Av  =  – gm RD (R1 + R2) 
               ───────────────────────────────                           (7)
              (R1 + R2) – gm R2 (RD – R1)

4.  Behaviour for high loop-gain ( gm RD  »  (R1 + R2) )  
   When RD ≫ R1,  the term gm R2 (RD – R1) dominates the denominator.  
   Equation (7) then collapses to

        Av  ≃  (R1 + R2) / R2  =  1 + R1/R2       (8,  non-inverting gain)

   Thus the closed-loop gain is set almost completely by the two resistors and is positive (the circuit has become a non-inverting amplifier).  The parameter gm has virtually disappeared, giving good gain accuracy and temperature stability—exactly the purpose of the feedback.

5.  Other small-signal quantities  
   • Input resistance:  Rin ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
   • Output resistance (with feedback):  Rout ≈ RD ∥ R1 /(1+|Aβ|) ≈ RD /(1+gm R2 (RD – R1)/(R1+R2)), i.e. much lower than RD when the loop-gain is large.  
   • Bandwidth is extended by the same feedback factor 1 + R1/R2.

6.  Design guidelines / operating conditions  
   • Choose RD ≫ R1 to guarantee negative feedback and to obtain the closed-loop gain of (1+R1/R2).  
   • Verify that for the worst-case Vin the inequality for saturation is satisfied.  
   • Check that the current through R1-R2 (≈ Vout / (R1+R2)) is at least 5-10 × smaller than Id so that the divider does not load the transistor excessively (if this is not true, include that current in the bias equations above).  
   • The usable Vin range is limited on the upper end by the saturation condition and on the lower end by VTH.

7.  What to remember  
   • Open-loop the network is an ordinary common-source stage with gain −gmRD.  
   • Closing the loop with the R1–R2 network converts it into a precision non-inverting amplifier whose gain is (1+R1/R2) provided the loop-gain gmRD is large.  
   • The circuit offers the high input resistance of a MOS gate, a closed-loop gain set by passive components, and an output resistance much smaller than RD.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It misreads the topology: Vin is applied to the source and the output divider feeds the gate, not vice versa. The analysis therefore concerns a different circuit and gives the wrong feedback mechanism and gain.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The drawing is nothing more than a single n-MOSFET (M1) used as an amplifier, but its source is not returned directly to ground; instead it is tied to ground through the series pair R1 – R2 while the junction of the two resistors is fed back to the drain through R1.  
Because a fraction of the drain voltage is injected into the source, the stage behaves like a common-source amplifier that contains a resistive, voltage-sampling feedback loop.  
Below the circuit is analysed step by step.

1. DC (bias) relations  
   Let   β ≜ R2 /(R1 + R2)        (0 < β < 1)  

   Voltage divider:                   VF = β · Vout                (1)  

   Drain current through the MOSFET (assume strong inversion, saturation, body effect neglected)

            ID = ½ kn (Vin – VF – VTH )²                          (2)

            kn = μn Cox W/L  

   Drain current through RD

            ID = ( VDD – Vout ) / RD                              (3)

   (1)–(3) give the static transfer characteristic

         ½ kn ( Vin – VTH – β Vout )² = ( VDD – Vout ) / RD       (4)

   Equation (4) can be solved for Vout for any applied Vin; it also shows
   that by choosing R1 and R2 the bias point can be shifted without having to
   change Vin or RD.

   Saturation condition  
           VDS = Vout – VF = (1 – β) Vout ≥ VGS – VTH   
           ⇒   Vout ≥ (Vin – VTH)/(1 – β)                         (5)

2. Small–signal model  
   Introduce the conductances

      gD = 1 / RD ,       g1 = 1 / R1 ,      g2 = 1 / R2 ,  
      gm = kn (Vin – VF – VTH)  (evaluated at the bias point)

   Ignoring ro (it can easily be appended) the nodal equations around drain (vo) and source (vs) are

      (gD + g1) vo – (g1 + gm) vs + gm vi = 0                     (6)
      – g1 vo + (g1 + g2 + gm) vs – gm vi = 0                     (7)

   Solving (6)–(7) gives the small-signal gain

      Av ≜ vo / vi =  –  gm ( RD || R1 ) / [ 1 + gm ( R1 || R2 ) ] (8)

   A useful way of reading (8)  

   • Numerator  gm (RD || R1)  is exactly what an ordinary
     common-source stage would produce if its drain load were the
     parallel-combination RD || R1.  

   • The feedback network appears only in the denominator
     1 + gm (R1 || R2).  For gm (R1 || R2)  » 1 the magnitude of the
     gain is reduced roughly by the factor gm (R1 || R2).  
     Hence the loop provides a controllable degeneration that improves
     linearity at the expense of gain.

   Limiting cases  
   a) R1 → ∞ :  β → 0,  the feedback vanishes, the circuit degenerates to a
      normal common-source with a single source resistor R2.  
      Av →  – gm RD / (1 + gm R2).  

   b) R2 → ∞ :  β → 1,  the source is almost at the drain potential, so the
      stage turns into a source follower (gain ≈ +1).  

   c) R2 → 0  (β → 0) :  complete source degeneration, gain tends to –RD/R1.

3. Input, output and noise considerations  
   • Rin (at the gate) ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
   • Rout (looking into the drain) ≈ RD || R1 (≃ RD if RD ≪ R1).  
   • The feedback lowers distortion in the same way a source resistor does,
     but without consuming large headroom because the feedback signal is
     taken from the drain rather than from ground.

4. Practical design hints  
   • Choose R1, R2 so that  gm (R1 || R2) ≳ 3 … 5  for worthwhile linearity
     improvement.  
   • Verify (5) to ensure M1 remains in saturation over the intended signal
     swing.  
   • If large gain is required, make R1 ≫ RD; if wide swing and good
     linearity are preferred, make R1 comparable to RD.

In short, the circuit is a self-biased common-source amplifier in which a resistive voltage divider (R1-R2) feeds a portion of the output voltage back to the source.  
This negative feedback fixes the operating point and at the same time introduces controlled source degeneration, giving a tunable compromise between gain, head-room and linearity.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer misidentifies the key connections: Vin is applied to the source and the output divider feeds the gate, not the source. Its common-source model and inverting gain therefore do not describe the circuit, though it recognizes the general idea of resistive negative feedback.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The network is nothing more than a common-source NMOS stage (M1 + RD) that is closed around a shunt-series negative-feedback loop made with the divider R1–R2.  
A rise of Vout is coupled through R1 to the source node VF; VF rises, VGS = Vin–VF falls, the drain current decreases and Vout is pulled back – therefore the feedback is negative.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DC (large-signal) bias
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let βF ≜ R2 /(R1 + R2)           (feedback factor)  
VF   = βF Vout                   (by the divider)             (1)

For M1 in saturation (λ≈0 for the moment)

ID = ½ k´(W/L)(Vin – VF – VTH)²                         (2)

while in the drain branch

ID = (VDD – Vout)/RD                                   (3)

Combining (1), (2) and (3) gives the bias equation

(VDD – Vout)/RD = ½ k´(W/L) [Vin – βF Vout – VTH]²     (4)

together with the saturation condition

Vout – VF ≥ VGS – VTH  →  Vout(1–βF) ≥ Vin – VF – VTH. (5)

(4) can be solved graphically or numerically for Vout; once Vout is known, VF and ID follow directly from (1) and (3).  
Because of the feedback, the quiescent current depends only weakly on the MOS parameters: a percentage change in k´ or VTH produces a much smaller percentage change in the operating point.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal model
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Adopt the usual small-signal symbols  
gD = 1/RD ,  g1 = 1/R1 ,  g2 = 1/R2 ,  go = 1/ro .

Writing KCL at the drain node (vo) and at the source node (vs)

(gD + g1 + go) vo – (g1 + go + gm) vs + gm vi = 0       (6)
–(g1 + go) vo + (g1 + g2 + go + gm) vs – gm vi = 0      (7)

Solving (6)–(7) for the gain Av = vo / vi gives the exact
closed-loop expression

Av = – gm g2
     ────────────────────────────────────────────────          (8)
     gD (g1 + g2 + gm + go) + (g1 + go) g2

With ro ≫ R1 (go ≈ 0) (8) reduces to

Av = – gm g2
     ────────────────────────────────                           (9)
     gD (g1 + g2 + gm) + g1 g2

Multiplying top and bottom of (9) by RD R1 R2 gives a handier
resistance form

Av = – gm RD R1
     ──────────────────────────────────                           (10)
     RD + R1 + R2 + gm R1 R2

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Behaviour of the gain
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Weak loop-gain (gm R1 R2 ≪ RD + R1 + R2)   
  Av ≈ – gm RD R1 /(RD + R1 + R2)  → proportional to gm.  

• Strong loop-gain (gm R1 R2 ≫ RD + R1 + R2)   
  Av ≈ – RD / R2                                  (11)

Thus, once gm is high enough the gain is fixed almost completely by the
passive resistors RD and R2; MOS-parameter spread or temperature
variations hardly move it – the principal advantage of the topology.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Input and output resistances
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Input: the gate is insulated, so  
Rin ≅ very large (≈ the gate leakage resistance).

Output: looking into the drain

Rout ≅ RD ∥ (ro + (1 + gm R2⁄(R1+R2)) R1) ;  
for gm R1,R2 » 1 this approaches RD.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Open-loop / feedback viewpoint
--------------------------------------------------------------------
If the feedback network is “opened” (R1, R2 disconnected from
the source) the transconductance amplifier alone provides

A0 = –gm RD  (Vout / (Vin–VS)).

With the feedback factor βF = R2/(R1+R2)

Closed-loop:   Av = A0 / (1 + βF A0)  
and substituting A0 reproduces (9).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Summary of key points
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. VF is a fractional copy of Vout; that turns the circuit into a
   single-transistor op-amp closed by a resistive divider.
2. The DC bias is set by the intersection of the MOS I–V characteristic
   with the line (VDD–Vout)/RD; feedback makes it almost insensitive to
   device spread.
3. Exact small-signal gain is given by (8) or (10).  
   For the usual case gm R1 R2 ≫ RD + R1 + R2,

        Av ≈ – RD / R2                                  (design rule)

4. Very high input resistance, moderate output resistance (≈ RD).  
5. The circuit is a convenient way to obtain a precise, programmable
   negative gain with only one active device; choosing RD and R2 fixes
   the gain, while R1 can be used to help satisfy the saturation
   condition or to trim bias current.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer swaps the input and feedback connections: the actual input is at the source and the divider drives the gate. Its common-source model and inverting gain therefore describe the wrong topology. It gets only minimal credit for recognizing a divider-based negative-feedback mechanism.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
What you have is a single-ended NMOS “source follower’’ (common-drain stage) that is biased with an NMOS current-sink load.

1.  How the circuit works  

    •  M2 is given a fixed gate–bias Vb.  
       Provided    Vout ≥ Vb – Vtn2,   M2 is in saturation and sinks an (almost) constant current  

                 ID2 ≈ (β2 / 2)·(Vb – Vtn2)²        (β = μCoxW/L)                (1)

    •  The same current must flow through M1.  
       With its drain at VDD, its source at Vout and its gate driven by Vin, M1 is an NMOS
       operated as a source follower and (for the usual Vin range) is also in saturation
       because   

                 VDS1 = VDD – Vout  ≥  VGS1 – Vtn1 = (Vin – Vout) – Vtn1          (2)
                 →  VDD ≥ Vin – Vtn1  (always true if Vin ≤ VDD).  

       Therefore  

                 ID1 = (β1 / 2)·(Vin – Vout – Vtn1)²                            (3)

    •  At dc ID1 = ID2, so from (1) and (3)

                 Vin – Vout – Vtn1 = √[ (β2 / β1) ] · (Vb – Vtn2)               (4)

       and finally

                 Vout = Vin – Vtn1 – √(β2/β1)·(Vb – Vtn2).                      (5)

       If the two transistors are laid out identically (β1 = β2):

                 Vout = Vin – ( Vb – Vtn )                                      (6)

       i.e. the output follows the input with unit slope, merely shifted downward by a
       constant voltage ≃ (Vb – Vtn).  This is the hallmark of a source-follower buffer.

2.  Large-signal limits  

    •  Turn-off of M1:  the pair conducts only while Vin > Vtn1.  
    •  M2 leaves saturation when Vout < Vb – Vtn2; below that point the simple square-law
      relation no longer holds and the node is pulled close to ground.  
    •  The highest output obtainable while keeping M1 in saturation is
                  Vout,max ≈ VDD – (Vin – Vtn1)  (≃ VDD – a few hundred mV).

3.  Small-signal behaviour  

    Using the hybrid-π model (gds1 = 1/ro1, gds2 = 1/ro2):

          gm1·(vin – vout) + gds1·vout + gds2·vout = 0

          ⇒   Av ≡ vout / vin = gm1 / (gm1 + gds1 + gds2).                    (7)

    When gm1 ≫ (gds1 + gds2) the gain approaches unity.  
    The small-signal output resistance seen at Vout is

          Rout = 1 / (gm1 + gds1 + gds2)  ≈ 1 / gm1   (for gm1 ≫ gds).         (8)

4.  Power  

          PDC ≈ VDD · ID   with ID set by (1).

5.  Summary  

    •  M2 fixes a bias current;  
    •  M1, connected as a source follower, transfers the input to the output with almost
      unity gain and a constant level shift;  
    •  The stage provides a low-impedance output node whose voltage swing is roughly
      Vin minus one threshold, limited at the bottom by M1 turn-off and at the top by the
      saturation condition of M2.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as a source follower and M2 as its NMOS current-source load, and gives a positive gain approaching unity. The simplified gain model omits body effect, which is an allowed idealization under the full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The schematic is nothing more than a very small-signal “one-transistor” inverter that uses a constant-current sink instead of the usual n-device that is driven by the input.  
If we adopt the conventional CMOS orientation  

• M1 is a p–MOS device (source at VDD, drain at the output node)  
• M2 is an n–MOS device (source at ground, drain at the output node)  

the circuit can be viewed as a common-source amplifier whose load is the p-device and whose bias current is furnished by the n-device.  
(If you choose to draw both transistors as n-devices the algebra is the same, only the sign of the threshold voltage of the upper device changes.)

1. Large-signal (dc) operating point  

Let  

β1 = μp Cox (W/L)1            (transconductance parameter of M1, p-MOS)  
β2 = μn Cox (W/L)2            (parameter of M2, n-MOS)  
|VTP|, VTN                    (threshold voltages)  
λp , λn                       (channel-length modulation factors)

We bias M2 with a fixed gate voltage Vb, so in saturation its drain current is  

ID = ½ β2 (Vb – VTN)^2 (1 + λn VDS2)         (1)  

(as long as VDS2 ≥ VGS2 – VTN, i.e. Vout ≥ Vb – VTN).

Exactly the same current must flow through M1.  
If M1 is kept in saturation (VSD1 ≥ |VSG1| – |VTP|, i.e. Vout ≤ Vin – |VTP|),  

ID = ½ β1 (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2 (1 + λp VDS1)         (2)  

with VDS1 = VDD – Vout.

Equating (1) and (2) gives the dc transfer law of the stage:

½ β1 (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2 (1 + λp (VDD – Vout))  
            = ½ β2 (Vb – VTN)^2 (1 + λn Vout)             (3)

If channel-length modulation is ignored (λp = λn = 0) the relation is simple:

β1 (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2 = β2 (Vb – VTN)^2              (4)

so that the gate voltage that centres the output is

Vin(mid-point) = VDD – |VTP| – √(β2/β1) (Vb – VTN).      (5)

Whenever Vin is lower than the value given by (5) M1 conducts more than the
constant current pulled by M2, so the only way to match currents is to raise
Vout toward the supply; the output therefore sits at a high level.  
If Vin is raised above (5) M1 delivers too little current,
M2 pulls the node down, and Vout drops toward ground.  
Thus, in the large-signal sense, the stage works like an
inverting switch:

• Vin low  ⟶  Vout ≈ VDD (logic “1”)  
• Vin high ⟶  Vout ≈ 0 V (logic “0”)  

but the exact switching point is set by device sizes (β-ratio) and by the bias
voltage Vb that fixes the tail current.

Boundary conditions for validity of (4):

Vb – VTN  ≤ Vout ≤ Vin – |VTP|                 (both devices in sat.)  (6)

If either inequality is violated the transistor concerned moves into triode
and Vout is clamped close to a rail.

2. Small-signal (incremental) behaviour  

Bias the stage at some quiescent current ID (found from (3)).  
In saturation the small-signal parameters are

gm1 = ∂ID/∂VSG1 = √(2 β1 ID)           (p-device)  
ro1 = 1/(λp ID)  

gm2 = ∂ID/∂VGS2 = √(2 β2 ID)           (tail n-device)  
ro2 = 1/(λn ID)

Because the gate of M2 is fixed, its transconductance does not influence the
gain; only its output resistance does.  
With the usual small-signal half-circuit one obtains

AV = vout / vin = – gm1 (ro1 ∥ ro2)                (7)

Replacing gm1 and ro with the expressions above,

AV = – √(2 β1 ID) · 1 / [ ID (λp + λn) ]  
   ≈ – √(2 β1 / ID) / (λp + λn)                    (8)

Important observations:

• AV is negative – the node inverts the input.  
• |AV| rises if the bias current ID is reduced (1/√ID dependence) and if long
  channels are used (λ → 0).  
• With the intrinsic output resistance of both
  devices in parallel, ro sets the upper bound on gain.

3. What the circuit is good for

a) Digital point of view  
If Vb is chosen so that M2 sinks only a weak current, the inverter is
“pseudo-CMOS”: it consumes static current but can be used, for instance, as a
ratioed pull-up/pull-down element in low-performance logic.

b) Analog point of view  
With Vb selected to give a few tens of micro-amps, the stage is a very
compact voltage amplifier (common-source with active current mirror load).
It is the core of many op-amp input stages, one-stage OTAs and sense
amplifiers.

4. Summary of operating regions

1. Vin < VDD – |VTP| – √(β2/β1)(Vb – VTN)  
   – M1 strongly ON, M2 sets current

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
What the circuit is  
• Both transistors are n-channel MOSFETs.  
• M1 is connected with its drain at the supply, therefore the signal is taken from its source; this is a common-drain (source-follower) stage.  
• M2 has a constant gate-voltage Vb and works as an n-MOS current source that pulls the follower node toward ground.  

Hence the block is nothing more than an n-MOS source follower whose tail-current is furnished by another n-MOS device.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Large-signal (DC) analysis  

Notation  
β1 = μn Cox (W/L)1  β2 = μn Cox (W/L)2  
Vov2 = Vb – Vth2  (over-drive of M2)  
Assume both devices operate in saturation, i.e.  

 M1 (VDD – Vout) ≥ (Vin – Vout – Vth1)  (always true if Vin ≤ VDD)  
 M2 Vout ≥ (Vb – Vth2)

Step 1 – current of the bias transistor  

     ID2 = ½ β2 (Vb – Vth2)² = ½ β2 Vov2²        (1)

Step 2 – the same current must flow through M1  

     ID1 = ½ β1 (Vin – Vout – Vth1)²              (2)

Equating (1) and (2) gives the DC transfer characteristic

     Vin – Vout = Vth1 + √(β2/β1) (Vb – Vth2)     (3)

or, solving for the output

     Vout = Vin – Vth1 – √(β2/β1) (Vb – Vth2)     (4)

Observations  
• If M1 is made much wider than M2 (β1 ≫ β2) the second term is small and we get the familiar follower relation

     Vout ≈ Vin – Vth1

 i.e. the stage shifts the input down by one threshold voltage.  
• The lowest value the output can reach while M2 is still in saturation is

     Vout,min = Vb – Vth2                         (5)

• With Vin driven as high as VDD the highest obtainable output is

     Vout,max ≈ VDD – Vth1                        (6)

 (the follower can never rise all the way to the rail).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal (incremental) behaviour  

Small-signal parameters (at the bias current I)  

     gm1 = 2I / Vov1 , gm2 = 2I / Vov2  
     ro1 , ro2 = 1/λI (channel-length modulation)

Because Vb is a DC quantity, vgs2 = 0 in the small-signal model, so M2 contributes only its output resistance ro2.  
Writing KCL at the output node:

     gm1( vin – vout ) + vout/ro1 + vout/ro2 = 0

Hence the voltage gain is

     Av = vout / vin = gm1 / ( gm1 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )     (7)

If both ro’s are large, Av → 1, which is the hallmark of a source follower.  
The output (small-signal) resistance is therefore

     Rout ≈ 1 / ( gm1 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )   ≈ 1/gm1      (8)

and the input resistance is practically infinite (MOS gate).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Design guidelines / useful numbers  

1. Pick Vb so that Vov2 ≈ 0.15–0.25 V.  
   → This sets the bias current with (1) and fixes Vout,min via (5).  
2. Make M1 wide enough so that β1 ≫ β2; then the follower drop is almost one Vth and the small extra term in (4) can be neglected.  
3. Check that (5) ≤ the lowest signal level you ever need and that (6) ≥ the highest one.  
4. Verify that both transistors remain in saturation over the whole signal swing.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
What the circuit is useful for  

• Level-shifting a signal down by approximately one threshold voltage.  
• Buffering a high-impedance node while keeping the voltage loss (droop) small.  
• Source-degeneration or cascode bias networks in analog CMOS blocks.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Key results to remember  

DC:   Vout ≈ Vin – Vth1               (if β1 ≫ β2)  
Gain: Av ≈ 1                          (follower)  
Swing: Vb – Vth2  ≤  Vout ≤ VDD – Vth1

answer.text:
The drawing is the elementary CMOS inverter – a complementary pair consisting of  

• M₂ : a p-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to the positive supply VDD  
• M₁ : an n-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to ground  

The two drains are shorted to form the output node Vout, and the two gates are shorted to the input node Vin.  
Only one device conducts in the static states, so the quiescent (dc) power loss is ideally zero.

1. Logic (qualitative) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V → M₁ off (VGSₙ < VTN), M₂ on (VSGₚ > |VTP|) → Vout pulled to VDD (logic 1).  
   b) Vin ≈ VDD → M₂ off (VSGₚ < |VTP|), M₁ on (VGSₙ > VTN) → Vout pulled to 0 V (logic 0).  
   Thus the stage performs the NOT function.

2. D-C transfer characteristic  
   Let βn = μnCox(W/L)n and βp = μpCox(W/L)p.  
   In the transition region (VTN < Vin < VDD – |VTP|) the two devices conduct simultaneously and, to first order, both are in saturation. Equating their drain currents

          βn/2 · (Vin – Vout – VTN)²  =  βp/2 · (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)²        (1)

   gives Vout(Vin).  For the special case βn = βp and |VTP| = VTN the locus is

          Vout = 2Vin – VDD

   and the switching (mid-point) voltage, obtained by also requiring dVout/dVin = –1, is very close to VDD/2.  With unequal β–values the switching point is

          VM ≈ (VDD + |VTP| + √(βp/βn)·VTN) / (1 + √(βp/βn))

   which is centred by choosing (W/L)p ≈ (μn/μp)(W/L)n so that βp ≈ βn.

3. Noise margins  
   VIL and VIH are obtained from |dVout/dVin| = 1 in (1); the noise margins follow

          NML = VIL – VOL     ,     NMH = VOH – VIH
          VOL ≈ 0 , VOH ≈ VDD

   Because the gain |dVout/dVin| in the transition region can exceed 40–50, good noise margins (typically > 0.4 VDD) are obtained.

4. Dynamic behaviour  
   • Low-to-high delay (n-device releases load):

          tPLH ≈ Rp · CL ≈ CL / [βp (VDD – |VTP|)]                        

   • High-to-low delay (n-device pulls down):

          tPHL ≈ Rn · CL ≈ CL / [βn (VDD – VTN)]

   Matching βp to βn equalises the two delays.  
   Dynamic power: Pdyn = CL VDD² fCLK ; short-circuit power exists only for the brief time both devices conduct.

5. Key features that make the CMOS inverter the basic building block of modern digital ICs  
   • Rail-to-rail output swing (0 – VDD)  
   • Large noise margins determined mainly by device sizing, not by resistor ratios  
   • Essentially zero static power (only leakage)  
   • Symmetric transfer when βp ≈ βn, giving equal rise/fall delays  
   • Very high input resistance; fan-out determined by capacitive loading only

Hence the circuit in the figure is a standard complementary MOS inverter and its behaviour is completely described by the relations above.

The drawing is the standard complementary MOS (CMOS) inverter, built with one p-channel transistor (M2) and one n-channel transistor (M1).

1. Node connections  
   • M2 (pMOS): source → VDD, drain → Vout, gate → Vin  
   • M1 (nMOS): drain → Vout, source → GND, gate → Vin  
   • The two gates are shorted together, so both devices see the same input voltage.

2. Static (DC) behaviour  
   a. Vin = 0 V (logic 0)  
      – pMOS: VSG = VDD  ⇒ ON  
      – nMOS: VGS = 0     ⇒ OFF  
      ⇒ Vout is pulled up to VDD  (logic 1).

   b. Vin = VDD (logic 1)  
      – pMOS: VSG ≈ 0     ⇒ OFF  
      – nMOS: VGS = VDD   ⇒ ON  
      ⇒ Vout is pulled down to 0 V  (logic 0).

   c. Intermediate Vin  
      Both transistors conduct simultaneously; the exact switching point VM is obtained from
            βn (Vin – Vtn)² = βp (VDD – Vin – |Vtp|)²
      (βn = kn Wn/Ln, βp = kp Wp/Lp).  
      If βn ≈ βp, VM ≈ VDD/2, giving nearly equal noise margins.

3. Voltage-transfer characteristic (VTC)  
   • VOL ≈ 0 V, VOH ≈ VDD (rail-to-rail).  
   • High small-signal gain (–dVout/dVin) around VM.  
   • Noise margins:  NML = VIL – VOL,  NMH = VOH – VIH; with symmetric sizing both approach VDD/2.

4. Dynamic operation  
   – Only one device conducts strongly while the other is OFF, so static power ≈ 0.  
   – During transitions both devices momentarily conduct, creating a short-circuit current but only for nanoseconds.  
   – Dynamic (switching) power:  Pdyn = CL VDD² fsw.  
   – Propagation delays (first-order):  
         tPHL ≈ 0.69 RN CL,  tPLH ≈ 0.69 RP CL,  
     where RN and RP are the equivalent on-resistances of the n- and p-devices.  
     Because μn ≈ 2–3 μp, designers make Wp ≈ 2–3 Wn to equalise tPHL and tPLH.

5. Summary of merits and drawbacks  
   + Rail-to-rail output swing  
   + Large noise margin  
   + Essentially zero static power  
   + Simple to cascade (output of one can directly drive the input of the next)  
   – Requires both n- and p-type devices (larger area than a single-device pull-up inverter).

Hence the circuit is a CMOS inverter that produces the logical complement of the input while delivering high switching speed, low static dissipation, and robust noise immunity.

The drawing is the textbook “static-CMOS inverter”, made with one p-channel MOSFET (M2) in series with one n-channel MOSFET (M1).  
• The two gates are shorted together and driven by the input node Vin.  
• The two drains are shorted together and form the output node Vout.  
• M2’s source is tied to the positive supply VDD; M1’s source is tied to ground.

1. Logical behaviour  
   – Vin = 0 (logic “0”):  
     • NMOS: VGS-N = 0 < Vthn  → OFF.  
     • PMOS: VSG-P = VDD > |Vthp| → ON, pulls Vout → VDD.  
     Result: Vout ≈ VDD (logic “1”).  
   – Vin = VDD (logic “1”):  
     • PMOS: VSG-P = 0 < |Vthp| → OFF.  
     • NMOS: VGS-N = VDD > Vthn → ON, pulls Vout → 0.  
     Result: Vout ≈ 0 (logic “0”).  

   Hence the circuit inverts the input.

2. Regions of operation  
   • For Vin ≤ Vthn  → NMOS off, PMOS on (usually linear once Vout reaches VDD).  
   • For Vin ≥ VDD – |Vthp|  → PMOS off, NMOS on.  
   • For intermediate Vin both transistors conduct simultaneously; this is the only time a d.c. path exists between VDD and ground.

3. Static transfer characteristic  
   Ignoring channel-length modulation and using the square-law model,

     Idn = (βn/2)(Vin – Vthn)²  (saturation, since Vout ≈ Vin)  
     Idp = (βp/2)(VDD – Vin – |Vthp|)²

   At the switching point VM (Vin = Vout, Idn = Idp):

     (VM – Vthn)² / (VDD – VM – |Vthp|)² = βp / βn

     ⇒ VM = ( VDD + |Vthp| + √(βn/βp)·Vthn ) / (1 + √(βn/βp))

   With matched devices (βn ≈ βp, |Vthp| ≈ Vthn) the trip point is close to VDD/2, giving a symmetrical VTC and large noise margins.

4. Noise margins and logic levels  
   VOH ≈ VDD,  VOL ≈ 0  
   VIL and VIH are found where |dVout/dVin| = –1 on the VTC.  
   NMH = VOH – VIH,  NML = VIL – VOL  
   Because the gain around VM is large, NMH and NML are typically close to VDD/2.

5. Power  
   • Static power: essentially zero, because in either stable state one transistor is OFF, so no direct path exists from VDD to ground (leakage excepted).  
   • Dynamic power: Pd ≈ α·CL·VDD²·fclk + Pshort, where Pshort is the brief shoot-through current that flows while Vin is crossing the transition region.

6. Propagation delay (with load capacitance CL)  
   tpHL ≈ CL·(VDD – VM) / Idsn(Vin = VDD)  
   tpLH ≈ CL·VM / Idsp(Vin = 0)  
   With equal β’s the high-to-low and low-to-high delays are comparable.

Summary  
The circuit is the fundamental CMOS inverter:  
• Rail-to-rail output swing (0 → VDD).  
• Very small static power.  
• Large noise margins and steep transfer characteristic.  
• Propagation delays and switching threshold that can be tailored through the βn/βp ratio.

answer.text:
The network is the basic CMOS (complementary-MOS) inverter.

1. Which device is which  
   • M1, the transistor tied to VDD, must be a p–channel MOSFET.  
     – Source at VDD, drain at the output node.  
   • M2, the transistor tied to ground, is an n-channel MOSFET.  
     – Drain at the output node, source at ground.  
   (If the upper device were n-channel its body diode would conduct whenever
   VDD > ground, so the circuit could not work.)

2. Logic (static) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V (logic 0)  
      – M1 : VSG = VDD > |VTP|  → ON  
      – M2 : VGS = 0            → OFF  
      → Output node pulled to VDD → VOH ≈ VDD (logic 1).  
      – No steady dc current because only the p-device conducts.

   b) Vin ≈ VDD (logic 1)  
      – M1 : VSG = 0            → OFF  
      – M2 : VGS = VDD > VTN    → ON  
      → Output node pulled to 0 V → VOL ≈ 0 (logic 0).  
      – Again no dc current; only the n-device conducts.

   c) Vin in the middle (around the switching point VM)  
      – Both devices partially ON; for a brief time there is a
        current path VDD → M1 → M2 → ground (the “shoot-through” or
        “crowbar” current).  This happens only while the input is
        switching, so the static power of the gate is essentially zero.

   Hence the gate produces the logical NOT of its input with rail-to-rail
   swing and almost zero static power-dissipation, which is why it is the
   work-horse of modern digital ICs.

3. Transfer characteristic and trip point VM  
   Using the long-channel square-law model in saturation and equating the
   drain currents of the two devices at the transition point:

        βn (VM – VTN)^2 = βp (VDD – VM – |VTP|)^2
        β ≜ μ Cox (W/L)

   Solving,

        VM = (βp (VDD + |VTP|) + βn VTN) / (βn + βp)

   • If |VTP| = VTN and the devices are sized so that βn = βp,
     VM = VDD / 2 (symmetrical inverter).

4. Noise margins (ideal abrupt transition)  

        NML ≈ VM – VOL       (≈ VM, because VOL ≈ 0)
        NMH ≈ VOH – VM       (≈ VDD – VM)

   For the symmetric case, NML ≈ NMH ≈ VDD/2 – VT, giving large
   tolerance to noise on both logic levels.

5. Dynamic behaviour with a load capacitance CL  

        tPHL ≈ (CL VDD) / (βn (VDD – VTN))   (high-to-low delay)  
        tPLH ≈ (CL VDD) / (βp (VDD – |VTP|)) (low-to-high delay)

   Delays are adjusted in practice by the W/L ratio (i.e. β) of the two
   transistors; typically the p-device is made wider to compensate for its
   lower mobility (µp ≈ 0.4 µn).

6. Power dissipation  

        Pstatic   ≈ 0                       (only leakage paths)  
        Pdynamic  = CL VDD² fSW             (plus the brief shoot-through
                                             component while Vin ≈ VM)

Summary  
The circuit is a complementary push-pull stage that inverts the input,
switches all the way between 0 V and VDD, exhibits large noise margins,
draws essentially no dc power, and forms the fundamental building block
for all CMOS digital logic.

answer.text:
The little two-transistor cell is nothing more than

• an n-channel MOSFET (M1) used as a common-source transistor whose gate is the input, and  
• a p-channel MOSFET (M2) whose gate is shorted to its drain, i.e. a “diode–connected” PMOS that behaves like a non-linear load tied to VDD.

Because the load is an active device rather than a passive resistor this structure is usually called a
“CMOS active-load inverter” or “common-source stage with PMOS load”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.   Useful notation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Vtn  = threshold of the NMOS  ( >0 )  
|Vtp|= absolute value of the PMOS threshold ( >0 )  
βn   = kn(W/L)n = μnCox(W/L)n      ( A/V² )  
βp   = kp(W/L)p = μpCox(W/L)p      ( A/V² )  
α    = √(βp/βn)                    (mobility- and size-weighted ratio)

We neglect channel-length modulation (λ≈0) to keep the algebra short; it does not change the
qualitative conclusions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.   DC operating regions and the transfer characteristic Vout(Vin)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
REGION 1 :  Vin < Vtn
   • M1 is OFF (Id1≈0).  
   • No current can flow through M2, therefore Vout rises to VDD.  
   VOH = VDD, the ideal logic-high level.

REGION 2 :  Vtn ≤ Vin ≤ VDD–|Vtp|
   • Both devices are ON and both are in saturation because  
       VDS1 = Vout ≥ (Vin–Vtn)   and   VSD2 = VDD–Vout ≥ |Vtp|.  
   • Current equality gives the square-law relation

         (½)βn (Vin – Vtn)²  =  (½)βp (VDD – Vout – |Vtp|)²      (1)

     Solving for Vout yields the mid-range section of the VTC.

REGION 3 :  Vin > VDD–|Vtp|
   • The PMOS is still saturated (gate and drain are shorted) but the NMOS enters the
     triode/linear region (because VDS1<VGS1–Vtn).  
   • Use the triode expression for M1 and the saturation expression for M2:

        βn[(Vin–Vtn)Vout – Vout²/2]  =  (½)βp (VDD–Vout–|Vtp|)²    (2)

     For Vin = VDD the solution of (2) is the static low level VOL.  If βn≫βp,
     VOL can be made a few tens of millivolts above ground; otherwise it will sit roughly
     around |Vtp|.

Switching (logic) threshold  VM  (by definition Vin = Vout):
   In region 2 set Vin = Vout = VM in (1):

        (VM – Vtn)² = α² (VDD – VM – |Vtp|)²                    (3)

        VM = [α (VDD – |Vtp|) + Vtn] / (1 + α)                 (4)

Notice that VM can be centred (≈VDD/2) by choosing the width ratio so that α≈1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.   Small-signal (incremental) gain
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Bias the input at any DC point where both devices are ON.  
Diode-connected M2 behaves as a resistor   rL ≈ 1/gmp.  
The small-signal equivalent resistance looking into the drain of M1 is its ro (ignored here).

A_v = – gm_n  / (gm_p + gds_n + gds_p)  ≈  – gm_n / gm_p  ≈ – 1/α

So with the usual mobility ratio μn/μp ≈ 2-3, a size ratio Wp/Wn ≈2-3 is needed to get |A_v|>1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.   Dynamic behaviour
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• t_pHL  (high→low): node is discharged by the strong NMOS – usually fast.  
• t_pLH  (low→high): node is charged through the saturated, diode-connected PMOS, whose
  incremental resistance is ≈1/gmp.  Because gm_p is modest, t_pLH is the slow edge.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.   Power consumption
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Unlike a complementary CMOS inverter, a DC current

        Istat(Vin) = ½ βn(Vin–Vtn)²   (region 2 value) 

flows whenever Vin sits between the rails.  Therefore the gate dissipates static power in the
logic “forbidden” region.  At Vin=0 or Vin=VDD the current is essentially zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.   Summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. VOH = VDD; VOL is set by the relative strengths βn, βp and can be made small but never
   exactly 0 V.  
2. The logic threshold is given by eq. (4); it can be centred by sizing.  
3. Small-signal gain ≈ –βn/βp½ ; with reasonable sizing |Av| of 3–10 is practical.  
4. The stage is compact (2 transistors) but
     – pulls static current when Vin is mid-range,  
     – has one slow edge,  
     – gives limited noise margin compared with a complementary CMOS inverter.  
   Consequently it is used mainly as an analog gain stage, a level shifter, or as the first
   stage of sense amplifiers rather than as a rail-to-rail logic inverter chain.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two-transistor network is nothing more than a common-source n-MOS stage (M1) that is loaded by a diode–connected n-MOS device (M2).  
Because the load is an “active” device the circuit is often called

• a saturated-load (or enhancement-load) n-MOS inverter when it is used as a logic gate, and  
• a common-source amplifier with a diode-connected load when it is used as an analog small–signal stage.

The analysis below covers both points of view.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Topology and qualitative operation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• M2 : gate and drain are hard–wired together, therefore  
        VGD2 = 0  and VDS2 = VGS2.   
  As long as VGS2 > VT the device is in saturation, so M2 behaves like an (almost) constant-current source that tries to pull the output node upward.

• M1 : conventional common-source transistor whose gate is the signal input.

Digital point of view  
  – Vin < VT1  → M1 is OFF, no dc current flows, Vout rises until VGS2 = 0, i.e.  
     VOH ≃ VDD (logic “1”).  
  – Vin ≫ VT1  → M1 turns ON and steals current from the node, pulling it down to a
     value VOL that is determined by the current balance between the two devices.
     Because M2 can never be completely cut off while Vout < VDD, VOL is higher than 0 V
     (the inverter does not swing all the way to the rails unless M1 is made much
     stronger than M2).

Analog point of view  
  With both transistors biased in saturation the small-signal voltage gain is finite
  (|Av| < 1 if channel-length modulation is neglected) and the stage can be used as the
  first gain cell in an op-amp, sense amplifier, etc.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. DC transfer characteristic Vout(Vin)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Introduce the usual square-law device constants

β1 = µn Cox (W/L)1 (for M1)     
β2 = µn Cox (W/L)2 (for M2)     
k  = β1 / β2    (ratio of drive strength)

Neglect channel-length modulation (λ ≈ 0).

Region A : M1 OFF (Vin ≤ VT)   
 ID1 = 0 ⇒ ID2 = 0 ⇒ Vout = VDD

Region B : Both transistors in saturation   
 ID1(sat) = ½ β1 (Vin – VT)^2  
 ID2(sat) = ½ β2 (VDD – Vout – VT)^2         (because VGS2 = VDD – Vout)  

Setting ID1 = ID2 gives

 β1 (Vin – VT)^2 = β2 (VDD – Vout – VT)^2  

⇒ Vout = VDD – VT – √k (Vin – VT)     (1)

Condition for M1 to stay in saturation:  
 VDS1 ≥ VGS1 – VT  → Vout ≥ Vin – VT.  
Using (1) this is satisfied as long as

 Vin ≤ VM1 = VT + (VDD – VT)/(1 + √k)

Region C : M1 linear, M2 saturation (Vin ≥ VM1)  
ID1(lin) = β1[ (Vin – VT)Vout – ½ Vout^2 ]  
ID2(sat) = ½ β2 (VDD – Vout – VT)^2  

Equating the two currents produces a quadratic in Vout:

 β1[ (Vin – VT)Vout – ½ Vout^2 ] – ½ β2 (VDD – VT – Vout)^2 = 0 (2)

Equation (2) can be solved explicitly, but for most practical work it is sufficient to
look at the special case Vin = VDD (logic high):

If Vout ≪ (VDD – VT) the Vout^2 term in (2) is negligible and

 β1 (VDD – VT) Vout ≈ ½ β2 (VDD – VT)^2  
⇒ VOL ≈ (β2 / 2β1) (VDD – VT) = ½ (VDD – VT)/k (3)

Thus a low logic level close to ground is obtained by making k (= β1/β2)
large (i.e. making the drive transistor much wider than the load transistor).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Logic parameters (square-law model, k ≫ 1)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
VOH  ≈ VDD  
VOL  ≈ (VDD – VT)/(2k)             (from 3)  
Switching point VM (~ where Vout = Vin) falls in region B and is obtained
by substituting Vout = Vin in (1):

 VM = VT + (VDD – 2VT)/(1 + √k)

Noise margins follow in the usual way once the points where |dVout/dVin| = 1
are found (those also lie in region B and give the customary expressions used for
enhancement-load n-MOS logic).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Small-signal gain (both devices saturated)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Include finite output resistance ro ≈ 1/λID for completeness:

gm1 = 2ID / (Vin – VT), gm2 = 2ID / (VDD – Vout – VT)  
Gout  = gm2 + gds1 + gds2

Mid-band gain

 Av = – gm1 / (gm2 + gds1 + gds2)

If λ → 0, gds1 ≈ gds2 ≈ 0:

 Av = – gm1 / gm2 = – √k             (|Av| < 1)

Hence the stage is a moderate-gain inverting amplifier whose gain is set by the
square-root of the W/L ratio.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Key take-aways
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. M2 is always in saturation (VDS2 = VGS2 ≥ VGS2 – VT) and therefore behaves like an active, almost constant, current source.  
2. At Vin = 0 the output rises to VDD; at Vin = VDD the output is limited to a value of order (VDD – VT)/2k, not to ground, so rail-to-rail logic swings are not obtained unless k is made very large.  
3. With both devices biased in saturation the small-signal gain equals –gm1/gm2 (≈ –√k), i.e. less than unity unless the driver transistor is much stronger than the load.  
4. The circuit is the basic “saturated-load n-MOS inverter” used in early NMOS logic families and is also the simplest active-load common-source amplifier encountered in analog design.

That completes the analysis of the circuit in the figure.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit identification  
M1 is an n–channel MOSFET whose source is at ground and whose drain is the output
node.  
M2 is a p-channel MOSFET whose source is at VDD.  Its gate is shorted to its drain, so
M2 is diode-connected and therefore always biased in saturation.  
Consequently the stage is nothing more than a common-source n-MOS amplifier
(M1) that is loaded by the small–signal resistance of a diode-connected p-MOS
(M2).  In digital language it looks like an “inverter with a
p-device wired as a load”, in analog language it is the most elementary
“active-load common-source” stage.

1. Regions of operation  

•  M2 – always in saturation (|VSD2| ≥ |VSG2 – VTP| automatically because
GD2 = DD2).  
•  M1 – normally kept in saturation by design:
      VDS1 = VOUT  ≥ VGS1 – VTN  →  VOUT ≥ VIN – VTN .
  When VIN is so large that VOUT falls below VIN – VTN the device slips into
  triode, but in the intended small-signal operating range both transistors
  are saturated.

2. D.C. operating point (λ ≈ 0)  

Equate the two drain currents (magnitudes)

   ID1 = ID2
 ⇒ ½ βn (VIN – VTN – VOUT)² = ½ βp (VDD – |VTP| – VOUT)²

Define k = βp/βn and solve for either voltage; for example

   VIN = VTN + √k (VDD – |VTP| – VOUT)               (1)

or

   VOUT = VDD – |VTP| + (VTN – VIN)/√k               (1′)

With equal transconductance parameters (k = 1) and similar
thresholds (VTN ≈ |VTP|) the static transfer characteristic is a
straight line of slope –1:

   VOUT ≈ VDD – VIN

so the quiescent point sits roughly in the middle of the supply
range.

3. Small-signal (incremental) model  

Diode–connected M2 looks like a resistor 1/gm2 in parallel with its intrinsic
output resistance ro2.  At low-to-moderate drain currents 1/gm2 ≪ ro2, so

   rL ≈ 1/gm2

Nodal KCL at the output (downward current positive, gm2 taken as a positive
number for clarity)

   gm1 v i – gm2 v o + vo/ro1 + vo/ro2 = 0

Neglecting ro-terms:

   vo/vi = – gm1 / gm2                                 (2)

Thus the stage gives voltage gain whose magnitude is the ratio of the two
transconductances; the minus sign shows that it is an inverting
amplifier.

Because  gm = √(2 β ID) , equation (2) can be rewritten

   |AV| = √(βn/βp) = √((μn/μp)(W/L)1 /(W/L)2)          (3)

Important consequences  
•  If the two devices are sized so that gm1 ≈ gm2, the magnitude of the
   gain is ≈ 1 (a very common choice for active loads in differential pairs).  
•  Higher gain can be obtained by making (W/L)1 larger or (W/L)2 smaller, or
   by operating at different channel lengths to profit from the mobility
   ratio.

With finite output resistances the gain becomes

   AV ≈ – gm1 (ro1 ∥ ro2 ∥ 1/gm2 ) ≈ – gm1 / (gm2 + go1 + go2)  ,
and can easily reach –5 … –15 in long-channel processes.

4. Logic-level interpretation  

VIN low (VIN < VTN) → M1 off → ID ≈ 0  
 VOUT rises to VDD through the weak leakage of M2.  
VIN high → M1 on → the node is pulled down until equation (1) is satisfied;
 VOUT never reaches 0 V because M2 keeps sourcing current, so the circuit
is not a full-swing CMOS inverter but a “pseudo-NMOS” type gate.

5. Design / use cases  

•  As a stand-alone amplifier that produces an inverted replica of the input,
  frequently used inside operational amplifiers and fully differential
  amplifiers.  
•  As the load of a differential pair, where the nearly –1 gain permits
  straightforward common-mode feedback.  
•  As a static logic element where area is more important than noise-margin.

Key expressions to remember  

D.C.:    ½ βn (VIN – VTN – VOUT)² = ½ βp (VDD – |VTP| – VOUT)²  
Gain:    AV ≈ – gm1 / gm2  (≈ –1 when devices are matched)  
Load:    rL(diode) ≈ 1/gm2

That fully characterises the behaviour of the circuit shown.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Transistor identification  
• M2 is a p-channel MOSFET: source at VDD , drain at the internal node Vout , gate driven by Vin.  
• M1 is an n-channel MOSFET: drain at Vout , source at ground, body tied to ground (arrow pointing toward the channel).  
• The gate of M1 is not connected to any signal in this drawing – it sits at 0 V.

Step-by-step operation

1. Vin = 0 (logic “0”)  
   – VSG2 = VDD  > |VTp|  ⇒ M2 turns ON.  
   – VGS1 = 0     ⇒ M1 is OFF.  
   – With no path to ground, Vout is charged through the low-resistance channel of M2 until Vout ≃ VDD.  
   – Result: Vout = VDD (logic “1”) and only a small static current (leakage) flows.

2. Vin = VDD (logic “1”)  
   – VSG2 = 0     ⇒ M2 turns OFF.  
   – M1 is still OFF.  
   – There is now no DC path either to VDD or to ground, so the node is high-impedance (open circuit).  
   – Whatever voltage was stored on the node’s capacitance just before Vin went high will remain there, slowly changing only through leakage.  If the previous phase left the node high, it stays high; if some external circuit had discharged it earlier, it will stay low.

Truth table (local view)

Vin   M2   M1   State of Vout  
0     ON   OFF  pulled up to VDD (logic 1)  
1     OFF  OFF  high-Z (voltage is whatever the node was carrying)

Interpretation

• The pair behaves as a unilateral (pull-up-only) tri-state driver.  
• It can actively assert a “1”; it can never actively force a “0”.  
• Because the node is left floating when Vin = 1, the circuit is useful only when some other circuitry can subsequently discharge the node or when a high-impedance “disconnect” is what is required.  Typical uses are:  
 – the pre-charge device in dynamic or domino logic (Vin is a clock’s complement, M1 represents the n-MOS evaluation stack that is not shown here),  
 – a simple high-side switch for power gating,  
 – “wired-OR / wired-AND” style busses where many pull-up-only drivers share a line and any one of them may pull it high.

Limitations

• On its own it is not a complete logic gate because it cannot create a valid low level.  
• When Vin goes from 0 → 1 the output is left floating; unless another path to ground exists the voltage on Vout is undefined after a long time (leakage).  
• The body diode of M1 is oriented from Vout to ground, so if an external circuit tries to drive Vout below ground it will conduct and clamp Vout near –VD, otherwise it is non-conductive.

In short, the schematic shows a p-MOS controlled high-side switch (M2) with an n-MOS device (M1) that is presently inactive.  The circuit pulls the node high when Vin is low and disconnects it when Vin is high, providing a pull-up-only, tri-state behaviour.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit identification  
The two transistors form the classical CMOS inverter (NOT gate).  
• M2 is a p-channel MOSFET (PMOS): source tied to VDD, drain tied to the output node.  
• M1 is an n-channel MOSFET (NMOS): source tied to ground, drain tied to the same output node.  
• The two gates are shorted together and driven by the input voltage Vin.  
• The bulks are returned to the appropriate supplies (PMOS bulk to VDD, NMOS bulk to GND), so body effects can be ignored for a first-order analysis.

1. Logic (qualitative) behaviour  
--------------------------------------------------  
Vin = 0 V (logic ‘0’) → PMOS ON, NMOS OFF → Vout ≈ VDD (logic ‘1’).  
Vin = VDD (logic ‘1’) → PMOS OFF, NMOS ON → Vout ≈ 0 V (logic ‘0’).  
Thus the gate inverts the input. Because only one device conducts in steady state, the static (dc) power dissipation is essentially zero (apart from leakage).

2. dc transfer characteristic  
--------------------------------------------------  
Assume long–channel devices, square-law model, same channel length for both
(Id = k/2 (VGS-VTH)² in saturation, VDS ≥ VGS-VTH).

Regions of operation when we sweep Vin from 0 → VDD:

A. Vin ≤ VTN                     (both transistors off)  
   Vout stays high (≈VDD).

B. VTN < Vin < VDD–|VTP|         (both devices on)  
   • NMOS: VGS = Vin – 0 > VTN → strong inversion, most likely saturated  
     (because VDS ≈ Vout and Vout > Vin–VTN in this region).  
   • PMOS: |VSG| = VDD – Vin > |VTP| → also saturated.  
   Equate their saturation currents to find Vout(Vin):

        kn/2 (Vin – VTN)² = kp/2 (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)²

        ⇒ (Vin – VTN) / (VDD – Vin – |VTP|) = √(kp/kn)

   For equal strength devices (kp ≈ kn) the numerator and denominator are equal, so  
        Vin = VM ≈ (VDD + VTN – |VTP|) / 2

   VM is the switching (trip) point; for VDD = 5 V, VTN ≈ |VTP| ≈ 0.7 V we get VM ≈ 2.6 V.

   Around VM the small-signal voltage gain is  

        Av = –dVout/dVin ≈ – ( √(kn/kp) + √(kp/kn) )

   which is typically greater than –10, giving large noise margins.

C. Vin ≥ VDD–|VTP|               (both transistors off)  
   Vout is already low; the PMOS is well turned off, the NMOS still on until Vin crosses VDD (rare in normal logic levels). Practically region C collapses to the high-input case where NMOS alone pulls the node to ground.

3. Logic-level summary and noise margins  
--------------------------------------------------  
VOH  ≈  VDD  
VOL  ≈  0  
VIL  ≈ VM – (1/Av)|VM|  
VIH  ≈ VM + (1/Av)|VM|  
With |Av| ≫ 1 the noise margins are roughly

        NML ≈ VM – VOL   and   NMH ≈ VOH – VM

and are close to VDD/2 for symmetric devices.

4. Power dissipation  
--------------------------------------------------  
Static: essentially zero because at most one transistor conducts when the input is at a valid logic level.  
Dynamic: Pdyn = α CL VDD² f, where α is the activity factor and CL is the total load capacitance seen at Vout.

5. Delay (first-order)  
--------------------------------------------------  
tpHL (high→low) ≈ (CL · VDD) / (kn (VDD – VTN)² / 2)  
tpLH (low→high) ≈ (CL · VDD) / (kp (VDD – |VTP|)² / 2)  
Sizing the PMOS wider by the mobility ratio (μn/μp ≈ 2-3) makes kn ≈ kp, equalizing the two delays and centring VM.

6. Advantages of the CMOS configuration  
--------------------------------------------------  
• Full-swing logic levels (0 V and VDD).  
• Very large input impedance (only capacitive).  
• Nearly zero static power.  
• Large noise margins, ratio-independent logic (unlike pseudo-NMOS or resistive-load gates).

7. Practical remarks  
--------------------------------------------------  
• The short period when both transistors are simultaneously on while Vin passes through VM produces a brief short-circuit current (ISSC), but its time integral is small compared with dynamic switching current.  
• Body effect slightly shifts the effective thresholds if the source voltages move away from the bulk potentials, but for an inverter this shift is small and usually absorbed into the empirical VT values.

Conclusion  
The circuit is a complementary MOS inverter. It provides rail-to-rail output swings, negligible dc power, large noise margins, and propagation delay that can be made symmetrical by appropriate transistor sizing (W/L ratios such that kn ≈ kp).

answer.text:
The two devices form the classical CMOS-inverter pull-up / pull-down pair.

1. Identifying the transistors  
   • M2 is a p-channel MOSFET.  Its source is hard-wired to the positive rail VDD, so when its gate voltage is low (relative to VDD) the device conducts and pulls the output high.  
   • M1 is an n-channel MOSFET.  Its source is tied to ground, so when its gate voltage is high (relative to ground) it conducts and pulls the output low.  
   • The gates of M1 and M2 are shorted together; that common node is the input Vin.  
   • The drains of M1 and M2 are shorted together; that junction is the output Vout.

2. Logic behaviour (truth table)  

   Vin = 0 (LOW)  
   – VGS2 = 0 – VDD = –VDD (|VGS2| > |VTP|)  →  M2 ON  
   – VGS1 = 0                  (< VTN)        →  M1 OFF  
   ⇒ Vout ≈ VDD  (logic ‘1’)

   Vin = VDD (HIGH)  
   – VGS2 = VDD – VDD = 0      (< |VTP|)      →  M2 OFF  
   – VGS1 = VDD – 0  =  VDD    (> VTN)        →  M1 ON  
   ⇒ Vout ≈ 0 V  (logic ‘0’)

   Thus the stage realises a NOT function.

3. DC transfer characteristic  
   Let kn = μn Cox (W/L)n and kp = μp Cox (W/L)p.  
   Around the switching point both devices operate in saturation, so the transition voltage VM is found from

        kn (Vin – VTN)^2  =  kp (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2

   If |VTP| ≈ VTN and kp ≈ kn (achieved by sizing Wp > Wn to compensate for mobility), VM ≈ VDD/2, giving large and nearly symmetrical noise margins.

4. Static power  
   Except for momentary overlap during switching, one transistor is always OFF, so the dc current drawn from the supply is essentially zero; static power dissipation is therefore negligible.

5. Dynamic behaviour  
   • When Vin makes a 0→1 transition, M2 turns off as M1 turns on.  The low-impedance path through M1 discharges CL (the total load capacitance on Vout) toward ground with a time constant τLH ≈ RN CL, where RN = (1/ kn(Vin–VTN)).  
   • For a 1→0 transition the roles reverse: M1 turns off, M2 turns on, and CL charges through the p-device with τHL ≈ RP CL, RP = (1/ kp(VDD–Vin–|VTP|)).  
   Proper sizing (Wp/Wn) not only centres VM but also makes RN ≈ RP so that rise- and fall-times are similar.

6. Small-signal (mid-transition) gain  
   At Vin ≈ VM both transistors are conducting in saturation.  The small-signal voltage gain is

        Av = – (gm1||gm2) (ro1 || ro2) ≈ – (gm1 ro1 + gm2 ro2)

   With long-channel devices gm ro ≈ |VA| / (VDSsat) >> 1, so |Av| can exceed 20–30, producing the sharp transfer curve characteristic of CMOS inverters.

7. Summary  
   • Function: logical inverter (NOT gate).  
   • Advantages: rail-to-rail output swing, nearly zero static power, large noise margins, and high gain in the transition region.  
   • Design knobs: device dimensions set VM, dynamic drive strength, and rise/fall symmetry; load capacitance CL and supply VDD set propagation delay and dynamic power (½ CL VDD² per transition).

That is the complete qualitative and quantitative analysis of the circuit in the figure.

1.  Apply a small test-voltage vtest at the output node; measure the resulting small-signal current itest that flows out of the node.  
    Rout = vtest / itest.

2.  Small-signal network (node names refer to the original circuit)  

    • ro1 between node X and the output node.  
    • ro2 between node X and a.c. ground (VDD).  
    • gm1⋅vgs1 current source between X and the output node  
      (vgs1 = –vX because the gate of M1 is at a.c. ground).  
    • gm2⋅vgs2 current source between a.c. ground and node X  
      (vgs2 = –vX).

   (Body-effect current sources, if relevant, are added exactly in
   the same way; they will just add gmb2 to gm2 in the final
   expression.)

3.  Solve the two node equations (node X and the output node).  
    With vout = vtest ,

    a)  KCL at node X  
        vX / ro2  +  gm2 vX  +  (vX – vout)/ro1  =  0
        ⇒ vX =  (ro1 / [1 + (gm2 + 1/ro2) ro1]) vout

    b)  Output-node current  
        itest = (vout – vX)/ro1  +  gm1(–vX)

        but for a biased device with its gate fixed, gm1 produces
        the same current that already appears through ro1; after
        substitution of vX from (a) the gm1-terms cancel out and the
        result depends only on ro1 , ro2 and gm2.

        itest = vout / [ ro1 + ro2 + gm2 ro1 ro2 ]

4.  Therefore

        Rout = vtest / itest
             = ro1 + ro2 + gm2 ro1 ro2

   For the usual case gm2 ro2 ≫ 1 (good cascoding):

        Rout ≈ gm2 ro1 ro2      (orders of magnitude larger than either
                                 transistor’s intrinsic r o).

   If body effect of M2 is included simply replace gm2 by
   (gm2 + gmb2).

So, the small-signal resistance seen at the output node of the two-transistor cascode stack is

Rout = ro1 + ro2 + gm2·ro1·ro2   ≈   gm2·ro1·ro2  when gm2·ro2 ≫ 1.

2. The cascode device M2 has a large gain gm2ro2 , therefore its source (node X) is almost a.c.–ground:
      vx  ≈ 0.

3. With the drain of M1 fixed (vx ≃ 0), a change vout appears directly –and with opposite sign– across
   the gate-to-source and body-to-source terminals of M1:

answers.question: How do we ensure that M2 is in saturation in the figure?

answer.text:
For the upper device M2 we have  

 Drain : VDD  
 Source : VX  
 Gate : Vb2  

The long-channel saturation condition for an n-MOSFET is  

 VDS2 ≥ VGS2 – VTHN              (1)

Substituting the node voltages

 VDS2 = VDD – VX  
 VGS2 = Vb2 – VX

gives

 VDD – VX ≥ (Vb2 – VX) – VTHN  
   ⟺ VDD ≥ Vb2 – VTHN                (2)

Equation (2) contains no term that depends on VX, so once the gate-bias Vb2 is chosen such that

 Vb2 ≤ VDD + VTHN                     (3)

M2 will be in saturation for every value that node X can take.

The device also has to be ON:

 VGS2 ≥ VTHN  ⇒ Vb2 ≥ VX + VTHN       (4)

Combining (3) and (4)

 VX + VTHN  ≤  Vb2  ≤  VDD + VTHN

is the complete range in which M2 is both conducting and saturated.

How this is done in practice

1. Generate Vb2 a few hundred millivolts below VDD (for example with a diode-
   connected NMOS carrying the same current, or with a resistive divider).  
   A common choice is  
  Vb2 ≈ VDD – VDSsat ≈ VDD – 200 … 300 mV  
   which automatically satisfies (3) and keeps M2 well into saturation.

2. Make sure the lowest allowed output voltage (Rout node) never lets VX rise so
   high that condition (4) is violated; this is normally guaranteed by the bias
   you choose for the lower transistor M1.

With the gate of M2 thus fixed, any movement of the output node affects only
the source of M2; the inequality (2) is always true, so M2 stays in saturation
and the cascode stack presents a high small-signal output resistance Rout.

For an NMOS transistor the saturation (pinch-off) condition is  

  VDS  ≥  VGS  –  Vth.                                     (1)

For the upper device M2 in the cascode

  VDS2  =  VDD  –  VX  
  VGS2  =  VB2  –  VX

so (1) becomes

  VDD – VX  ≥  (VB2 – VX) – Vth   
  ⟺         VDD  ≥  VB2 – Vth .                       (2)

Notice that VX cancels out; therefore M2 will be in saturation for every possible value of the node X as long as its gate is kept at least one threshold voltage below the supply:

       VB2  ≤  VDD – Vth   (with a few hundred mV of margin preferably).     (3)

How do we guarantee (3) in practice?

1. Generate VB2 with a bias circuit referenced to VDD.  
   The usual way is to pass the same bias current through a diode-connected NMOS (or a source-follower) that is identical to M2 and whose drain is tied to VDD.  
   The voltage that appears at its source is  

       VB2  =  VDD – (Vth + Vov) ,

   so the distance between VB2 and VDD is automatically larger than Vth and tracks process, temperature and supply variations.

2. Make sure M2 is turned on: VB2 – VX ≥ Vth.  
   With the bias of step 1, VX is clamped near VB2 – (Vth + Vov), so this inequality is also satisfied.

3. Provide enough head-room for the whole stack:  

       Vout,min  ≈  VDSsat1 + VDSsat2 + Vth

   so that both M1 and M2 stay in saturation over the required output-voltage range.

In short, choose (or generate) the gate bias VB2 so that

       VB2 is at least one Vth below VDD,

and M2 can never leave saturation regardless of what happens at the intermediate node X or at the output node.

VDS ≥ VGS − Vth       (1)

Apply (1) to M2 in the cascode stack.

Node voltages
   Drain of M2 : VDD
   Source of M2 : VX                 (the M1 drain / M2 source node)
   Gate of M2  : Vb2

Hence

VDS2 = VDD − VX
VGS2 = Vb2 − VX

Insert these expressions in (1):

VDD − VX ≥ (Vb2 − VX) − Vth2
⟺ VDD ≥ Vb2 − Vth2                    (2)

Notice that VX cancels out; therefore the condition for M2 to be in saturation is independent of the actual value of the intermediate node X.

Practical rule
Choose the gate-bias voltage of the cascode device at least one threshold voltage below the supply:

Vb2 ≤ VDD − Vth2                      (3)

If you leave a small safety margin (≈50–100 mV) to cover process/temperature spread, M2 will remain in saturation for any movement of the output node Rout.

How to generate Vb2
A convenient way is to fabricate a diode-connected NMOS of the same type and run (roughly) the same current through it. Its source will sit at ≃ VDD − Vth, producing exactly the bias required by (3); this voltage can be buffered and used as Vb2.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit name  
The schematic is the classical “telescopic n-MOS cascode” (common-source transistor M1 with a cascode transistor M2 that is biased by the dc voltage Vb1 and is loaded by an ideal current source I1).

1. DC (large-signal) bias  

Let the constant bias current delivered by the source I1 be I1 = ID.  
Because the two devices are in series,

      ID = ID1 = ID2 = I1.                                      (1)

(a) Lower device (M1, the input transistor)  
    ID1 = ½ µnCox(W/L)1 (Vin – VTH1)^2(1 + λ1VDS1)

    VDS1 = VX – 0  ≥  Vov1   (to keep M1 in saturation)          (2)

    so choose VX ≈ Vov1 (= Vin – VTH1) + 0.1…0.2 V margin.

(b) Upper device (M2, the cascode)  
    VX is forced by the bias voltage Vb1:

      VX = Vb1 – VGS2 = Vb1 – (VTH2 + Vov2).                     (3)

    Equation (3) together with the chosen VX fixes Vb1.  
    Condition for M2 to stay in saturation for every output swing:

      VOUT ≥ Vb1 – VTH2.                                         (4)

    Hence Vb1 is usually picked as low as possible while still
    supplying the required VGS2 so that (4) gives the widest head-room.

2. Small-signal equivalent  

Gate leakages are ignored (Rin ≈ ∞).  
ro1, ro2 … intrinsic drain-source resistances  
gm1, gm2 … transconductances

               gm1Vin + vx/ro1
      ro1 ↓            ↑ gm2vx + (vx–vout)/ro2
         |              |
ground ——M1——─X——─M2——─Vout——(ideal current source, ro → ∞)

Writing nodal equations yields

      vout / vin = –gm1 ro1 (1 + gm2 ro2).                       (5)

If gm2ro2 ≫ 1 the gain is

      Av ≈ –gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2  = –gm1 Rout.                       (6)

3. Output resistance  

With Vin set to ac ground (vin = 0) apply a test voltage VT at the
output and calculate the resulting small-signal current IT :

      vx (1/ro1 + 1/ro2 + gm2) = VT/ro2
      IT = (VT – vx)/ro2 – gm2vx

      ⇒  Rout ≡ VT / IT = ro1 + ro2 + gm2 ro1 ro2                (7)

      ≈ gm2 ro1 ro2               (when gm2ro1, gm2ro2 ≫ 1).     (8)

4. Important properties  

• Input resistance   Rin ≃ ∞ (MOS gate).  
• Transconductance  Gm = gm1.  
• Voltage gain       Av of (5) typically tens of thousands
  (60–80 dB) with realistic gm·ro products, largely exceeding the
  –gm1ro1 that a simple common-source stage could provide.  

5. Output-swing limits  

Low-side:  from (4) Vout,min ≈ Vb1 – VTH2.  
High-side:  Vout,max ≈ VDD – VDSSAT of the bias current source.

6. Design hints  

1. Pick the overdrive of M1 to obtain the required gm1 at the chosen
   bias current I1.  
2. Set VX ≈ Vov1 + safety margin.  
3. Choose (W/L)2 such that M2 carries I1 with an overdrive Vov2 small
   enough to preserve head-room, then set Vb1 = VX + VTH2 + Vov2.  
4. A larger gm2 or longer-channel M1/M2 increases gm2·ro1·ro2 and
   therefore both Rout and the voltage gain.

Thus the two-transistor cascode converts the moderate gain of a
common-source stage (≈ –gm1ro1) into

      Av  ≈ –gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2                              (high gain)

while retaining a very high input impedance and a moderately large
output swing.

Omitting body effect is allowed; the remaining bias and output-resistance discussion is consistent with the topology.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two-transistor stack M1–M2 that is connected to the ideal current-sink I1 is nothing more than a single–ended cascode amplifier:

1. What each device is doing  
   • M1 : signal device (common-source).  
   • M2 : cascode device whose gate is fixed at the bias voltage Vb1; it keeps the drain of M1 (node X) at an almost constant voltage, greatly increasing the small-signal output resistance.  
   • I1 : an (almost) infinite-resistance load that forces a dc current I1 through the MOS pair.  
   • Vout : the high-impedance output node.  

2. DC (large–signal) analysis  
   Assume both transistors are to be biased in saturation.

   a) Drain current  
      I D1 = I D2 = I1                                             (1)

   b) Voltage at the internal node X  
      VX ≃ VGS1 = Vov1 + VTH1                                      (2)  

      where Vov1 = VGS1 – VTH1 is the over-drive of M1.

   c) Bias for the cascode gate  
      The gate of M2 must be high enough to let I1 flow but low enough to leave M2 in saturation over the full output-voltage range:

      VB1 ≃ VX + Vov2 + VTH2                                       (3)

   d) Output-voltage compliance  
      • For M2 to stay in saturation: VDS2 ≥ Vov2  
        ⇒ Vout,min ≃ VX + Vov2 = Vov1 + VTH1 + Vov2                (4)

      • For the current source to stay in saturation:  
        VDS,I1 ≥ VDSsat,I1 ⇒ Vout,max ≃ VDD – VDSsat,I1            (5)

      Hence the admissible output swing is

           ΔVout ≃ VDD – VDSsat,I1 – (Vov1 + VTH1 + Vov2).         (6)

3. Small-signal (incremental) model  
   With ro,I1 ≫ ro2, ro1 we can neglect the finite output resistance of I1.

   Small-signal parameters  
      gm1 , ro1 → M1  
      gm2 , ro2 → M2  

   Node equations  

      At node X :   –gm1·vin – (vx/ro1) – gm2·vx   + (vout – vx)/ro2 = 0
      At node Vout: +(vx – vout)/ro2 – (vout/roI1)                   ≈ 0

      (roI1 → ∞ ⇒ the second term vanishes.)

   Solving for the open-circuit gain Av = vout / vin gives, to first order,

           Av ≃ –gm1 · (gm2·ro2·ro1 + ro2 + ro1)                   (7)

      Because the cascode raises the resistance seen looking into M2’s drain,

           rout ≃ ro2 + gm2·ro2·ro1  ≈ gm2·ro2·ro1                  (8)

      and since ro1,ro2 ≫ 1/gm1 , Av reduces to

           Av ≃ – gm1 · rout ≃ – gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2.                  (9)

      If ro1 ≃ ro2 ≃ ro,

           Av ≃ – gm1 gm2 ro².                                     (10)

      Thus the gain is the product of the two g m ’s multiplied by the square of a single-device r o – often hundreds or thousands, i.e. tens of decibels.

4. Salient features of the topology  
   • Very high intrinsic gain because rout is boosted by the cascode.  
   • Node X is nearly ac-ground (small swing ≈ vx ≪ vout), so the Miller capacitance of M1 is suppressed and the input pole is shifted to a higher frequency.  
   • Good power-supply rejection: the high-resistance current source isolates Vout from VDD noise.  
   • Output swing is limited on the low side by two over-drives plus one threshold, on the high side by the current-source compliance.  
   • Only one bias voltage (Vb1) is required for the cascode.

5. Practical design procedure  
   1) Choose I1 from the required transconductance gm1 (gm1 ≈ 2·I1 / Vov1).  
   2) Pick Vov1 (speed vs. swing trade-off), giving VX from (2).  
   3) Choose Vov2 (typically 150–200 mV) and determine Vb1 from (3).  
   4) Check that the resulting Vout,min from (4) leaves enough room for the desired signal swing below VDD – VDSsat,I1.  
   5) Lay out M2 with a longer channel (larger ro2) if still higher gain is needed.

In short, the circuit is a classical n-channel cascode stage: a common-source transistor M1 loaded by a current sink, with its drain shielded by a common-gate device M2 that dramatically increases the output resistance and hence the voltage gain, at the expense of reduced output-voltage swing.
