answer.text:
The network is nothing more than a common-source gain stage (M1) whose drain has been
“protected’’ by a cascode transistor (M2) and is loaded by an (ideally) constant current
source I1.  
Because of the cascode, the stage exhibits

• a very high small-signal output resistance,  
• consequently a large voltage gain,  
• a small signal swing at the sensitive internal node X (hence little Miller
  multiplication of Cgd1 and little channel-length-modulation error).

Below is a compact dc and small-signal analysis and the usual design limits.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  dc (large-signal) operating point
--------------------------------------------------------------------
At equilibrium     I1 = ID2 = ID1  ≜ I  (a design value).

Let

VOV1 = VGS1 – VTH1        (over-drive of M1)  
VOV2 = VGS2 – VTH2        (over-drive of M2)  
VX    = dc voltage at node X.

Conditions for saturation

M1 :       VX  ≥  VOV1                                  (1)  
M2 :   VOUT – VX ≥  VOV2                                (2)  
I1 :   VDD  – VOUT ≥ VDSAT,I1                           (3)

With M2 saturated, VX is fixed by its gate bias:

ID = (½)kn2(VB1 – VX – VTH2)²      ⇒    VX = VB1 – VTH2 – VOV2    (4)

Choose VB1 so that (1)–(3) are comfortably met when VIN is at its quiescent value.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  small-signal (ac) model
--------------------------------------------------------------------
gm1, ro1     – transconductance and output resistance of M1  
gm2, ro2     –      “             “          “        M2  
roI          – small-signal output resistance of I1  
(All taken at the dc bias current I.)

With the current source ideal (roI → ∞) the incremental
circuit contains only gm1, ro1, gm2, ro2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  node-X behaviour
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Writing KCL at X gives

gm2(VB1 – vX) + (vX – vOUT)/ro2  =  gm1 vIN + vX/ro1

Solving for vX (roI → ∞)

vX ≈ [gm1 / (gm2 + 1/ro2)]  vIN  ≈  (gm1 / gm2) vIN    for  gm2ro2 ≫ 1.  (5)

Thus only a small fraction (≈ gm1/gm2) of the input signal appears at X.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  output resistance
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Apply a test voltage vT at VOUT with vIN = 0:

Rout ≡ vT / iT  ≈  ro2 + (1 + gm2ro2)ro1                 (6)  
               ≈  gm2 ro2 ro1     if  gm2ro2 ≫ 1.

With a finite current-source resistance roI the three resistances are in series:

Rout ≈ roI + (gm2ro2 ro1) + (ro1 ∥ ro2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  small-signal voltage gain
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Av  =  vOUT / vIN  =  –gm1 · Rout                        (7)

Using (6) and gm2ro2 ≫ 1

Av  ≈  –gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2.

Hence the intrinsic gain of a single NMOS (gm1ro1) is multiplied by
the intrinsic gain of the cascode device (gm2ro2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  signal swing limits
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Lower limit at the output (to keep M2 in saturation):

     VOUT,min  =  VX + VOV2  (use VX from (4)).

• Upper limit (set by the head-room of I1):

     VOUT,max  =  VDD – VDSAT,I1.

• Maximum input excursion before M1 leaves saturation
  (using VX from (5) with largest negative vIN):

     |vIN|max  ≈  (gm2/gm1)(VOV1 – safety margin).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  rôle of each element
--------------------------------------------------------------------
M1   converts vIN to a drain current (g m1).  
M2   fixes (almost) the drain voltage of M1, boosting Rout and suppressing Miller
     feedback through Cgd1.  
I1   supplies a nearly constant current, providing a high-impedance load.  
VB1  sets the drain voltage of M1 and guarantees M2 is always saturated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8.  practical design hints
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Choose VOV1 ≈ 0.2–0.25 V for low noise and high gm.  
2. Pick VOV2 slightly larger (≈ 0.25–0.3 V) to leave a few hundred mV at node X.  
3. Set VB1 from (4).  
4. Make sure VDD ≥ VOV1 + VOV2 + VDSAT,I1 + desired output swing.

With these choices the stage delivers a gain of many hundreds (or thousands)
while using only one transistor length for the signal path and only one supply
rail, a common solution in the input and gain stages of CMOS op-amps.

answers.question: Is the circuit shown in the figure a cascode structure?

answer.text:
Yes.  
What you see is the textbook NMOS “common-source / common-gate” cascode:

1. M1 (bottom device) is the amplifying transistor. Its source is at ground, its gate is the signal input Vin, so it works in common-source mode and converts the input voltage into a small-signal drain current gm1·vin.

2. M2 (the upper NMOS) is stacked on top of M1 and its gate is held at the fixed bias voltage Vb1. With its gate AC-grounded it operates in common-gate mode; it keeps the drain of M1 at an almost constant voltage and therefore:
   • forces M1 to stay in saturation,  
   • greatly increases the small-signal output resistance seen looking into the stack,  
   • suppresses the Miller (Cgd1) feedback to the input.

3. The current flowing through the two transistors is turned into an output voltage by the load resistor RD. For small-signal analysis VDD is an AC ground, so the node Vout is indeed the drain of the common-gate device, exactly where the output of a cascode is taken.

Using a resistor instead of an active current source does not change the fact that the core of the circuit (M1 + M2) is a cascode. A current source load would give an even higher gain, but the basic “cascode” function is already provided by the two stacked transistors with the upper one in common-gate configuration.

answer.text:

answer.text:

The two stacked NMOS devices form the classic “common-source + common-gate” combination that defines a cascode:

2. M2 sits on top of M1 with its gate held at a fixed bias VB1, so it works as a common-gate stage.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect multiplies the capacitance that connects two nodes by the gain that exists between those nodes.  
For a single-stage common-source MOS/​BJT amplifier the small-signal gain from gate/base (input) to drain/collector (output) is large and negative (A_v ≈ −gm·R_D).   
Seen from the input, the gate-to-drain (or base-to-collector) capacitance, Cgd, therefore appears as

C_Miller = Cgd · (1 – A_v) ≈ Cgd · (1 + |A_v|)          (|A_v| » 1)

so the effective input capacitance becomes C_in ≈ Cgs + C_Miller, often an order of magnitude larger than the physical Cgd. This swollen capacitance lowers the high-frequency bandwidth.

What changes in a cascode?

1. Structure  
   The cascode puts a common-gate (or common-base) device on top of the common-source device. The drain of the lower (input) transistor is now the source of the upper transistor.

2. Small AC swing at the drain of the input transistor  
   The common-gate transistor presents a very low AC impedance at its source (≈ 1/gm₂). As a result, the drain of the input transistor hardly moves with the signal: it is an almost “AC-grounded” node.

3. Very small gain from gate to drain of the input transistor  
   Because that drain node hardly moves, the small-signal gain that appears across Cgd of the input transistor is no longer large; in fact

   A_v(gate→drain)  ≈  0  (instead of −10, −20, …)

4. Miller multiplication collapses  
   With A_v ≈ 0 the Miller factor becomes

   C_Miller = Cgd · (1 – A_v) ≈ Cgd

   i.e. Cgd is no longer multiplied. The input capacitance of the cascode stage is essentially

   C_in ≈ Cgs + Cgd   (only the physical values)

5. Consequence  
   • Far less capacitive loading at the input → higher bandwidth.  
   • Reduced phase shift caused by Cgd feedback → better stability.  

In short: the cascode isolates the drain of the input device from large voltage swings, so the gain that drives the Miller capacitor is almost zero. With no significant gain across Cgd, the Miller effect is greatly diminished.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
Miller-effect capacitance is the product of a physical capacitance (the gate–drain, Cgd) and the voltage gain that exists between the two terminals of that capacitance.  
    Equivalent input capacitance = Cgd · (1 – AvGD)

1. In a simple common–source/-emitter stage AvGD ≈ –gm·RL, so |AvGD| can easily be 20–50. The small Cgd (tens of femtofarads) is therefore “magnified” into several hundred femtofarads or more, slowing the stage badly.

2. In a cascode the upper device is wired as a common-gate/-base stage whose gate (or base) is at AC ground. That stage tries to keep the drain (or collector) of the lower, input device at a nearly constant voltage; small-signal analysis shows

        AvGD ≈ rd1 / (rd1 + 1/gm2)   (MOS)
             ≈ 1 / (1 + gm2·ro1)      (BJT or MOS)

Because gm2·ro1 is large, AvGD is close to 0 (typically < 1). With essentially no gain between gate and drain, the feedback capacitance is not multiplied:

        C-Miller,cascode ≈ Cgd · (1 – AvGD) ≈ Cgd

3. The only remaining capacitances that the signal source “sees” are the raw Cgd of the input device and its Cgs/Cπ, so the input node no longer has to charge an enlarged Miller capacitor. The pole formed with the source resistance therefore moves to a much higher frequency, giving the cascode its characteristically wide bandwidth.

Summary  
The cascode keeps the drain/collector of the input transistor from moving, so the voltage gain across the gate-to-drain (or base-to-collector) capacitance collapses to ≈ 1. Without that gain there is almost no Miller multiplication, hence the Miller effect is far less pronounced in a cascode amplifier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies that the common-gate device presents a low-impedance node at the input transistor’s drain, reducing Miller effect. However, it says the drain gain is nearly zero and the Miller multiplication nearly disappears; the gain is typically about −1, so the Cgd multiplier is roughly 2. This overstates the reduction, but the core mechanism is correct.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
Miller-effect enlargement of a device’s reverse (gate-drain or base-collector) capacitance requires two things

1. A capacitance that connects the input node to a node whose a.c. voltage moves a lot with respect to the input.  
2. An inverting gain between those two nodes so that the difference voltage across the capacitor is approximately (1+|A v|) times the input swing.

In an ordinary common–source / common–emitter stage both conditions are satisfied: the drain/collector voltage makes a large inverted excursion (≈-g m R D times the input swing), so the small C gd /C μ is multiplied by (1+|A v|).

What the cascode does
---------------------

A cascode is obtained by placing a common-gate (MOS) or common-base (BJT) device on top of the input transistor.

• The input transistor (M1/Q1) is still used as a trans-conductance element.  
• The upper transistor (M2/Q2) keeps the drain/collector of the input device at an almost constant a.c. voltage because its source/emitter is a low-impedance node (≈1/g m2) looking into the common-gate/base.  
  – With M2’s gate/base held at a fixed d.c. bias, the small-signal voltage at M1’s drain is only a few tens of millivolts, independent of the large voltage swing that finally appears at the cascode output node.

Consequences for the Miller capacitor of the input device

Let v g1 be the small-signal voltage at the gate/base of the input device and v d1 the voltage at its drain/collector:

Common-source: v d1 ≈ −A v v g1   (|A v|≫1)  
Cascode:    v d1 ≈ κ v g1 ,  |κ|≪1 (typically |κ|≤0.1)

The current through C gd /C μ is i = C ( d/dt )(v g1 − v d1).  
Hence the capacitance seen at the input becomes

C in = C gs + C gd (1 − v d1/v g1) = C gs + C gd (1 − κ)

For a common-source amplifier (κ≈−A v) ⇒ C in ≈ C gs + C gd(1 + |A v|)  ⇒ large.  
For a cascode          (κ≈0)   ⇒ C in ≈ C gs + C gd      ⇒ barely enlarged.

In other words, the cascode “bootstraps” the drain/collector of the input transistor so that almost the same instantaneous voltage appears on both plates of C gd /C μ; with little voltage across the capacitor, little current is required to charge or discharge it, and the input does not feel a multiplied capacitance.

Additional points

1. The upper (cascode) transistor itself does not introduce a Miller problem because its gate/base is at a.c. ground, so its own reverse capacitance connects a.c. ground to the output node, not back to the signal source.  
2. Because the input device now only has to drive its intrinsic capacitances, the dominant pole of the amplifier is pushed to a much higher frequency, giving the cascode its characteristic high bandwidth.  
3. The gain that was lost in the first (now low-gain) stage is recovered by the second transistor because the current from the input device is delivered into a high-impedance load at the cascode’s collector/drain.

Therefore the Miller effect is far less pronounced in a cascode because the node that would normally experience the large inverting voltage swing is held nearly constant by the common-gate/common-base transistor, eliminating the large voltage across the reverse capacitance and hence eliminating its Miller multiplication.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer correctly identifies the low-impedance cascode node and why it reduces Miller effect, but overstates the reduction by treating the input transistor’s drain as nearly AC-grounded. Its gain is often about −1, so Cgd still has roughly a factor-of-two Miller multiplication rather than almost none.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
1. What the circuit is  
   • M2 is an n-channel MOSFET whose source is not at ground but is held at the fixed
     bias Vb1.  
   • M1 is a p-channel MOSFET connected between the positive rail VDD and the output
     node; its gate is kept at the bias Vb2.  
   • The two devices are in series, so the same drain current ID flows through both of
     them.  
   • M1 behaves like an (almost) ideal current source, therefore the circuit is nothing
     more than a common-source amplifier (M2) with an active p-MOS load (M1).

2. Large–signal (DC) relations  
   We assume both transistors are intended to work in saturation.

   ID1 = ID2 = ID

   ID2 = ½ μn Cox(W/L)2 (Vin – Vb1 – VTHn)²(1+λnVDS2)  
   VDS2 = Vout – Vb1

   ID1 = ½ μp Cox(W/L)1 (VSG1 – |VTHp|)²(1+λpVSD1)  
   VSG1 = VDD – Vb2 ,         VSD1 = VDD – Vout

   Setting the two currents equal gives the static Vin-to-Vout characteristic
   (usually solved numerically because Vout appears inside ID through VDS2 and VSD1).

   Saturation limits:

        For M2 :  Vout ≥ Vin – VTHn                 (keeps M2 in sat.)  
        For M1 :  Vout ≤ VDD – |VOV1|,    VOV1 = VSG1 – |VTHp|  (keeps M1 in sat.)

   So the usable output range is

        Vin – VTHn  ≤  Vout  ≤  VDD – |VOV1|.

   If Vin ≤ Vb1+VTHn → M2 is OFF → Vout ≃ VDD.  
   If Vin is very large → M2 enters triode and pulls Vout down close to Vb1.

3. Small-signal (incremental) analysis  
   Let

        gm2 = ∂ID/∂VGS2 = 2ID / VOV2 ,     ro2 = 1/gds2 ≃ 1/(λnID)  
        ro1 = 1/gds1 ≃ 1/(λpID)

   (VGS2 is Vin – Vb1; VOV2 is Vin – Vb1 – VTHn.)

   Because VGS1 is fixed (Vb2 is a dc node), gm1·vgs1 = 0 in small signal; M1
   contributes only its output conductance gds1.  
   KCL at the output gives  

        gm2 vin + gds2 vout + gds1 vout = 0

   Therefore

        Av = vout/vin = –gm2 / (gds1 + gds2) = –gm2 (ro1 || ro2).

   Because ro1 and ro2 are both large, Av can easily reach –20…–40 V/V with
   minimum-length devices and well over –100 V/V with long-channel devices.

4. Input and output impedances  
   Rin ≅ ∞ (MOS gate).  
   Rout = ro1 || ro2 (tens to hundreds of kΩ).  
   The stage can only drive high-impedance loads; a source follower or second
   gain stage is normally added afterward.

5. Bias-point design procedure  
   1. Choose ID from required gain-bandwidth or power.  
   2. Pick VOV1 and VOV2 that give enough swing; typical 0.15…0.25 V in deep sub-µm.  
   3. Fix M1 size from ID and VOV1:  (W/L)1 = 2ID / (μp Cox VOV1²).  
   4. Fix M2 size from ID and VOV2 similarly.  
   5. Generate the two bias voltages:  
        Vb2 = VDD – (|VTHp| + VOV1)  
        Vb1 = desired source level (often ground, but can be lifted for
              common-mode considerations).

6. Qualitative behaviour  
   • With M2 off the output is high (≈ VDD).  
   • As Vin rises above Vb1+VTHn the output falls, inverting the input.  
   • Because M1 forces almost constant ID, even a small change in Vin must be
     absorbed by a comparatively large change in Vout → high gain.  
   • Finite λ (ro) of the two devices limits the gain to a finite value.

7. What the circuit is used for  
   This two-transistor “n-MOS with p-MOS current-source load” is the basic
   gain stage of most CMOS op-amps, comparators and analog building blocks.
   By simply adjusting Vb2 the designer can set the quiescent current and hence
   gm and gain, without disturbing the dc level of Vin.

In short:  
M2 works as a common-source transistor, Vb1 sets its source potential, M1 is an
active p-MOS load that fixes the bias current.  The small-signal gain is

        Av ≃ –gm2 (ro1 || ro2),

and the allowable output swing is bounded by

        Vin – VTHn ≤ Vout ≤ VDD – |VOV1|,

so, with the proper choice of Vb1 and Vb2, the stage provides a high-gain,
inverting voltage amplifier using only two MOSFETs and two dc bias voltages.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer places Vin at M2’s gate and treats the circuit as an inverting common-source stage. The required topology has Vin at M2’s source and is a non-inverting common-gate stage; the golden solution assigns 0 to this topology error.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
What you see is nothing more than the elementary “gain” stage that appears in most MOS linear
and mixed–signal ICs:

• M2 is a common–source NMOS whose gate is the signal input.  
• M1 is a PMOS biased as an (almost) constant-current source and therefore behaves as an
active load for M2.  

            VDD
              │         PMOS current source load
              │ISAT1≈constant
              ▼
            ┌──┴───┐  M1  (W/L)1 , gate = Vb2
            │      │
            │  Vout├───────────►   signal output
            │      │
            └──┬───┘
               │ID
               │
            ┌──┴───┐  M2  (W/L)2 , gate = Vin
            │      │
            │      │◄── Vb1  (source reference)
            └──────┘
               │
              Vb1  (usually ground in single–supply designs)

The two external dc voltages Vb2 and Vb1 establish the quiescent current and the allowable input /
output swings, while Vin carries the information.  Below is a concise large- and small-signal
analysis.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Large-signal (dc) behaviour
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume both devices are kept in saturation (normal design intent).

   PMOS current:    ID1 = ½ βp (VSG1 – |VTP|)^2  [1 + λp VSD1]
                    where VSG1 = VDD – Vb2
                          VSD1 = VDD – Vout

   NMOS current:    ID2 = ½ βn (VGS2 – VTHn)^2  [1 + λn VDS2]
                    where VGS2 = Vin – Vb1
                          VDS2 = Vout – Vb1

In the quiescent state ID1 = ID2 = I0, so to first order (neglect λ’s)

        I0 = ½ βp (VDD – Vb2 – |VTP|)^2
           = ½ βn (VinQ – Vb1 – VTHn)^2

⇒  Vin (bias point) = Vb1 + VTHn + √(βp/βn) (VDD – Vb2 – |VTP|) .        (1)

-------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Saturation limits (signal swing)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
To keep both devices in saturation:

   For M2 (NMOS):   VDS2 ≥ VGS2 – VTHn  ⇒  Vout ≥ Vin – VTHn          (2)
   For M1 (PMOS):   VSD1 ≥ VSG1 – |VTP| ⇒  Vout ≤ Vb2 + |VTP|         (3)

Thus the output node is allowed to move only inside

        Vin – VTHn  ≤  Vout  ≤  Vb2 + |VTP| .

Equation (2) also gives a practical upper limit for Vin:

        Vin,max ≈ Vb2 + |VTP| + VTHn .

At the low end Vin must be at least Vb1 + VTHn to create an inversion layer in M2.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Small-signal (incremental) gain
-------------------------------------------------------------------
With both devices saturated the incremental drain current produced by a small
input variation vin is

        id = gm2 · vin ,          gm2 = √(2 βn I0)

This current flows through the parallel output resistances of the two devices

        ro1 ≃ 1/(λp I0)    ,    ro2 ≃ 1/(λn I0)    ,   ro = ro1 || ro2 .

Hence the mid-band gain is

        Av = vo / vin = – gm2 · ro
           ≈ – √(2 βn I0) / (λp + λn) .                            (4)

Because ro1 is normally much larger than ro2 in deep-sub-micron processes,
|Av| can easily reach 20–40 dB with only two transistors.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Power and bias flexibility
-------------------------------------------------------------------
The quiescent dissipation is

        Pdc = I0 · (VDD – Vb1) .

Biases Vb2 and (less frequently) Vb1 give the designer two convenient knobs:

   • Vb2 fixes I0 (and therefore gm and gain).  
   • Vb1 shifts the allowable input common-mode level without touching gm.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
5. What the circuit is used for
-------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Linear: the “second stage” of a two-stage CMOS op-amp, gain boosters, basic
   video/IF amplifiers, etc.  
2. Digital/mixed-signal: level shifter or CMOS inverter with an adjustable
   switching threshold (Vb1/Vb2 place the trip point almost anywhere in the
   supply window).

-------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
-------------------------------------------------------------------
The schematic is a common-source NMOS amplifier (M2) loaded by a PMOS
current source (M1).  Vb2 sets the drain current, Vb1 defines the lower
reference for the input, Vin modulates the current through M2 and the output
node responds inversely with a gain

        Av ≈ – gm2 (ro1 || ro2) ,

provided that

        Vin – VTHn  ≤  Vout  ≤  Vb2 + |VTP| .

Those few equations capture virtually everything you need to know to
design or use this ubiquitous little circuit block.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit identification  
• M1 is a p-MOSFET whose source is tied to VDD and whose gate is held at the fixed bias Vb2.  
 With Vb2 constant the device behaves like a (almost) constant-current source – an “active
 load” for the stage.  
• M2 is an n-MOSFET.  Its source is not at ground but at the bias voltage Vb1, while its gate is
 the signal node Vin.  It therefore works as the amplifying transistor of a common-source
 stage.  
• The drain terminals of the two devices are shorted; that node is the output Vout.  

Thus the drawing is the elementary CMOS common-source amplifier with an active load
(often one half-circuit of a CMOS differential pair).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Large-signal (d.c.) operation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The same drain current I flows through the two series devices, therefore

            Idn(Vin) = Idp(constant)                                       (1)

Assume long–channel devices and both transistors in saturation:

            Idn = ½ kn(W/L)n (Vin – Vb1 – VTN)²                  (2)
            Idp = ½ kp(W/L)p (VDD – Vb2 – |VTP|)²                (3)

(kn = µnCox , kp = µpCox).

Because Vb2 is fixed, (3) is a constant, so (2) must deliver the same value.
Solving (2) = (3) for the gate voltage that yields the quiescent bias current:

        Vin,Q = Vb1 + VTN
                 + √( kp(W/L)p / kn(W/L)n ) · (VDD – Vb2 – |VTP| )      (4)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Region limits (input common-mode window)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
To keep both transistors in saturation

1. M2 : VDSn ≥ VGSn – VTN  ⇒  Vout ≥ Vin – VTN                    (5)
2. M1 : VSDp ≥ VSGp – |VTP| ⇒  Vout ≤ Vb2 + |VTP|                 (6)

Combine (5) and (6):

        Vb1 + VTN  ≤  Vin  ≤  Vb2 + |VTP| + VTN                     (7)

Below the lower limit M2 turns off and Vout is pulled to VDD.
Above the upper limit M1 leaves saturation and the gain collapses.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Small-signal model and gain
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let gm2, ro2 be the transconductance and output resistance of M2;
gm1, ro1 for M1.  The small-signal circuit is:

 • Input node: open-circuit (MOS gate).  
 • Output node resistance:  Ro = ro1 || ro2.  
 • Small-signal current injected by M2:  gm2 · vin.  

The incremental voltage gain is therefore

        Av = vout / vin = – gm2 · ( ro1 || ro2 )                   (8)

If λn ≈ λp = λ, Id = IQ,

        ro1 = 1/(λ·Id) ,  ro2 = 1/(λ·Id)  ⇒  Ro ≈ 1/(2λ Id)       (9)

Using gm2 = 2Id / Vov,n  (with Vov,n = Vin – Vb1 – VTN),

        |Av| ≈ ( 2 / Vov,n ) · ( 1 / 2λ ) = 1 / ( λ Vov,n )       (10)

Hence the gain is large when channel-length modulation (λ) is small and when
the n-MOS overdrive Vov,n is small.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Output swing
--------------------------------------------------------------------
High level: When M2 is off (Vin < Vb1+VTN) the tiny load current in M1
raises Vout ≈ VDD (minus a few hundred millivolts caused by ro1).

Low level: The lowest usable Vout while keeping M2 in saturation is

        Vout,min ≈ Vb1 + Vov,n                                    (11)

and must also satisfy (6):  Vout,min ≥ Vb1 + Vov,n  ≤  Vb2 + |VTP|.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Frequency response (first–order)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
 Dominant pole:   fp ≈ 1 / (2π Ro Ctot)  
where Ctot is the sum of Cdb1, Cdb2, load capacitance and the Miller-reflected
Cgd of M2 (≈ gm2Cgd2Ro).  Because the input node is capacitive only, the input
pole is usually far beyond the dominant pole and the stage behaves like a
single-pole amplifier over most of its bandwidth.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Qualitative transfer characteristic
--------------------------------------------------------------------
 • Vin < Vb1 + VTN → M2 off, Vout ≈ VDD (logic ‘1’).  
 • Vb1 + VTN < Vin < Vb2 + |VTP| + VTN → linear region with negative gain
   given by (8).  
 • Vin above upper limit → M1 enters triode, current rises sharply,
   Vout is forced close to Vb1 + VDS(sat)n (logic ‘0’).

Thus the stage behaves like an analog inverting amplifier around its bias
point and like a digital inverter at the extremes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
The circuit is a CMOS common-source gain stage:

• M1 (pMOS) is a current-source load set by Vb2.  
• M2 (nMOS) is the amplifying device controlled by Vin and referenced to Vb1.  
• Within the bias window the small-signal voltage gain is approximately
  Av = –gm2·(ro1||ro2); outside that window the output rails to the supply
  limits.  
Such a cell is the basic building block for the gain stages of CMOS op-amps,
sense amplifiers and logic level shifters.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit shown in the figure have?

answer.text:
In the small–signal picture every high-impedance node that can store charge contributes one pole.  
Looking at the schematic we can identify three such nodes:

1. Gate node of M1 (between Rs and the gate).  
   Capacitances connected to it: Cgs and one side of Cgd.  

2. Intermediate node (drain of M1 / source of M2).  
   Capacitances connected to it: Cgd, Cgd2 and Cdb.  

3. Output node (drain of M2, Vout).  
   Capacitances connected to it: Cdb2 and any external load capacitance.

Although five MOS capacitances are drawn, the ones that terminate on the same node simply add together; they do not create additional independent energy-storage points. Consequently the transfer function is third-order:

The circuit has 3 poles.

   • CGD goes from this node to the internal node.  
   Because the node is reached through the finite source resistance RS, it is a high-impedance node and therefore contributes a pole.

2. Internal node (drain-1 / source-2)  
   • CGD from the previous item returns here.  
   • CDB (drain-bulk capacitance of M1) is to ground.  
   • The small-signal resistance seen looking into the node is large (≈ ro1 ∥ 1/gm2), so this node gives another pole.

3. Output node

1. Gate of M1 (behind the series resistance RS).  
   – Capacitances connected to this node: CGS to ground and CGD to the drain node.

2. Drain of M1 / source of M2 (the output node Vout).  
   – Capacitances connected to this node: CDB to ground, CGD to the gate node, and CGD2 to ground (because the gate of M2 is tied to ac ground).

All the other terminals in the schematic (source of M1, gate of M2, drain of M2, supply rails) are at ac ground, so the capacitors connected there do not introduce additional dynamic nodes.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The network is nothing more than two identical n-MOSFETs that are placed in series (a “stack”) and whose gates are shorted to the same driving node Vin.  
The drain of the upper device M2 is pulled-up to the supply by the resistor RD, so the drain node is the output Vout.  
Because the two transistors conduct exactly the same drain current ID (they are in series), the circuit may be analysed with only two unknowns:

 • the current ID  
 • the intermediate node voltage VX  ( VX = drain of M1 = source of M2 )

The behaviour is easiest to see in three regions of Vin.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Vin < VTH  (both devices OFF)  
ID ≃ 0  ⇒ Vout = VDD , VX = 0

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. VTH < Vin < 2 VTH  (both devices in saturation)

Neglect channel–length modulation in the first pass (λ = 0) so the familiar square-law
 ID = ½ k (VGS – VTH)^2 , k ≜ μn Cox W/L
may be used for both MOSFETs.  
Because the two gate voltages are identical while the sources are different we write

 ID = ½ k (Vin – VTH)^2            (for M1)  
 ID = ½ k (Vin – VX – VTH)^2        (for M2)

Equating the two currents gives

 (Vin – VTH)^2  =  (Vin – VX – VTH)^2    
 ⇒ (Vin – VTH + Vin – VX – VTH)(Vin – VTH – Vin + VX + VTH) = 0   
 ⇒ VX = 0 or VX = 2(Vin – VTH)

When ID ≠ 0 the physically acceptable solution is

 VX = 2 ( Vin – VTH )          [1]

which is indeed smaller than Vin as long as Vin < 2 VTH, so VGS2 is positive and M2 conducts.

Hence in this region

 ID = ½ k (Vin – VTH)^2         [2]  
 Vout = VDD – RD·ID = VDD – ( RD k /2 ) (Vin – VTH)^2 [3]

The dc transfer characteristic is therefore parabolic and inverted.

Small-signal (around some bias Vin = VBIAS in this region) :

 gm = ∂ID / ∂Vin = k (Vin − VTH)        [4]  
 ∆Vout = – RD · gm · ∆Vin ⇒ Av ≡ ∆Vout/∆Vin = – RD k (VBIAS – VTH) [5]

So the magnitude of the gain is the usual product gm·RD, exactly as for a simple
common-source stage; but because M2 sits on top of M1 the drain–source
voltage of the amplifying device (M1) is almost constant, giving a very large intrinsic output resistance (cascode effect).  If channel-length modulation is included

 ro,eq  ≃  ro2  + (1 + gm2 ro2) ro1  »  ro1

and the small-signal gain becomes

 Av  ≃  – gm1 [ RD ∥ ro,eq ] .

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Vin ≥ 2 VTH  (top device cuts off)

For Vin ≥ 2 VTH eqn. [1] would give VX ≥ Vin which makes VGS2 ≤ 0,
so M2 is forced out of conduction.  As the drain path is pinched off the
current can no longer increase; Vout rises back toward VDD and the
circuit is no longer a useful amplifier.  Hence the practical linear
input range is limited to Vin < 2 VTH and usually chosen a few hundred
millivolts above VTH to obtain a reasonable gm.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary of important results (λ = 0, VTH < Vin < 2 VTH) :

 Intermediate node:      VX = 2 ( Vin – VTH )

 Drain current:        ID = ½ k (Vin – VTH)^2

 Output dc level:       Vout = VDD – (RD k /2)(Vin – VTH)^2

 Small-signal transconductance: gm = k (Vin – VTH)

 Small-signal voltage gain:   Av = – gm · RD = – RD k (Vin – VTH)

Because M2 stands as a common-gate (cascode) device, the effective
output resistance is greatly increased, so with realistic λ the gain is
actually

 Av ≈ – gm1 ( RD ∥ ro,eq )  with  ro,eq ≈ (1 + gm2 ro2) ro1 .

The circuit is therefore an inverting voltage amplifier whose dc
transfer is parabolic, whose gain is set (to first order) by
gm1 RD, and whose output resistance is boosted by the cascode action of
M2 while requiring no separate bias for that cascode transistor (its
gate is simply tied to the input).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes the common-gate series NMOS stack, but incorrectly treats both devices as saturated and the circuit as a cascode with strongly boosted output resistance. The essential mechanism—M1 in triode extending M2's effective channel length—is missed.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The network is nothing more than a resistively-loaded n–MOS inverter, except that the pull-down device has been replaced by two identical n-MOSFETs (M1 and M2) placed in series and driven from the same gate.  
Because the two devices share the same VGS their i-v laws can be written very compactly and the dc transfer characteristic can be obtained in closed form.

Assumptions used below  
• Both transistors are identical, enhancement type, body tied to the source (no body effect).  
• Channel-length modulation is neglected (λ ≃ 0).  
• Process transconductance parameter β = μn Cox (W/L)  (A V–2).  
• Vth is the threshold voltage.

Nodal definitions  
VX  : source of M2 ( = drain of M1)  
ID  : drain current of the stack  
x   : Vin – Vth  (MOS over-drive)

1. Region A – both devices off (cut-off)  
Vin ≤ Vth   →   ID ≃ 0,  Vout = VDD,  VX = 0.  
The circuit delivers a logic ‘1’.

2. Region B – both devices in saturation  
This region starts as soon as Vin exceeds Vth and lasts until the top device just reaches the edge of saturation.

Currents (square-law saturation):
ID = ½ β x²        (for M1)                (1)  
ID = ½ β (Vin – VX – Vth)²   (for M2)     (2)

Equating (1) and (2) gives the intermediate node voltage

VX = 2 x  = 2 (Vin – Vth).                 (3)

Output voltage (Kirchhoff on RD)

Vout = VDD – ID RD = VDD – ½ β RD x².      (4)

Small-signal gain in this region

Av = dVout/dVin = –β RD x.                 (5)

Boundary of Region B  
M2 remains in saturation as long as  
VDS2 ≥ Vov2    →    Vout – VX ≥ Vin – VX – Vth  →  Vout ≥ x.

Inserting (4) gives the inequality that defines the end of Region B:

½ β RD x² + x – VDD ≤ 0.                  (6)

Solve the quadratic equality to obtain the largest admissible over-drive

xmax = [ –1 + √(1 + 2 β RD VDD) ] / (β RD).   (7)

For Vin ≤ Vth + xmax all previous formulas are valid and both transistors stay in saturation.

3. Region C – M1 still in saturation, M2 has entered the triode region  
For Vin > Vth + xmax  the top device can no longer keep the drain node high enough, hence it operates in the linear (resistive) region while M1 is still in saturation.

Equations to be solved simultaneously in this region:

ID  = ½ β x²                                        (M1, still saturation)  
ID  = β[ (x – VX)(Vout – VX) – ½ (Vout – VX)² ]    (M2, triode)  
Vout = VDD – ID RD.                                 (resistor)

They can be reduced to a single algebraic expression (omitted for brevity),
but two useful approximations are worth keeping:

• As Vin continues to rise, ID grows ∝ x² while Vout falls almost linearly,
   so after only a few hundred millivolts above the boundary value,
   Vout is already very close to ground; hence for digital use one may safely write

    VOL ≈ 0 at Vin ≥ Vth + xmax + 0.2 … 0.3 V.      (8)

• The effective on-resistance of the two-device stack when Vin is high is

    Ron ≈ 1 / [ β (Vin – Vth) ]                    (9)

   which is roughly twice the on-resistance of a single transistor of the same size, as expected, because two identical devices are in series.

4. Key expressions collected

VOH  = VDD                                                 (logic ‘1’)  
VOL  ≈ 0                                                   (logic ‘0’)  
Transition (switching) point VM obtained from Vout = Vin:

VM = Vth + ½ [ √(1 + 2 β RD VDD) – 1 ] / (β RD).        (10)

Maximum small-signal gain (magnitude) occurs at the edge of region B

|Av|max = β RD xmax = √(1 + 2 β RD VDD) – 1.            (11)

5. Qualitative behaviour

•   When Vin < Vth the stack is open and the resistor pulls the output to VDD.  
•   As soon as Vin exceeds Vth both MOSFETs conduct; because the current rises with the square of the over-drive, the voltage drop on RD rises fast and the transition is significantly steeper than that of the ordinary single-transistor inverter.  
•   Once Vout falls below Vin – Vth the upper MOSFET leaves saturation, its channel resistance adds to the pull-down path, and Vout is rapidly driven to almost 0 V.  
In other words, the extra device gives a “gm boost”: the inverter has
larger gain in the transition region and therefore better noise margins, while still being built with n-channel devices only.

That completes the large-signal and small-signal analysis of the circuit.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes a resistively loaded inverter with a series, common-gate NMOS stack, but the core analysis is wrong: the devices do not have equal VGS, the lower device operates in triode while the upper is saturated, and the effective-channel-length mechanism is missed. The claimed gm boost and region equations are incorrect.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Below is a self–contained dc and small-signal analysis of the two-transistor
stage of Fig.-1.  
(Notation : β = μn Cox W/L ,   Vov = VGS–Vth = over-drive voltage.)

1. Operating regions (dc)

a) Cut-off Vin ≤ Vth  
 Both M1 and M2 are OFF → ID = 0, Vout = VDD.

b) Both devices in saturation Vin > Vth, head-room still available  
 Because the two gates are shorted, the channel current of the two
saturated devices is identical

  ID = ½ β (Vin – Vth)^2                                (1)

 The load resistor converts this current into the output voltage

  Vout = VDD – RD ID
     = VDD – ­½ β RD (Vin – Vth)^2                 (2)

 Saturation requires

  VDS1 ≥ Vov and VDS2 ≥ Vov
  ⇒ Vout ≥ VDS1+VDS2 ≥ 2 (Vin – Vth)                 (3)

 Combining (2) and (3) gives the admissible input range for which both
devices really stay in saturation:

  ½ β RD (Vin – Vth)^2 + 2 (Vin – Vth) – VDD ≤ 0     (4)

 Solving (4) for x = Vin – Vth (take the positive root) gives

  x ≤ xMAX = [–2 + √(4 + 2 β RD VDD)] / (β RD).       (5)

c) M1 still saturated, M2 driven into triode Vin > Vth + xMAX  
 ID is still limited mainly by M1 (≈ expression (1)); Vout continues to
decrease almost linearly with increasing Vin until, when both transistors
enter deep triode, Vout approaches ground.

2. Large-signal transfer characteristic (region b)

 For Vth < Vin ≤ Vth + xMAX :

  ID(Vin)  = ½ β (Vin – Vth)^2  
  Vout(Vin)= VDD – ½ β RD (Vin – Vth)^2

 Hence the Vout–Vin curve is parabolic and the stage behaves as an
inverting “square-law” amplifier.

3. Small-signal gain (bias chosen inside region b)

 gm1 = gm2 = β(Vin – Vth) = β Vov

 With ro » RD for simplicity, write the a-c node equations
(vo = small-signal output, vin = small-signal input, vx = node between the
two devices):

 (1) vo/RD + gm2 (vin – vx) = 0  
 (2) gm2 (vin – vx) = gm1 vin

 If the two transistors are identical, gm1 = gm2 ⇒ from (2) vx ≃ 0 (an
a-c virtual ground).  Substituting in (1):

  Av = vo / vin = – gm2 RD = –β RD (Vin – Vth) = –gm RD         (6)

 So the small-signal gain is exactly the same as that of a simple
common-source amplifier with load RD, but

 • the internal node vx is a-c grounded → no Miller effect for M1  
 • the input capacitance is therefore only CGS, giving a higher bandwidth
   for the same voltage gain.

4. Output– and input–swing limitations

 Minimum output voltage while keeping both devices saturated follows from
(3):

  Vout,min = 2 (Vin – Vth) = 2 Vov.                     (7)

 As soon as Vout drops below (7), M2 is the first to leave saturation.
The positive swing is limited only by VDD.  
The maximum permissible input excursion that keeps both devices in
saturation is given by (5).

5. Summary of key relations (region with both devices saturated)

 ID              = ½ β (Vin – Vth)^2  
 Vout            = VDD – ½ β RD (Vin – Vth)^2  
 Small-signal gm = β (Vin – Vth)  
 Voltage gain    Av = – gm RD  
 Input range     0 < Vin – Vth ≤ xMAX   [eq.(5)]  
 Output swing    2 (Vin – Vth) ≤ Vout ≤ VDD.

The circuit therefore realises a voltage-controlled current sink whose
square-law current is turned into an inverted output voltage through RD.
For small excursions about a bias point it behaves like a common-source
amplifier with gain –gm RD but with greatly reduced input Miller
capacitance because the intermediate node is boot-strapped to a-c ground.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes the stacked, common-gate NMOS topology but incorrectly assumes both devices can be saturated and builds an invalid small-signal analysis around that assumption. It misses the key mechanism: M1 operates in triode and the pair behaves approximately like one transistor with a longer effective channel.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit topology  
• M1, M2 and the ideal current source I1 form an NMOS source-coupled (differential) pair.  
• M1’s drain is hard-wired to the positive supply VDD, so M1 never delivers signal current to the
output – it is used only to “steal” part of the tail current away from M2.  
• The whole tail current I1 must flow through the two transistors, therefore any change of the
current drawn by M1 is reflected as an opposite change of the current that flows through M2 and
the load resistor RD.  
• The voltage Vb is a dc bias (reference) applied to M2, while Vin is the signal applied to M1; the
circuit therefore behaves like a single-ended differential pair that converts the difference
(Vin − Vb) into a single-ended voltage Vout.

Assumptions for the calculations  
1. identical transistors, long-channel, λ ≃ 0 (ro → ∞)  
2. strong inversion saturation so that  
 ID = ½ β (VGS − VTH)² with β = μn Cox W/L  
3. I1 is an ideal, temperature-independent current source

1. Quiescent (balanced) operating point  
Set Vin = Vb so that the pair is perfectly balanced.  
Each device then carries half of the tail current:

 ID1 = ID2 = I1/2

The overdrive voltage of each transistor at the quiescent point is

 Vov0 = VGS0 − VTH = √(2 ID1/β) = √(I1/β)

The common-source node voltage is therefore

 VS0 = Vin − (VTH + Vov0).

The corresponding quiescent output voltage is

 Vout0 = VDD − RD (I1/2).

2. Large-signal transfer characteristic  
Let ΔV = Vin − Vb.  Define x = VGS1 − VTH, y = VGS2 − VTH ⇒ y = x − ΔV.

Because the sum of the branch currents is fixed,

 ½β(x² + y²) = I1.                          (1)

Solving (1) for y gives the drain current of M2:

 ID2 = ½βy²  
    = ½ I1 − (I1/2Vov0) ΔV     (approximation for |ΔV| ≪ 2Vov0)           (2)

The exact solution is obtained from the quadratic in (1), but the linear form (2) is accurate in
the region of interest for small signals.

The current through the load resistor is hence controlled by ΔV, and the output node obeys

 Vout = VDD − RD ID2.

Limiting behaviour  
• ΔV ≥ +2Vov0 → ID2 → 0, Vout → VDD (high level).  
• ΔV ≤ −2Vov0 → ID2 → I1, Vout → VDD − I1 RD (low level).

Thus the circuit can be viewed as a hard-limiting comparator when driven far enough or as a
linear amplifier around ΔV = 0.

3. Small-signal analysis (ΔV kept small)

Small-signal transconductance of each device at the bias point:

 gm0 = ∂ID/∂VGS = β(VGS0 − VTH) = 2(ID1)/Vov0 = I1/Vov0.

Applying an incremental change vin (= ΔVin) to the gate of M1 while keeping Vb fixed gives the
small-signal set

 id1 = gm0 (vin − vs),     id2 = −gm0 vs ,     id1 + id2 = 0

⇒ vs = vin/2                               (common source rises half as much)

⇒ id2 = −gm0 vin/2.

The output voltage variation is therefore

 vout = −RD id2 = + (gm0 RD / 2) vin

so the small-signal voltage gain is

 Av = vout / vin = (gm0 RD)/2 = (RD I1) / (2 Vov0).    (positive gain)

4. Output-swing / saturation requirement for M2  
M2 must stay in saturation even when it carries the full tail current:

 Vout,min = VS + Vov0 ≃ Vin,min − VTH.

The designer therefore chooses RD so that

 VDD − I1 RD ≥ VS + Vov0.

This places the upper limit

 RD,max ≃ (VDD − VS − Vov0) / I1.

5. Summary of key points  
• The circuit is a single-ended NMOS differential pair with a resistive load.  
• It realises a voltage-controlled current steering function:

 ID2 varies linearly with (Vb − Vin) for |Vin − Vb| < 2Vov0  
 and is limited to 0 or I1 outside that range.

• Small-signal gain: Av = (gm RD)/2, non-inverting with respect to Vin.  
• Input resistance is practically infinite (MOS gate), output resistance ≃ RD (if ro neglected).  
• By choosing Vb as a fixed reference the circuit can be used as a low-power, high-gain
comparator; with Vb chosen as a bias point it serves as a linear amplifier stage in many
integrated-circuit op-amp and band-gap reference cores.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the circuit as a source-coupled differential pair with M2 biased at Vb and the output taken at M2’s drain. Its small-signal gain is also non-inverting, consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The network is nothing more than a “one-sided” long-tailed pair.

•  M1 and M2 are identical n-channel MOSFETs that share the same source
   node (VS).  
•  A bias current source I1 forces a constant tail current IT = I1 to flow
   from the common source node to ground.  
•  The gate of M2 is kept at the dc bias voltage Vb, the gate of M1 is the
   signal input Vin.  
•  The drain of M1 is hard-wired to the positive rail, therefore M1 never
   leaves saturation (as long as VS < VDD – VDSAT).  
•  The drain current that does not go through M1 is steered through M2 and
   the load resistor RD, producing the single-ended output voltage  
        Vout = VDD – ID2 RD.

Because the two devices form a current-steering pair, ID1 + ID2 = I1 at all
times; which of the two transistors conducts the greater share of I1 is
decided by the difference Vin – Vb.

1. Large-signal (dc) behaviour  

   Long-channel square-law model, β = μnCoxW/L (same for both devices):

        ID1 = β/2 (Vin – VS – VTH)²
        ID2 = β/2 (Vb  – VS – VTH)²
        ID1 + ID2 = I1                                         (1)

   Define a = Vin – VTH and b = Vb – VTH.  
   From (1)

        (a – VS)² + (b – VS)² = 2I1 / β                       (2)

   Solving (2) for VS gives

        VS = (a + b)/2  ± ½ √[ 4I1/β – (a – b)² ]              (3)

   (The “–” sign is selected so that VS lies between a and b.)

   The drain currents then become

        ID1 = I1/2 + (β/4)(a – b) √[ 4I1/β – (a – b)² ]        (4)
        ID2 = I1 – ID1                                         (5)

   Finally

        Vout = VDD – ID2 RD                                    (6)

   Qualitative picture

   •  If Vin ≪ Vb  ⇒  ID1 ≈ 0, ID2 ≈ I1,  Vout ≈ VDD – I1 RD (LOW).  
   •  If Vin ≫ Vb  ⇒  ID2 ≈ 0, ID1 ≈ I1,  Vout ≈ VDD         (HIGH).  
   •  Around Vin = Vb the currents share the tail current and
      the transfer characteristic is the smooth S-shaped curve
      described by (6).  The circuit therefore behaves as a high-gain
      voltage comparator / inverter.

2. Small-signal gain around the crossing point (Vin = Vb)

   At Vin = Vb the pair is perfectly balanced:

        ID1 = ID2 = I1/2

   Transconductances

        gm1 = ∂ID1/∂Vin = √(2β ID1) = √(β I1)
        gm2 = √(β I1)                       (identical)

   A small perturbation δVin produces

        δID1 = gm1 (δVin – δVS)
        δID2 = –δID1  (because δIT = 0)

   From Kirchhoff at the source node
        (gm1 + gm2) δVS = gm1 δVin

   Hence source node gain
        δVS = (gm1/(gm1 + gm2)) δVin = ½ δVin

   and

        δID2 = –gm1 (δVin – δVS) = –gm1 (½ δVin) = –gm1 δVin / 2

   Finally

        δVout = –δID2 RD = (gm1 RD / 2) δVin

        Small-signal voltage gain  |Av| = gm RD / 2, with
        gm = √(β I1).

   Example: β = 500 μA/V², I1 = 100 μA  →  gm ≈ 0.224 S,  
            RD = 10 kΩ                →  |Av| ≈ 1.1 × 10⁴ ≃ 11.

3. Necessary bias inequalities

   •  Saturation of M1:       VDD – VS ≥ VDSAT  
   •  Saturation of M2:       Vout(min) – VS ≥ VDSAT  
   •  Both devices on (at least near the switching point):  
         VS ≤ min(Vin – VTH, Vb – VTH)

   These relations put limits on the acceptable ranges of
   Vin, Vb, RD and I1.

4. What the circuit is good for

   •  Single-ended sense amplifier / comparator: the output toggles
     between VDD and (VDD – I1 RD).  
   •  Trans-conductor: around Vin ≈ Vb the transfer is nearly linear
     with gm/2.  
   •  Building block of latch, regenerative sense amp, decision
     circuit, etc.

In short, the circuit is a current-steering amplifier that converts the
difference between Vin and a fixed reference Vb into a rail-to-rail output
through the resistor RD, with small-signal gain gm RD / 2 and large-signal
“digital” behaviour for inputs several VOV (≈ 100–200 mV) away from the
reference.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the circuit as a source-coupled differential pair with M2 biased at Vb and output taken at M2’s drain. Its small-signal analysis gives the correct non-inverting gain; minor terminology and numerical-unit slips do not undermine the essential answer.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
(1)  What the circuit is  

The two NMOS transistors share the same source node.  
• M1 is a common-source device whose drain is hard-wired to VDD and whose gate is the signal input Vin.  
• M2 is another common-source device whose drain is the output node Vout; a load resistor RD connects that node to VDD.  
• A constant current sink I1 forces a dc current I1 out of the common source node.  
• The gate of M2 is held at a fixed bias voltage Vb.

Thus the circuit is nothing more than a “half” differential pair.  The tail current I1 is steered between the two branches; only the current that flows through the right-hand branch (M2) produces an output voltage, so the cell behaves as a single-ended transconductance stage that compares Vin with the reference Vb.

(2)  Large-signal (dc) relations  
Assume both MOSFETs operate in saturation and ignore channel-length modulation.

ID1 = (β1 /2)(Vin – Vth – VS)^2         (1)  
ID2 = (β2 /2)(Vb  – Vth – VS)^2         (2)  

with βi = μnCox(W/L)i.  The tail current constraint is  

I1 = ID1 + ID2                                 (3)

Solving (3) for the source potential VS gives

VS = Vth + (β1Vin + β2Vb – √(β1β2)(|Vin–Vb|) ) /(β1+β2)         (4)

(Exact algebra for the general β1≠β2 case is messy; for matched devices β1 = β2 = β the solution simplifies to)  

VS = Vth + ½(Vin + Vb – |Vin – Vb|)                             (4a)

Once VS is known, the right-branch current is obtained from (2) and converted into a voltage by RD:

Vout = VDD – ID2 RD                                             (5)

Boundary values  
• Vin ≪ Vb  ⇒  ID2 ≈ I1 , Vout ≈ VDD – I1RD (LOW).  
• Vin ≫ Vb  ⇒  ID2 ≈ 0 ,  Vout ≈ VDD (HIGH).  
• Vin = Vb  (matched devices)  ⇒  ID2 = I1/2 , Vout = VDD – ½I1RD.

Hence the transfer characteristic is a soft “S-shaped” curve that swings between VDD and VDD – I1RD and centred at Vin = Vb.

(3)  Small-signal analysis  

Let gm1 , gm2 be the incremental transconductances of M1 and M2 at the operating point.

At the source node:

id1 + id2 = 0          (the tail current source keeps the total current constant)
⇒ gm1 (vin – vs) – gm2 vs = 0
⇒ vs = gm1/(gm1+gm2) · vin                            (6)

The small-signal drain current of M2 is

id2 = –gm2 vs = –gm1gm2/(gm1+gm2) · vin              (7)

The incremental transconductance seen at the output is therefore

Gm,eff = – gm1gm2 /(gm1+gm2)                      (8)

For matched devices (gm1 = gm2 = gm)

Gm,eff = – gm /2                                        (9)

The minus sign means that an increase in Vin reduces the downward current through M2, i.e. raises Vout.  Including the resistor,

small-signal voltage gain:    Av = –Gm,eff RD  
                         = + (gm RD)/2 (matched case)           (10)

Thus, although only one resistor is used, the stage provides a moderate positive gain (~gmRD/2) together with a high input impedance.

(4)  Saturation conditions  

To keep both MOSFETs in saturation:

M1 : VDD – VS ≥ VGS1 – Vth = Vin – Vth – VS  
M2 : Vout – VS ≥ VGS2 – Vth = Vb  – Vth – VS

These inequalities put an upper limit on the tail current (hence on |VDD – VS|) or, equivalently, on the maximum value of RD that can be used for a given swing.

(5)  What the circuit is useful for  

1.  Single-ended sense amplifier / comparator (Vin compared to the fixed reference Vb).  
2.  Front end of an op-amp where one side of the differential pair is reused as a diode-connected load to save area.  
3.  Variable‐gain transconductor by changing Vb.  
4.  Simple linearised common-source stage with source degeneration created by the current-steering action.

In summary:  
The cell steers the constant current I1 between M1 and M2 according to the difference (Vin – Vb).  The current that reaches M2 is turned into a voltage by RD, giving a transfer function whose slope (gmRD/2 for matched devices) makes the circuit a useful, compact voltage-to-voltage amplifier or comparator.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the circuit as a source-coupled differential pair with M2 biased at Vb and the output at M2’s drain, and gives the correct non-inverting gain. Although its large-signal source-voltage formula is flawed, the golden full-credit rule makes the correct topology identification sufficient.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
Think in small-signal terms and look into the source of M1, i.e. into the node that has been labelled Vout.

1. Elements that the small-signal current can use  
   • the intrinsic gate-source capacitor of M1, Cgs  
   • the resistor that connects the gate to the ac ground, RS  
   • the transconductance of the device, gm (current source gm·vgs)  
   • the large drain resistance ro (it can be added at the end – it does not change the argument)

2. Gate–source relationship  
   At the gate node the only current that can leave is the current through Cgs, therefore

           Vg / RS  =  s Cgs (Vg – Vs)

   →  Vg = (s Cgs) Vs / (1/RS + s Cgs)

   →  Vgs = Vg – Vs = – Vs / (1 + s RS Cgs)               (1)

   A change of the source voltage therefore produces a gate–source
   voltage that is phase-lagged by 90° for the frequencies for which
   sRS Cgs  ≪  1.

3. Current that is produced by the device  
   The total small-signal current that leaves node Vs is

           Iout = –gm Vgs – s Cgs Vgs                (the second term is the current through Cgs)

   Insert (1):

           Iout = –Vs (gm – s Cgs) / (1 + s RS Cgs)          (2)

4. Output impedance Zout = Vs / Iout  

           Zout(s) = – (1 + s RS Cgs)/(gm – s Cgs)

   For frequencies well below the zero ωz = 1/RS Cgs (i.e. sRS Cgs ≪ 1)
   the denominator may be written gm(1 – s Cgs /gm) and one obtains the
   series expansion

           Zout(s) ≈ –1/gm  +  s (RS Cgs /gm + Cgs /gm²)          (3)

   The constant term –1/gm is the familiar resistance of a source
   follower.  The term that is proportional to s, however, represents an
   inductance

           Leq  ≈  RS Cgs / gm                                  (4)

   (the second term Cgs/gm² is usually negligible because gm is large).

5. Interpretation  
   • The gate resistor and Cgs form an RC low-pass.  
   • When the source node is shaken, the gate voltage follows with a
     90° phase lag.  
   • The transconductance gm converts this delayed vgs into a current
     that leads the node voltage by 90°, exactly the behaviour of an
     inductor (v = L di/dt).  
   • Mathematically the RC network that is seen at the gate is
     “reflected” to the source through gm; in other words the MOSFET
     acts as a gyrator converting a capacitance into an inductance.

Therefore the impedance that an external circuit sees at Vout can have a positive imaginary part; i.e. it can look like a physical inductor of value

           L ≃ RS Cgs / gm  (in series with the small resistance 1/gm and
                              the large ro of M1).

This “active inductor” property is widely exploited in IC design for
shunt/series peaking, on-chip filters, and RF matching networks, because
it provides an inductive load without requiring a bulky, area-hungry
spiral inductor.
