answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
Think of what happens when a small -signal current ix is injected into the output node.

1.   The only element that is directly connected between the output node and another node is the gate-to-source capacitance of M1,  
     Cgs1.  Thus the first thing that happens is that Cgs1 is charged or
     discharged.

2.   The current that flows through Cgs1 has no place to go except through
     the series resistor RS that ties the gate of M1 to the ac ground
     (Vin is at ac ground when we measure Zout).  
     Hence the instantaneous gate voltage Vg is

           Vg = – RS · iC = – RS · jωCgs1 (Vg – Vout)             (1)

     so Vg lags Vout by 90° and is proportional to dVout/dt.

3.   The source of M1 is the output node, therefore

           Vgs1 = Vg – Vout.                                     (2)

     Substituting (1) in (2) gives

           Vgs1 = – Vout /(1 + jωRS Cgs1).                        (3)

     For the frequency range in which  |ωRS Cgs1|  ≫ 1   we obtain  
           Vgs1 ≈ – j /(ω Cgs1 RS) · dVout/dt                      (4)

     i.e. Vgs1 is proportional to the time derivative of Vout.

4.   The small-signal current delivered by M1 is

           igm = gm1 · Vgs1 ≈ – gm1 RS Cgs1 · dVout/dt.            (5)

     Because igm is proportional to dVout/dt, the transistor
     looks like an inductor:  for an inductor  v = L di/dt or,
     equivalently, i = (1/L) ∫ v dt.  Comparing (5) with the
     inductor relation we obtain

           Leq = RS Cgs1 / gm1.                                   (6)

5.   The lower device M2 is simply a (large-signal) current sink that
     provides a high ro so the impedance contributed by M1 dominates.
     Thus the small-signal output impedance seen at Vout is

           Zout ≈ 1/gm1  (a small series resistance)
                    +  jωLeq  (an inductive term).                (7)

In other words, the resistor RS, the gate-to-source capacitor Cgs1
and the transconductance gm1 form a gyrator that turns the capacitor
into an equivalent inductor Leq = RS Cgs1 / gm1.  
Because of this gyrator action, the circuit presents an inductive
output impedance even though it contains only transistors, a resistor
and (parasitic) capacitors.  This “active inductor” property is often
used for on-chip shunt/series peaking or for synthesising resonant
loads without bulky spiral inductors.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the relevant RS–CGS1–gm1 interaction and reaches the possible inductive conclusion, but its derivation is inconsistent and it treats the impedance as inductive without the required condition RS > 1/gm1. It also misses the key transition from about 1/gm1 at low frequency to RS at high frequency.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
Think small-signal, set the input ac-grounded (Vin = 0) and look into the node Vout.

1.  Small-signal model of M1  
    • Gate-to-source capacitance: Cgs  
    • Controlled current source: gm1·vgs flowing from drain (ac ground) to source (Vout)

2.  Gate circuit  
    The only ac current that can leave the gate is the displacement current through Cgs, and it has to flow through the external resistor RS to ground:

        iCgs = jωCgs (Vout – Vg) = Vg / RS      (1)

    hence

        Vg = jωRS Cgs
             ─────────── Vout =  jωRS Cgs
                            1 + jωRS Cgs        1 + jωRS Cgs
                                                    (2)

    and

        vgs = Vg – Vout = – Vout / (1 + jωRS Cgs)               (3)

3.  Current that M1 draws from the node  

        iM1 = (gm1 + jωCgs) · vgs                           (4)
             = – (gm1 + jωCgs)            Vout
                 ─────────────────────────────────           (5)
                     1 + jωRS Cgs

4.  Output impedance Zout = Vout / (–iM1)

        Zout =  1 + jωRS Cgs
                ─────────────────   ≈  RS Cgs      · s  +  RS
                   gm1 + jωCgs         ────────             ───
                                       gm1                  gm1
                                      ⎧──────── inductive term⎫
                                      ⎩──────── resistive term⎭     (6)

    For the frequency range  

        1 / (RS Cgs)  «  ω  «  gm1 / Cgs                       (7)

    the denominator is almost gm1 and the numerator is almost jωRS Cgs, so

        Zout  ≈  j ω (RS Cgs / gm1)                           (8)

    which has the form jωL, i.e. a pure inductance

        L ≃ RS Cgs / gm1                                      (9)

    with a small series resistance R ≃ RS / gm1 that becomes visible outside the band of (7).

5.  Physical interpretation  
    • A change in Vout is capacitively coupled to the gate through Cgs.  
    • Because this current must pass through RS, the gate voltage cannot follow the source instantly; it lags by ≈90°.  
    • The drain current gm1·vgs therefore lags the node voltage by ≈90° as well.  
    • An element whose current lags its voltage by 90° behaves like an inductor, hence the node presents an inductive impedance equal to L of (9).

6.  Role of M2  
    M2 is biased as a current source; its large ro2 isolates the node from ground so that the inductive impedance produced by M1 + RS is what the outside world “sees”.

Thus the combination of the gate resistor, the transistor’s gm and its gate capacitance acts as a gyrator that converts the capacitance Cgs into an equivalent inductor, making the output impedance of the circuit inductive over a useful mid-frequency range.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The exact output-impedance expression and the stated midband approximation correctly show inductive behavior, with the frequency range implying the required large gm1·RS. However, the claimed series-resistance term RS/gm1 is incorrect, and the physical explanation reverses the gate-voltage phase relationship.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The schematic is nothing more exotic than a one–transistor current mirror (M2 is the sensing/diode device, M1 is the output device) that drives a load-resistor, RD1.  
The mirror converts the input current Iin into a current n·Iin ( n = (W/L)1 ⁄ (W/L)2 ) and that current is then converted into a voltage across RD1, so the whole block behaves as a simple trans-impedance amplifier.

Assumptions used below  
• Long-channel MOSFETs, square-law model, channel-length-modulation neglected unless stated.  
• All devices are NMOS, body tied to 0 V.  
• M1 and M2 operate in saturation.  

1. Node X voltage (large-signal)  
The input current is forced into the diode-connected transistor M2, therefore

 Iin = ID2 = ½ kn (W/L)2 (Vx – VTH)²     (1)

⇒ Vx = VTH + √[ 2 Iin / (kn (W/L)2) ]    (2)

2. Mirror action  
The same gate voltage Vx appears on M1, so (still neglecting λ)

 ID1 = ½ kn (W/L)1 (Vx – VTH)²  
   = (W/L)1 ⁄ (W/L)2 · Iin ≜ n Iin      (3)

Thus the mirror ratio n = (W/L)1/(W/L)2 sets how much of the input current is reproduced by M1.

3. Output voltage (large-signal)  
KCL at node Vout gives

 (VDD – Vout)/RD1 = ID1 = n Iin       (4)

⇒ Vout = VDD – n Iin RD1         (5)

Equation (5) is the DC transfer characteristic.  
The polarity is inverting: a positive input current drives the output voltage downward.

4. Range of validity (M1 must stay in saturation)  
M1 remains in saturation as long as

 Vout ≥ VDSsat1 = Vx – VTH        (6)

Combining (2), (5) and (6) gives the maximum admissible input current

 Iin ≤ (VDD – (Vx – VTH)) / (n RD1) .   (7)

If that limit is exceeded M1 enters triode and the slope |dVout/dIin| rolls off.

5. Small-signal parameters  
• Trans-impedance (assuming λ ≈ 0)

 T ≡ ∂Vout/∂Iin ≈ –n RD1        (8)

With channel-length modulation,

 T ≈ –n RD1 / (1 + gds1 RD1) .  

• Input resistance

 Rin ≈ 1 /(gm2 + gds2) ≈ 1/gm2 (because M2 is diode-connected).  

Rin is usually only a few hundred ohms, so the stage behaves like a Norton-to-Thevenin converter.

• Output resistance

 Rout ≈ RD1 ∥ 1/gds1 .  

6. Qualitative operation summary  
1. Iin is forced through the diode-connected M2; the resulting VGS sets node X.  
2. The same VGS appears on M1, mirroring a current n Iin into the output node.  
3. RD1 turns that current into a voltage swing, giving Vout = VDD – n Iin RD1.  
4. The conversion gain is set by the mirror ratio n and the resistor RD1, while the largest current the circuit can handle without distortion is limited by the need to keep M1 in saturation.

In other words, the circuit is a very simple current-to-voltage converter whose gain is programmable with one resistor and the W/L ratio of two transistors.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer treats M2 as diode-connected and the circuit as a current mirror, missing the gate-of-M2 connection to Vout and the resulting positive-feedback loop, instability, and latching. It earns limited credit for recognizing a current input at X and the inverting M1/RD1 output behavior.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit description  
• M2 is an n-MOS transistor whose gate and drain are shorted (diode-connected).  
• M1 is another n-MOS whose gate is tied to the same node X.  
• The dc current source Iin forces a current into node X.  
• RD1 connects the drain of M1 (node Vout) to the supply VDD.

Thus M1 and M2 form the familiar two-transistor current mirror; RD1 merely turns the mirrored current into a voltage.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Large–signal (dc) analysis
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume both transistors are in saturation and neglect channel–length
modulation for the moment.  Let

β1 = μnCox (W/L)1      and      β2 = μnCox (W/L)2
VT  = threshold voltage (take the two devices identical).

(1) Current through the diode-connected device M2  
      Iin = ID2 = ½ β2 (VX – VT)²    ⇒ 
      VX = VT + √( 2Iin / β2 )

(2) Current through M1  
      ID1 = ½ β1 (VX – VT)²
           = ½ β1 · 2Iin / β2
           = (β1 / β2) Iin                … current-mirror law

(3) Output voltage  
      Vout = VDD – RD1 ID1
            = VDD – RD1 (β1/β2) Iin        …   dc transfer law

Hence the circuit converts the input current into an output voltage with a
large-signal transimpedance

      RT (dc) = ∂Vout/∂Iin = – RD1 (β1/β2) = – RD1 (W1/L1)/(W2/L2)

The minus sign simply means that a positive Iin lowers Vout.

Saturation conditions  
• M2 is always in saturation because VDS2 = VGS2.  
• M1 must satisfy Vout ≥ VX – VT.  Using the equations above this gives an
upper limit for Iin:  
      VDD – RD1(β1/β2)Iin  ≥  √(2Iin/β2) – VT

Choose RD1 and the geometry ratio β1/β2 so that the expected Iin range
respects this inequality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal analysis
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Small-signal parameters (both devices in saturation)

      gm1 = 2ID1 / (VX – VT) ,     gm2 = 2ID2 / (VX – VT)

Because ID1/ID2 = β1/β2 and VX – VT is common,

      gm1 / gm2 = ID1 / ID2 = β1 / β2

Node-X equation (gate currents ≈ 0)

      iin = gm2 vx            ⇒   vx = iin / gm2

Drain current of M1

      id1 = gm1 vx = gm1 / gm2 · iin

Small-signal output voltage

      vout = – id1 RD1 = – (gm1/gm2) RD1 · iin
            = – (β1/β2) RD1 · iin          (same result as dc)

Thus the incremental (ac) transimpedance equals the dc slope:

      ZT = vout / iin = – RD1 (β1/β2)

Other small-signal quantities  
• Input resistance  Rin = vx / iin = 1/gm2  (typically a few tens of Ω, a
  very low impedance – useful for photodiode or TIA front ends).  
• Output resistance  Rout ≈ RD1  ∥  ro1.  
• Voltage gain to node X (vx) is unity for M2 but the overall stage gain
  to Vout is the negative transimpedance above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Effect of channel-length modulation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
If λ ≠ 0,

      ID ≈ ½ β (VGS – VT)² (1 + λVDS)

The mirror ratio β1/β2 is still the dominant term but Vx appears inside the
(1 + λVDS) factors, so the current transfer and hence RT acquire a small
dependence on Vout.  Using long-channel devices for M1, M2 or adding a cascoded
mirror can minimise this error.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Summary of circuit function
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• M1–M2 constitute a current mirror; their W/L ratio sets a precise current
  gain  ID1 / Iin = β1/β2.  
• RD1 converts that mirrored current into a voltage, yielding a linear,
  negative transimpedance

          Vout = VDD – (W1/L1)/(W2/L2) · RD1 · Iin

• The small-signal gain is the same number:  –(W1/L1)/(W2/L2)·RD1.  
• The input node exhibits a very low resistance (≈1/gm2), so the circuit is
  well suited as a wide-band current-to-voltage converter or as the input
  stage of a photodiode pre-amplifier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies M1 as a common-source device driven by input current at X, but incorrectly treats M2 as diode-connected and therefore misses the positive-feedback loop and its instability.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit description  
• M2 is an n-MOS transistor whose gate and drain are tied together: it is diode–connected.  
• The dc input current Iin is forced into the node X, therefore it must flow through the channel of M2.  
• Node X is also the gate of the second transistor M1, so VGS1 = VGS2 = VX.  
• M1 is an n-MOS working as the output device of a current mirror; its drain is the output node that is loaded by the resistor RD1.  
• RD1 converts the drain current of M1 into the output voltage Vout.  
The whole block is therefore a MOS current mirror followed by a resistor; i.e. a current-to-voltage (trans-impedance) converter.

1. DC relations (long–channel, λ ≈ 0)  
β1 = k′(W/L)1 ,   β2 = k′(W/L)2 ,

Iin = ID2 = ½ β2 (VX – VTH)²               (Diode-connected M2 in saturation)     (1)

⇒ VX = VTH + √(2 Iin/β2)                                                   (2)

The same VGS is applied to M1, so

ID1 = ½ β1 (VX – VTH)² = (β1/β2) Iin ≜ k Iin                               (3)

with k = (W/L)1 /(W/L)2, the mirror ratio.

The output voltage is the supply minus the drop across RD1:

Vout = VDD – RD1 ID1 = VDD – k RD1 Iin                                    (4)

Thus the dc trans-impedance of the stage is

ZT = ∂Vout/∂Iin = –k RD1                                                    (5)

2. Operating-region constraints  
M2 is automatically in saturation because VDS2 = VGS2.  
For M1 we need VDS1 ≥ VGS1 – VTH :

Vout ≥ VX – VTH = √(2 Iin/β2)                                               (6)

Using (4) this gives the maximum input current that can be handled without leaving saturation:

VDD – k RD1 Iin(max) = √(2 Iin(max)/β2)                                    (7)

A designer chooses RD1 and the size ratio k so that (7) is satisfied for the largest expected Iin.

3. Small-signal behaviour  
Diode-connected M2 provides a large transconductance gm2 = √(2 β2 Iin).  
Hence the input impedance seen at node X is roughly 1/gm2 (typically only a few-tens of ohms for micro-amp bias currents), so the circuit behaves as a low-impedance current shunt that translates the current into a voltage at the drain of M1.  
Including channel-length modulation, the small-signal trans-impedance becomes

ZT,ac ≈ –k RD1 (1 ‖ ro1)/(1 + gm1 ro1)    ≈ –k RD1/(1 + k λ1 RD1)

(λ1 is the channel-length modulation coefficient of M1).

4. Summary of key points  
• Iin is mirrored by M1 with a gain set by the device-width ratio k.  
• That mirrored current flows through RD1, so Vout drops linearly with Iin.  
• ZT = –k RD1; the polarity is negative (larger input current → smaller Vout).  
• Input compliance (VX) is only a few hundred millivolts above ground, making the circuit attractive as a trans-impedance front-end for low-voltage current sources such as photodiodes.  
• To keep the mirror in saturation we must satisfy equation (7); otherwise M1 enters the triode region and the transfer becomes nonlinear.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer treats M2 as diode-connected and concludes the circuit is a current mirror, missing the actual positive-feedback loop and its instability or negative-input-resistance consequence. It does correctly identify X as the input node and M1’s gate, with M1 driving the resistor-loaded output, warranting minimal credit.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The schematic is nothing more than a shunt-feedback (trans-impedance) amplifier that has been implemented with only two n-MOS devices and two passive load resistors.  
• node S (the junction that receives the photocurrent Iin, RF and the source of M1) is the “summing node” of the TIA;  
• M1 and RD1 constitute the first gain stage;  
• M2 and RD2 constitute the second gain stage and furnish the output node;  
• RF closes the dc- and a-c-feedback loop that forces the input node to a (nearly) constant potential so that almost the whole sensed current is conveyed through RF and translated into a voltage at Vout.

1. DC operating point  

   – Vb fixes the quiescent gate-source voltage of M1 → the drain current ID1.  
   – RD1 determines the dc value of VX (drain of M1 / gate of M2) :  
          VX ≃ VDD – ID1·RD1.  
   – The current that flows in M2 is therefore ≃ ID1 (neglecting gate current).  
     Choosing RD2 so that Vout ≃ VDD/2 gives the largest signal swing:  
          RD2 ≃ (VDD/2) / ID2.  
   – Both transistors must obviously remain in saturation for the expected
     excursion of Iin.

2. Small-signal model (ro of the MOSFETs is ignored for clarity).  

   Symbols: gm1 , gm2 ­– trans-conductances; RD1 , RD2 , RF ­– resistors;  
             vs , vx , vout – small-signal voltages at nodes S, X and OUT.

   a. Current generated by M1  
         id1 = gm1·(vgs1)  with vgs1 = Vb (ac ground) – vs ⇒ id1 = –gm1·vs.
   b. Voltage at node X (drop across RD1)  
         vx = – RD1·id1 = gm1·RD1·vs (negative sign kept explicit).  
   c. Output voltage produced by M2  
         vout = – gm2·RD2·vx = – gm2·RD2·(–gm1·RD1·vs)  
               =  (+) gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2 · vs.                  (1)

   Open-loop gain (from node S to node OUT)  
         A ≡ vout / vs =  gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2.                 (2)

   d. KCL at the summing node S (ro → ∞)  
         Iin + (vs – vout)/RF  – gm1·vs = 0.               (3)

   Combine (1), (2) and (3) to obtain the closed-loop trans-impedance:

         ZT ≡ vout / Iin = – RF · (1 + A) / (1 + A + gm1·RF).  (4)

   If the loop-gain A ≫ 1 and gm1·RF ≪ A (the usual design target),

         ZT  ≈  – RF           (ideal TIA behaviour)          (5)
         Zin ≡ vs / Iin ≈ RF / (1 + A) ≈ RF /A  ≪ 1 Ω.        (6)

   Hence the input node is a low-impedance “virtual ground” and the sensed
   current is almost completely forced through RF, converting it into the
   output voltage –Iin·RF.

3. Stability and bandwidth  

   There are two high-impedance nodes (X and OUT) → a two-pole loop.  
   The small capacitor that is drawn between VX and the gate of M2 is a
   Miller-compensation (or “lead”) capacitor that moves the dominant pole to
   node X and gives a left-half-plane zero to cancel part of the phase shift
   of the second pole, insuring ≥60° phase margin.

   A rough bandwidth estimate:  fbw ≃ 1 / [2π (RD1·CX)] , with CX the total
   capacitance at node X (RD1 is chosen far larger than 1/gm1 so that this
   pole dominates).

4. Noise  

   – Thermal noise of RF (4kT/RF) and channel noise of M1 are the dominant
     contributors at the amplifier input.  
   – Noise coming from M2 and RD2 is divided by the loop-gain before it is
     referred to the input (20- to 30-dB relief for A ≳ 10-30).

5. Practical design hints  

   • Make gm1 high (large W/L or a small drain current) to minimise the input
     impedance and to raise the loop-gain.  
   • RD1 must be big enough to give a large gain gm1·RD1 but still leave VX
     high enough to keep M1 in saturation over the full Iin range.  
   • Choose RD2 from the desired output swing and ID2.  
   • Vb is placed roughly one VGS(th) + 0.2-0.3 V above the desired quiescent
     input-node voltage (often 0 V for a photodiode TIA).  
   • Verify that the two poles are well separated or add the shown
     compensating capacitor.

6. Summary of key formulas  

   Open-loop gain:                 A = gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2  
   Closed-loop trans-impedance:    Vout / Iin ≈ – RF (for A ≫1)  
   Input impedance:                Zin ≈ RF /A                (very small)  
   Loop-gain:                      LG ≈ A (since β = 1 through RF)  

The circuit therefore behaves exactly like an operational-amplifier-based
inverting TIA, but it is implemented with the minimum amount of active
devices (only two MOSFETs) and gains its accuracy from the large product
gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2 rather than from a high-performance op-amp.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies M1 as the gate-biased, source-input common-gate device, M2 as the X-driven common-source stage, and RF as feedback from Vout to the input node forming a shunt-feedback TIA, meeting the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
1. What the circuit is  
• The two MOSFETs and the two resistors form a two–stage voltage-amplifier.  
• The feedback resistor RF returns a portion of the output voltage to the input node, so the whole network is a shunt-shunt (current-voltage) feedback system.  
• Because the input variable is a current and the output variable is a voltage, the quantity of interest is the transimpedance   ZT = Vout / Iin.  
Typical use: front-end of a photodiode receiver, or any other application that needs a low-impedance node converting current to voltage.

2. DC bias (large-signal)  
M1 is biased as a common-gate device: its gate is held at the fixed voltage Vb, so its source node (the input node) sits roughly at  
    VS ≈ Vb – VGS1(on).  
The drain current of M1 flows through RD1, creating a dc voltage VX.  
The coupling capacitor insures that the dc bias of M2 is (almost) independent of M1, while ac variations at X are delivered to the gate of M2.  
M2 is a conventional common-source stage; its quiescent current flows through RD2 and sets the dc value of Vout.

(A very large resistor, or the bias network of the following stage, is usually placed in parallel with the capacitor so that the gate of M2 has a dc return; it has been omitted in the sketch for clarity.)

3. Small-signal model  
Let  

 vs  = small-signal voltage at the input node (source of M1)  
 vx  = small-signal voltage at node X (drain of M1, gate of M2)  
 vout = small-signal output voltage  
 gm1 , gm2 = transconductances of M1 and M2.  
Body effect and ro are neglected for clarity, but they can be added easily.

(i) Current through M1  
id1 = gm1 (vg1 − vs) = −gm1 vs                             (1)

(ii) Voltage at node X  
vx = −id1 RD1 = gm1 RD1 vs                                (2)

(iii) Output of M2  
id2 = gm2 vx  
vout = −id2 RD2 = −gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2 vs             (3)

Hence the (open-loop) voltage gain from the input node to the output node is  

 Av = vout / vs = −gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2.               (4)

4. Open-loop transimpedance (feedback open)  
Without RF, the input node sees the small impedance 1/gm1, so  

 vs = (1/gm1) Iin.  

Combining with (3) gives  

 ZOL = vout / Iin = −gm2 RD1 RD2.                (5)

5. Feedback relations  
The feedback current is  

 iRF = (vs − vout)/RF    (direction: from the input node toward the output, as indicated in the drawing)  

and the feedback factor that relates the fed-back current to the output voltage is  

 β = 1/RF.  

Loop-gain magnitude  
 T = β ZOL = −(gm2 RD1 RD2)/RF.                (6)

6. Closed-loop transimpedance  
Using the usual expression ZT = ZOL /(1 + βZOL):

 ZT = −gm2 RD1 RD2 /[1 − (gm2 RD1 RD2)/RF].    (7)

If |gm2 RD1 RD2| ≫ RF → |T| ≫ 1, the denominator is dominated by the second term and

 ZT ≈ RF    (with the expected sign inversion).           (8)

That is, the transimpedance accuracy is set by the passive element RF, while the active devices only have to provide sufficient loop gain.

7. Input impedance  
Rin = vs / Iin = ZT / Av  
  = RF /(1 + |T|) ≈ 1/(gm1)·(1/|T|) ≪ 1 Ω for large loop gain.  
A low Rin is precisely what a current source (e.g. photodiode) needs.

8. Bandwidth  
Because the loop gain multiplies the input node admittance by (1 + |T|), the −3 dB bandwidth roughly extends to  

 f3dB ≈ (1 + |T|) /[2π (CIN + CS1) / gm1]  

where CIN is the sensor capacitance and CS1 the parasitic capacitance at the source of M1.  
The dominant high-frequency poles are at node X (RD1 ‖ 1/gm2 with the capacitances of that node) and at the output node (RD2 with CLOAD).

9. Noise (spectral densities)  
Equivalent input-referred current noise:  

 Si,in ≈ 4kT γ gm1              (M1, dominant)  
     + 4kT/RF                (feedback resistor)  
     + 4kT γ gm2 /|T|²       (M2, suppressed by loop gain)  

so a large |T| both sets the gain and keeps the contribution of the second stage small.

10. Qualitative summary  
• M1 + RD1 create a transconductance stage whose low input impedance captures the external current.  
• The voltage at node X is ac-coupled to M2, which supplies high voltage gain.  
• The large gain around the shunt-shunt loop forces the input node to a virtual ground; consequently the closed-loop transimpedance is almost exactly RF, the input impedance is very small, and the bandwidth is widened by the loop-gain factor.  
• Proper choice of RD1, RD2, VB and the coupling capacitor value defines the bias point, maximises loop gain, and guarantees stability (phase margin).  
• Dominant noise comes from M1 and RF; the contribution of the second stage is suppressed by feedback.

In short, the circuit is a two-stage, gain-boosted transimpedance amplifier that provides precise gain ≈ RF, very low input impedance, wide bandwidth and low noise—an architecture well suited to high-speed or low-light photodetector interfaces.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, M2 as the common-source stage, and RF as feedback from the output to the input. But its signed loop equation uses 1 + βZOL with ZOL < 0, yielding a 1 − |T| denominator and an inconsistent transimpedance limit—effectively modeling the feedback with the wrong sign. This contradicts the required negative-feedback mechanism and caps the score at 2.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The schematic is nothing more than a two-stage, shunt–shunt-feedback MOS transimpedance amplifier (TIA).

• M1 (common–gate) performs the first current-to-voltage conversion:  
 IX = –gm1 VS flows into node X, and RD1 converts it into VX.

• A coupling capacitor ties VX to the gate of M2 (common-source).  
 For dc that capacitor is an open circuit, so M2 has no influence on the
 quiescent voltages; for signal frequencies above the high-pass corner it
 is effectively a short, so the voltage gain of M2 (≈ –gm2 RD2) is inserted
 in the feedback loop.

• RF returns the amplified signal to the input node, closing a shunt-shunt
 negative-feedback loop.  That loop simultaneously
 1) fixes the low-frequency transimpedance at –RF, so the gain is set with a
 single, precisely trimmable resistor, and  
 2) forces the input node close to ac ground, greatly reducing the input
 impedance and therefore increasing bandwidth.

Below is a concise dc and small–signal analysis (ro’s omitted for clarity;
add them in parallel with the RD’s if a more exact result is desired).

1.  dc operating point (Cc = open):
  ID1 = (VDD–VX)/RD1,  ID2 = (VDD–VOUT)/RD2  
 (The dc value of VS is set by the sum of IIN and the current through RF.)

2.  Small-signal equations (Cc = short):

 • Node X (drain of M1)  
  –gm1 VS + VX/RD1 = 0  ⇒ VX = gm1 RD1 VS (1)

 • Node OUT  
  VOUT/RD2 + gm2 VX + (VOUT – VS)/RF = 0  (2)

 • Input node (source of M1)  
  IIN = gm1 VS + (VS – VOUT)/RF         (3)

3.  Solve (1)–(3) for VOUT/IIN:

 Let A ≡ (1/RD2 + 1/RF) and B ≡ (1/RF – gm1 gm2 RD1)

 Zt ≡ VOUT/IIN = B RF /
        [(gm1 RF/RD2 + gm1) + (1/RD2) + gm1 gm2 RD1]  (4)

 If the loop-gain factor
  T ≃ gm1 gm2 RD1 RF / (1 + RF/RD2) ≫ 1

 then (4) collapses to the textbook result for a shunt-feedback TIA

  Zt ≈ –RF    (5)

 while the input impedance becomes

  ZIN = VS/IIN ≈ 1 / [gm1 (1 + gm2 RD1 + RF/RD2)]  (6)

 so the bandwidth is extended roughly by the multiplier  
 (1 + gm2 RD1 + RF/RD2) compared with a passive-RF TIA.

4.  Design hints

 • Choose gm1 from noise and head-room requirements.  
 • RD1 fixes VX ≃-gm1 RD1 VS; pick it so M1 never leaves saturation.  
 • Make gm2 RD2 as large as possible (voltage gain), respecting head-room.  
 • RF sets the wanted low-frequency transimpedance.  
 • Place the Cc high-pass corner at least one decade below the signal band
   so the feedback is active over the whole band but dc bias is untouched.

5.  Qualitative summary

 a. At dc the circuit is simply a resistor-feedback TIA (gain = –RF).  
 b. Above the Cc corner M2 amplifies the error at node X and drives it back
    to the input through RF; the loop makes the input look like a virtual
    ground, pushing the input pole and therefore the bandwidth upward.  
 c. The loop also cancels a large part of M1’s and M2’s channel noise,
    lowering the overall equivalent-input-noise current.

Hence the two-transistor / one-resistor network realises a wide-band, low-noise, well-defined-gain transimpedance amplifier well suited, for example, to photodiode front ends or wideband resistive-feedback LNAs.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, M2 as a common-source stage driven by X, and RF as negative feedback from Vout to the input node, forming a shunt-shunt TIA. The extra capacitor and DC/noise claims are not needed for full credit under the golden solution’s rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Circuit topology  
The two MOSFETs and the three current sources form what is usually called a
“regulated-cascode” (or “re-gained cascode”) trans-impedance stage:

• M1 is the input device.  
• M2 is diode-connected and, together with the load current source I1, works as a
  one-transistor voltage amplifier that regulates the voltage at the source of M1.  
• The lower current source (Ib) biases the branch; the external signal is a small
  differential current Iin that is injected into (or drawn from) the same node.  

Because the small-signal behaviour is what makes the cell attractive, the analysis is
done in two steps: dc operating point and ac (small-signal).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  dc bias (Iin = 0)

Let the bias current supplied by the lower source be Ib.  
With Iin = 0 the same current must flow through the whole branch, hence

ID1 = ID2 = I1 = Ib                                                    (1)

Pick Vb so that M1 is in saturation with the desired over-drive VOV1:

Vx  ≃ VOV1  = 2ID1 /k´(W/L)1                                    (2)

M2 is diode-connected, therefore Vy (Vout) is simply

Vout = Vy = Vx + VGS2(ID2)                                      (3)

Thus the quiescent voltages are fully determined by the two current
sources and the chosen transistor dimensions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Small-signal model

Small-signal parameters  
gm1 , ro1 – M1  
gm2 , ro2 – M2 (diode-connected)  
roL        – small-signal resistance of the load I1  
roB        – output resistance of the bias source (usually very large)

Node names  
vx – small-signal voltage at the source of M1 (input node)  
vy – small-signal voltage at Vout

KCL at node x (input):

iin + gm1(–vx) + (vx–vy)/ro2 + gm2(vy–vx) + vx/roB = 0        (4)

KCL at node y (output):

(vy–vx)/ro2 – gm2(vy–vx) + vy/roL = 0                         (5)

Because roB  ≫ 1/gm1 it can be dropped.  Solving (4) and (5) gives

Input resistance

Rin = vx / iin ≈ 1 / [ gm1 ( 1 + gm2(ro2||roL) ) ]            (6)

If gm2(ro2||roL) ≫ 1 (easily satisfied with sub-micron MOSFETs),

Rin ≈ 1 / ( gm1 gm2 roL )   →  a few ohms or even sub-ohm     (7)

Voltage gain from node x to Vout

Av = vy / vx ≈ –gm2 (ro2||roL)                                (8)

Output resistance seen at Vout (input port open):

Rout ≈ roL + (1+gm2ro2)ro2  ≈ roL (high)                      (9)

Trans-impedance (the quantity for which the cell is normally used)

ZT = vy / iin = Av · Rin ≈ – roL                              (10)

So, to first order, the current source resistance roL sets the current-to-voltage
conversion factor.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Intuitive explanation

1. The diode-connected M2 and the load current source form a high-gain
   inverting amplifier that senses vx and drives the gate of M2 (vy).
   The loop gain gm2(ro2||roL) forces vx to stay almost constant (“virtual
   ground”).  
2. Because vx hardly moves, essentially the whole signal current Iin is
   diverted through M1, reflected into the high-impedance node vy and turned
   into a voltage ΔVout = –Iin·roL.  
3. The extra loop gain multiplies the intrinsic input conductance gm1 of the
   transistor, giving the very small input impedance expressed in (7).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Design / practical notes

• To obtain a low Rin, design for gm2(ro2||roL) ≥ 20…50.  
• Head-room:   Vout,min ≈ Vx + VDS,sat(M2);  
                Vout,max ≈ VDD – VDS,sat(I1).  
• The feedback path involves only one dominant pole (node vy) so the loop is
  unconditionally stable, although a few pF of compensation can be added from
  vy to vx when large parasitics are present.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

The circuit is a regulated-cascode trans-impedance amplifier.  The local
feedback created by the diode-connected transistor M2 multiplies the
input transistor’s conductance, yielding

Rin ≈ 1/(gm1 gm2 roL)  – very low  
ZT  ≈ –roL             – high current-to-voltage gain

making the structure ideal as the front-end of photodiode receivers or any
other application that requires both a virtual ground input node and a large
output swing from a small input current.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes a low-input-resistance feedback effect, but misreads M2 as diode-connected and derives the wrong loop and transimpedance. In the actual circuit M2 is a PMOS feedback device driven by Vout, with transimpedance and output resistance on the order of 1/gm2.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The network is nothing but the two-MOS “regulated-cascode” (or “shunt-feedback common-gate”) transimpedance stage that is used in many low-noise photo-diode and current-mode front ends.

1.  Large-signal (dc) operating point  
    •  M1 is an n-channel device whose gate is held at the bias voltage Vb.  
       Because it is run in saturation, its source (node X, the input node) is
            VX ≃ Vb – VGS1(sat)                                  (1)  
       and therefore – except for process spread – is almost constant.  
    •  M2 is another n-channel transistor that is diode-connected (gate tied to
       drain).  It forms the “error amplifier’’ that tries to keep VD1 (= Vout)
       so high that VDS1 stays only a few 100 mV (≈VDS(sat)).  
    •  I1 is an ideal current source that pulls a constant current out of the
       output node.  In quiescence
            ID1,0 = I1 – IIN,0 .                                 (2)  
       So the static drain current of M1 is the difference between the bias
       current I1 and the dc component of the applied input current IIN.  
    •  As long as  
            0 < ID1 < I1  and  VDS1 ≥ VDS(sat)              (3)  
       both transistors remain in saturation and the stage is linear.  
       When |IIN| becomes too large, either M1 cuts off (Vout pulled to ground)
       or it is forced into triode (Vout ≈ VDD).

2.  Small-signal model  
    Denote  
        gx = gm1 + go1 + gm2 + go2 .  
    Writing KCL at the two nodes gives  
        Iin = gx vx – go1 vout                         (4a)  
      –gm1 vx + go1(vx – vout) = 0                    (4b)  
    Solving (4a, 4b) for vout / iin yields the incremental
    transimpedance of the stage
        RTIA = vout / iin
             = (1 / gm1) (1 + gm2 ro2 + ro1(gm2 + go2)) ≈ (1 / gm1)(1 + gm2 ro2) .   (5)

3.  What the equations mean  
    •  gm2 ro2 ≡ Afb is the open-loop gain of the little local feedback
      amplifier built by M2; for modern CMOS Afb ≈ 10…100.  
    •  Because of that feedback, the input impedance is driven down to
            Zin  ≈  1 / [ gm1(1 + Afb) ]   ≪  1 / gm1         (6)
      so the current source that is attached to the input sees an almost
      short circuit (a key requirement for photodiode TIAs).  
    •  Conversely, the output resistance is multiplied:
            Rout ≈ ro1 (1 + Afb)                              (7)
      which allows a large voltage swing from the rather small drain current.

4.  Range of admissible input current  
      –I1 < Iin < Imax  ,  with  
      Imax set by the point at which M1 leaves saturation:
         Imax ≃ (β1/2)(VDD – VDSsat2 – Vb + VT)^2 .            (8)

5.  Advantages and caveats  
    +  Only two MOSFETs and one bias current.  
    +  Very low input impedance, very wide bandwidth, practically no Miller
       effect.  
    –  Consumes a few hundred millivolts of head-room at the input node
       (VX ≈ Vb – Vth).  
    –  Output swing is limited by the diode-connected M2.  
    –  Handles only one polarity of input current unless duplicated with a
       complementary branch.

In short, the circuit converts the input current Iin into an output voltage

        Vout ≈ (1 / gm1)(1 + gm2 ro2) · Iin                     (9)

while pinning the input node within a few tens of millivolts, giving the
combination of low input impedance and high transimpedance gain that makes the regulated-cascode topology so popular.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly recognizes M1 as a common-gate NMOS and claims low input impedance, but misreads M2 as a diode-connected NMOS instead of the Vout-driven PMOS feedback device. Consequently, it misses the actual feedback path and gives incorrect transimpedance and output-resistance results.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
(The node between the two current sources is called X, the drain / gate of the p-MOS M2 and the drain of the n-MOS M1 is the output node Vout.)

1. Bias principle and large-signal behaviour  

• M2 is a diode-connected p-MOS whose source is tied to VDD.  
  The device therefore generates a fixed drop |VSD2|=|VSG2|,
  I2 = βP (|VSG2|–|VTP|)^2 /2 , that pulls the output node a
  threshold-plus-over-drive below the supply.

• I1 is a (nearly) ideal current sink connected in parallel with M2.
  At DC the two currents must add up to the drain current of M1 plus the external
  input current Iin:

        I1  =  ID1  +  ID2  +  Iin.                     (A-1)

• M1 is an n-MOS whose gate is biased at a constant voltage Vb.
  Its source node (X) therefore settles to  

        VX  =  Vb  –  VOV1 ,      VOV1 = √(2ID1/βN).    (A-2)

  If Vb is only a few hundred millivolts above ground, VX is
  forced to stay very close to ground.  This is the key idea: the circuit
  realises a “virtual ground” for the input current Iin while the voltage
  appearing at Vout can swing over several hundred millivolts.

2. Small-signal model  

Let  

      gm1 , ro1  – transconductance / output-resistance of M1  
      gm2 , ro2  – corresponding quantities of M2 (ro2 ‖1/gm2 = rD of the
                   diode-connected p-MOS)  
      rI         – small-signal output resistance of the current sink I1  
      vx , vo    – small-signal voltages of node X and Vout, respectively  
      iin        – small-signal input current.

Node X (input node)  
      iin = gm1(–vx) + gm2(vo – vx) + gds1(vo – vx) + gds2(–vx)      (B-1)

        ⇒  iin = (gm2 + gds1) vo – (gm1 + gm2 + gds1 + gds2) vx      (B-2)

Node Vout  
      Current to ground through the three elements tied to Vout must sum to zero:

      vo/rI  +  vo/ro2  +  gm2(vo – vx)  +  gds1(vo – vx)  = 0.       (B-3)

Collecting terms

      vo [(1/rI)+(1/ro2)+gm2+gds1]  –  vx(gm2+gds1) = 0.              (B-4)

3. Input impedance (looking into node X)

Solving (B-2) and (B-4) for vx/iin gives

      Zin ≡ vx / iin  =  1 /(gm1 + gm2) •
                         (1 + (gm2+gds1) rO) / (1 + rO G)            (C-1)

      with   rO = 1 /[(1/rI)+(1/ro2)]     and     G = gm2+gds1.  

If rO ≫ 1/gm1 and gm2 ≫ gds1 (usual in deep--sat), (C-1) degenerates to

      Zin  ≈  1 /(gm1 + gm2).                                        (C-2)

Because gm’s of practical MOSFETs are a few mS, Zin can be of the order of
10-50 Ω – the hallmark of a “regulated-cascode” transimpedance input stage.

4. Transimpedance gain  

From (B-2) and (C-2) one derives

      vo / iin  ≡  ZT  ≈  – 1 / gm1.                                 (C-3)

Hence the current-to-voltage conversion factor is set almost exclusively by
gm1, which in turn is fixed by the same bias current that establishes I1,
resulting in good process and temperature tracking.

5. Dynamic limits  

• Lower limit on Iin: ID1 must remain ≥ 0.  
• Upper limit on Iin: neither device may leave saturation:  
      Vout ≥ VDSsat1 + VX   and   Vout ≤ VDD – |VSDsat2|.  
• Output swing is finally restricted by the headroom needed by the current
  source I1 (VDSsat of its sink transistor).

6. Key points  

a) M2 + I1 produce a high-impedance node at Vout and, through the
   diode-connected p-MOS, feed back any change of Vout to the source node of
   M1; the feedback “regulates” VX and therefore realises a very low input
   impedance.  
b) The circuit converts input current into a voltage with gain ≈ 1/gm1 while
   isolating the input from the often large capacitance present at the output
   node.  
c) This topology is the classical regulated-cascode TIA widely used in optical
   receivers, ΔΣ modulators and current-steering DACs because of its
   simultaneously low Zin, reasonably high output swing and excellent
   bandwidth–power trade-off.

That completes the analysis of the circuit in the figure.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer misreads M2 as diode-connected at Vout; in the circuit, its gate is driven by Vout while its drain feeds the input node. This misses the actual feedback path and leads to incorrect input-impedance and transimpedance expressions, despite correctly identifying M1 as an NMOS and noting low input resistance.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No.  
A three-inverter ring oscillator does not depend on a tuned resonance; it oscillates simply because a transition that starts at one node is inverted three times and therefore comes back as a transition of the opposite polarity. For the oscillation to continue all that is required is that

1. a node voltage can change far enough to cross the switching point of the following inverter, and  
2. that change gets around the loop in a finite time.

Making the load capacitance CL larger only affects how long it takes an inverter to charge or discharge its output node through its finite on-resistance.  
Propagation delay per stage ≈ Ron·CL·ln( VDD /(VDD – VTH) ).  
Hence

oscillation period ≈ 2 · N · Ron · CL ,          (N = 3 stages)
oscillation frequency ≈ 1 /( 2N Ron CL ).

As CL is increased the time constant grows proportionally, so the frequency drops proportionally, but nothing in the loop gain or the phase condition is lost. With any finite CL the node will eventually reach the next inverter’s switching threshold and the edge will keep propagating. Only in the (unphysical) limit CL → ∞, or if leakage currents become comparable with the drive current, would the edge never move and the oscillation cease.

Therefore, for any practical (finite) value of capacitance the circuit still oscillates—it just does so more slowly.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that all three capacitors slow the transitions and lower the oscillation frequency, while finite capacitance does not stop oscillation. The delay-based justification satisfies the full-credit rule.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No.  
The three extra capacitors do not take the necessary conditions for oscillation away – they only make the loop slower.

1. What makes a ring oscillator start?
   • An odd number of inverting stages guarantees a ­180° phase shift (-540° in this case, which is the same as -180° modulo 360°).  
   • Each inverter has a very large small–signal gain at dc (|A| >> 1).  
   Therefore |Aβ| > 1 and the Barkhausen phase condition is already satisfied at ω ≈ 0, so the mid-rail operating point is unstable and any noise kicks the loop into oscillation.

2. What do the shunt capacitors do?  
   Putting a capacitor at each node simply adds a pole (low-pass behaviour) to every stage.  
        A(jω) = −A0 / (1 + jωRoutCL)  
   The dc gain A0 is unchanged, so |Aβ| is still > 1 at low frequency.  
   The added pole just moves the frequency at which |Aβ| falls to 1 downward:

        fosc ≈ 1 / (2 N τd)  with τd ≈ Rout CL  
        → fosc ∝ 1 / CL

   As CL is made larger, τd grows, the propagation delay grows, and the oscillation frequency drops in inverse proportion. For CL → ∞, fosc → 0, but for any finite CL the frequency is finite (just perhaps seconds or minutes per cycle instead of MHz).

3. When would it actually stop?  
   Only if the load were literally infinite (so the node voltage could never be moved) or if the inverter could not supply enough static current to move the voltage by at least one threshold in any reasonable time. With real but finite transistors and capacitors, the nodes will eventually charge and discharge, so the loop will still flip state and continue to oscillate.

Hence the circuit does not “fail to oscillate” merely because the capacitors are made very large; it simply oscillates more and more slowly.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that all three capacitors slow the ring and reduce its frequency, with a valid delay-based 1/CL trend. The low-frequency Barkhausen phase wording is imprecise, but the delay argument independently supports the answer and the golden solution’s full-credit rule applies.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No.  
A three-inverter ring oscillator will always meet the Barkhausen start-up
condition as long as every inverter still has more than unity small-signal
gain; making the load capacitances large only pushes the oscillation
frequency toward zero, it does not remove the possibility of oscillation.

Sketch of the argument

1. Small-signal model of one inverter  
  A(s)=−A0 /(1+s/ωp) with  
  A0 = g m r o  (dc gain, independent of CL)  
  ωp = 1/(ro CL)  (single pole set by the load capacitance).

2. Loop transfer function of the 3-stage ring  
  L(s)=A(s)^3 = (−A0)^3 /(1+s/ωp)^3.

3. Characteristic equation (1+L(s)=0) gives the three roots  
   s/ωp = A0 e j2πk/3  −1  (k = 0,1,2).

 • k = 0  ⇒  s0 = (A0 −1) ωp   (real, positive when A0>1)  
 • k = 1,2 ⇒  real part = −(1+A0 /2) ωp  < 0.

 Thus, for any A0 > 1 there is always one root with Re{s}>0, i.e. the loop is
unstable and will start to grow from noise.

4. Effect of enlarging CL  
 CL ↑  ⇒  ωp ↓  ⇒  all roots move toward the origin.  
 s0 becomes smaller in direct proportion to 1/CL, so the oscillation
frequency

  fosc ≈ Re{s0}/2π ≈ (A0 −1)/(2π ro CL)

   decreases as 1/CL, but never vanishes for any finite capacitance.

In practice

• If CL is made very large the period can become seconds, minutes or longer,
so the circuit may look “stuck’’ on an oscilloscope, but it is still an
oscillator.  
• Only in the limit CL → ∞ (or if the inverter gain drops below unity or the
devices cannot supply enough current to move the nodes at all) would
oscillation truly cease.

Therefore the circuit does not fail to oscillate merely because the three
capacitors are made arbitrarily large; it just oscillates more and more
slowly.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The conclusion and lower-frequency trend are correct. However, the small-signal derivation has a sign error: it predicts a real growing pole, not an oscillation, then treats that growth rate as the oscillation frequency; its A0 > 1 startup criterion is also incorrect. Thus the answer merits partial rather than full credit.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in the figure are doubled?

answer.text:
Each of the three capacitors is the load that, together with the output resistance of its inverter, determines  

 tPD ≃ k · RL · CL    (propagation delay per stage)

The oscillation frequency of a 3-stage ring therefore is  

 fOSC ≃ 1 / (6 · tPD) ∝ 1 / CL

Doubling all three capacitors

1. doubles every stage-delay,
2. so the period T doubles and the carrier frequency is cut in half.

How does this affect phase noise?

Thermal‐noise current of the transistors (4 kT γ gm) is essentially unchanged; it is turned into a
voltage at the output node by the impedance 1/s = RL ∥ 1/(s CL) and integrated during the switching transient:

 v n,rms ≈ √(Si ­· tSW) / CL  with tSW ≈ RL CL

 ⇒ v n,rms ∝ √(RL / CL)

The noise expressed as time jitter at a switching crossing is

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
The network is nothing more than a three-stage ring oscillator.  
With an odd number of inversions the loop already possesses the required 180° phase shift at dc, so the only other requirement for oscillation is that the magnitude of the loop gain exceed unity at some frequency.  

Placing the extra capacitance CL on one node

1. adds another low-frequency pole to the open-loop transfer function, and  
2. increases the delay through that particular inverter,  

but it does not change the dc (low–frequency) gain of the inverter, which is still very large (|A0| ≫ 1).  
Hence, even when CL is made very large the loop-gain magnitude is still well above one at ω = 0, and there will always be a (lower) frequency at which |Aβ| = 1 while the total phase shift is 180° + 360°k.  

What changes is the oscillation frequency:

fosc ≈ 1 / [2N (tp0 + Δtp)]  with Δtp ≅ Rout·CL

so fosc falls roughly in inverse proportion to CL.  
As CL → ∞ the period (and the start-up time) → ∞, i.e. the oscillator becomes arbitrarily slow, but the small-signal conditions for oscillation are still satisfied.

Practical limit: the circuit will appear “dead” only when CL is so large that the transistors’ finite static currents (or leakage) can no longer move the node past the switching threshold in any reasonable time. For any finite CL that the devices can eventually charge or discharge, the ring will still start and oscillate—just at a proportionally lower frequency.

answer.text:
Take the three–inverter ring oscillator in two steps.

1.  What sets the oscillation frequency  
   Each inverter has an effective output resistance R and is driving the
   capacitance that appears at its output.  
   The small-signal (first-order) transfer function of one stage is  

        A(s) = –A0 /(1+s R Ctot)          with   Ctot = Cint + CL

   (A0 is the low-frequency gain, Cint the intrinsic node capacitance and
   CL the external load that we have added).

   •  The – sign supplies the fundamental 180° phase shift of an inverter.  
   •  The pole at ωp = 1/(R Ctot) contributes an additional phase
      –tan-1(ω/ωp).  
   With three identical stages the total phase is

        Φloop(ω) = 3·(–π ­– tan-1(ωRCtot))

   The ring will oscillate at the frequency ω0 for which Φloop = –2π,
   i.e.

        3π + 3 tan-1(ω0 R Ctot) = 2π  →  tan-1(ω0 R Ctot) = π/3
        ⇒  ω0 = (π / 3) · 1/(R Ctot)

   Thus      f0 ≈ 0.17 / (R Ctot)  ∝ 1/CL.

   As CL is made larger the pole moves down, the required –60°/stage is
   obtained at a proportionally lower frequency, so the oscillation
   simply slows down.

2.  Is the start-up gain still high enough?  
   The loop-gain magnitude at ω0 is

        |Aloop(jω0)| = [ A0 / √(1+(ω0 RCtot)²) ]³
                      = [ A0 / √(1+(π/3)²) ]³ ≈ (0.69 A0)³

   A0 (the dc gain of a CMOS inverter) is independent of the external
   capacitive load, so |Aloop| is essentially the same no matter how big
   CL is.  As long as A0 ≳ 2 the cube of 0.69·A0 is well above unity and
   the oscillation starts and grows.

   Only two non-ideal effects can really stop it:

   •  CL → ∞ ⇒ ω0 → 0, the period becomes infinite, so in the limit of an
     infinite capacitance the circuit never changes state – but this is
     a mathematical limit, not a practical one.

   •  A load so large that the static leakage currents of the devices
     equal the charging / discharging current; then the node cannot be
     driven far enough from the switching threshold.  In ordinary CMOS
     logic this would require capacitances many orders of magnitude
     larger than those encountered on a chip.

Conclusion  
For any finite, practical value of CL the ring oscillator will still
oscillate; its frequency merely drops approximately in inverse
proportion to CL.  It “fails” only in the unphysical limit where CL
becomes infinite (or when leakage rather than dynamic current dominates
– again an impractical situation for normal values of CL).

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
A single-ended ring oscillator keeps oscillating as long as two conditions are satisfied  

1. Static loop gain magnitude > 1 and an odd number of inversions (180° phase shift).  
2. Each stage is able to move its output far enough past the switching threshold of the next stage that the latter will in turn switch.

The first condition is completely independent of the load capacitance that happens to be connected to one of the nodes; the dc (low-frequency) gain of a CMOS inverter is set by device transconductance/resistive output and does not change when a capacitor is hung on the output.

The capacitor only adds delay.  
For one stage the small-signal transfer function is approximately  

  Vout(s)/Vin(s) ≈ −A0 /(1 + sτ) ,  τ ≃ Ron · CL

so the pole moves toward the origin as CL grows.  
For an N-stage ring, the oscillation frequency is

  fosc ≈ 1/(2Nτ)

therefore fosc falls roughly in inverse proportion to CL. If CL is made “arbitrarily large”, τ becomes “arbitrarily large” and the frequency tends toward zero, but the Barkhausen phase-condition can still be satisfied, so mathematically the circuit still oscillates – it just does it very, very slowly.

What stops it in practice?

• Finite output current: the edges rise and fall at Iout/CL. If CL is so large that leakage currents (or any dc load) dominate before the node has been charged/discharged past the switching threshold, the stage will never complete the transition and oscillation will die.  
• Limited noise margin: with an enormous CL the transition is so slow that noise can disturb the state or the loop may get trapped in a metastable operating point.  
• Device leakage, charge sharing, and subthreshold conduction eventually balance the small charging currents for very slow edges and prevent rail-to-rail motion.

Hence:

Ideal, small-signal point of view – No, the oscillator does not fail; its frequency merely approaches zero as CL→∞.

Real hardware – Yes, beyond some finite CLmax (set by the maximum drive current of the inverters, leakage, and required noise margin) the ring will fail to start or will stall.

The key mechanism is that the dominant pole on the singly loaded node causes enough loop gain/phase roll-off for oscillation to fail.

1. 2× larger transconductance (g m ∝ W)  
2. 2× larger gate / diffusion capacitance (C ∝ W)  
3. About the same delay per stage (because t pd ≈ RC and R∝1/W , C∝W → RC ≈ const, so the oscillation frequency hardly moves).

Noise-voltage power at the switching node therefore falls:

S v  ≈  S i /(ω 2 C 2 )  ∝  W /(2W) 2   →   1/2

so the rms noise voltage is smaller by √2.

The edge slope dv/dt at the switching point is unchanged because I ∝ W and C ∝ W, therefore

dv/dt  ≈  I/C  ≈  (2I)/(2C)  =  const.

Timing uncertainty (jitter) is

σ t  ≈  σ v /(dv/dt)  →  σ t,new  =  σ t,old /√2 .

Phase-noise power is proportional to the square of the jitter, so the single-sideband phase-noise density improves by a factor of two, i.e. about

–3 dB.

Hence:

Doubling the widths lowers (improves) the phase noise by roughly 3 dB, while doubling transistor area and roughly doubling the dynamic (and short-circuit) power consumption.

1. Drain current ∝ W → doubles.  
2. Trans-conductance gm ∝ W → doubles.  
3. All node capacitances (gate-, diffusion-, wiring) ∝ W → double.

Because the delay of a CMOS inverter is roughly

tpd ≈ CL VDD / IDsat ,

and both CL and IDsat scale in the same way (both ∝ W), the stage delay – and therefore the oscillation frequency – stays practically unchanged.

White phase-noise / jitter of a ring oscillator can be written (one of several equivalent forms)

L(Δf) ≈ (4 kT γ / gm VSW²) (fosc / Δf)²

or, in time domain,

σt² ≈ (4 kT γ gm / ω² C²) / (dV/dt)² ,

with dV/dt = ID / C.

Plugging in the W-dependences:

• gm → 2 gm  
• C  → 2 C     → (dV/dt) unchanged  
⇒ Sν (and hence σt², L) scale as gm / C² ∝ W / W² = 1/W.

σt ² ≈ ( kT · C ) / I²         →   L{Δf}  ∝ σt ²

where

1. Current capability  
   gm and the dynamic switching current, I, are proportional to W, so I → 2 I.

2. Node capacitance  
   The gate- and diffusion capacitances are also proportional to W, so C → 2 C.

3. Transition slope  
   dv/dt = I / C ≈ (2 I)/(2 C) = I / C → essentially unchanged, so the oscillation frequency hardly moves.

4. Thermal-noise voltage on the node  
   For a capacitor driven by a noisy conductance the mean-square noise voltage is ≈ kT/C, so
   v n,rms ² → kT /(2 C) = ½·v n,rms ².

5. Time (phase) fluctuation  
   σt ² = v n,rms ² /(dv/dt)² ∝ (kT/C)/(dv/dt)² ∝ (kT)/(W) ,

   therefore with W doubled:  σt ² → ½·σt ²  
   (σt,rms is reduced by √2).

• Oscillation frequency is almost the same.

answers.question: Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in the figure.

answer.text:
For a CMOS ring oscillator the supply current that is drawn is almost completely dynamic.

1. Energy needed for one switching event  
 Each inverter charges and discharges its load capacitance CL once every period.  
 Energy per transition E = CL VDD²

2. Average power of an N-stage ring oscillator oscillating at the frequency f  
 Every period each of the N stages switches once, so  

 P = N CL VDD² f

3. Average supply current  
 I = P ⁄ VDD = N CL VDD f                                                 (1)

4. Frequency versus supply voltage  
 The delay of an inverter is approximately  

 tp ≈ k  VDD ⁄ (VDD – VTH)²

 The oscillation period is 2 N tp, therefore  

 f = 1 ⁄ (2 N tp) ≈ (VDD – VTH)² ⁄ (2 N k VDD)

5. Insert f from above into (1)

 I = N CL VDD · (VDD – VTH)² ⁄ (2 N k VDD) = CL (VDD – VTH)² ⁄ (2 k)

 Notice that VDD has canceled out – the average current is (in this simple model) independent of the supply voltage.

6. Small-signal conductance seen from the supply node  

 gx = dI ⁄ dVDD = 0

7. Small-signal resistance  

 Rx = 1 ⁄ gx → ∞

So, to a small-signal (low-frequency) perturbation the ring oscillator looks like an open circuit; the resistance seen looking into its VDD node is essentially infinite.

answer.text:
Let  

VDD = dc supply voltage  
VT  = threshold voltage of the MOS devices  
N   = number of stages in the ring ( N = 3 in the figure )  
CL  = total capacitance that one inverter output drives  
β   = µCox(W/L) of the conducting transistor (the p-device during a 0→1
      transition, the n-device during a 1→0 transition)  
k   ≈ 1 … 1.5 is the constant that appears in the usual delay expression  
( tp ≈ k CL VDD / ION ).

1. Average supply current of the oscillator  

Every node performs one 0→1 and one 1→0 transition each period.  
During a 0→1 transition the supply delivers the charge  

     Q = CL VDD   →   energy Esw = ½ CL VDD².

Therefore the energy drawn from the supply in one period is  

     Ecycle = N · CL VDD² .                                (1)

With oscillation frequency f, the average power is P = Ecycle f and the
average supply current is  

     IDD = P / VDD = N CL VDD f .                          (2)

2. The oscillation frequency as a function of VDD  

For a CMOS inverter

     tp ≈ k CL VDD / ION ,               ION = β (VDD – VT)².     (3)

Hence  

     f = 1/(2N tp) = β (VDD – VT)² /( 2N k CL VDD ).       (4)

3. IDD versus VDD  

Insert (4) into (2):

     IDD(VDD) = N CL VDD · β (VDD – VT)² /( 2N k CL VDD )
              = β (VDD – VT)² /( 2k ).                     (5)

Notice that the load capacitance and the number of stages have dropped
out of the result.

4. Small-signal resistance seen into the supply pin  

     Rx = ( dIDD / dVDD )⁻¹ .

From (5)

     dIDD / dVDD = β (VDD – VT) / k ,

so

     Rx = k / [ β (VDD – VT) ].                            (6)

5. Numerical feel  

For a typical β ≈ 3×10⁻⁴ A/V², VDD – VT ≈ 0.8 V and k ≈ 1,

     Rx ≈ 1 / (3×10⁻⁴ × 0.8) ≈ 4 kΩ.

Thus the 3-stage CMOS ring oscillator presents only a few-kilohm
(positive) small-signal resistance to its supply node, given
approximately by

     Rx ≈ 1 / [ (µ Cox W/L) (VDD – VT) ].

   is  
  Rinst ≈ 1/gmn + 1/gmp.

   RX(t) is practically infinite.

 • most of the time it is very large (≈ ∞),  
 • for short intervals it drops to ≈ 1/gmn + 1/gmp.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
M7 is the ‘tail-switch’ of the sense amplifier.  
When the clock (CK) goes high it is supposed to behave like an ideal dc current source – i.e. it should present a very high small-signal impedance to the common-source node of the differential pair M1–M2.

Small-signal impedance of M7  
Looking into the drain of M7 we see  

    rtail ≈ 1 / gm7                 (if ro7 ≫ 1/gm7)

gm7 = 2ID /(VGS – VTH) ∝ W7

So, if we increase the width W7 :

1. The drain current ID7 increases.  
2. gm7 increases roughly in proportion to W7.  
3. The tail impedance rtail (= 1/gm7) therefore decreases.

Influence on the initial (t = 0+) voltage gain  
The differential-mode small-signal gain of the latch just after it is enabled can be written (simplified) as

    Av0 ≈ (gm1 ⋅ roeff) / (1 + gm1 ⋅ rtail /2)

where roeff denotes the effective output resistance seen at the output nodes (including the cross-coupled devices). A lower tail resistance rtail (produced by a larger gm7) appears in the denominator and behaves like source-degeneration for the differential pair. Consequently:

• As W7 (and therefore gm7) is increased, rtail decreases.  
• The term 1 + gm1 rtail/2 becomes larger.  
• The initial small-signal voltage gain Av0 becomes smaller.

In other words, making M7 wider turns the “current source” into a stiffer path to ground, shunting some of the differential signal current and reducing the instantaneous voltage gain with which regeneration starts. Therefore

  Increasing the width of M7 lowers the initial voltage gain of the latch (and, in turn, tends to lengthen the regeneration time).

But its main explanation is incorrect: looking into M7's drain is not generally 1/gm7, and the stated gain equation predicts that reducing rtail increases gain, contradicting the prose. answers.question: In the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain if we increase the capacitance at nodes P and Q?

answer.text:
During the very first instants after the clock turns-on, the pair M1–M2 works only as a transconductor and the drains P and Q are loaded almost exclusively by the parasitic (and any intentional) capacitances present at those two nodes.  
The small-signal chain is therefore

ΔVin  →  ΔI = gm ΔVin  →  charge / discharge C P,Q  →  ΔVPQ

For a short time interval Δt

ΔVPQ = (ΔI Δt)/CPQ = (gm ΔVin Δt)/CPQ

so the instantaneous (or “initial”) voltage gain of the input pair is

Av,init = ΔVPQ / ΔVin = (gm Δt)/CPQ ∝ 1/CPQ.

Hence, if the capacitance seen at P and Q is increased,

1. The same differential current has to charge (or discharge) a larger C.  
2. The slope dV/dt at those nodes is reduced.  
3. Consequently the initial differential voltage that appears at P and Q for a given ΔVin is smaller, i.e. the initial voltage gain is lowered.  

The cross-coupled latch (M3–M6) will still drive the outputs to the rails, but it will start its positive-feedback action later, so the overall decision time becomes longer. In short:

Increasing the capacitance at nodes P and Q reduces the initial small-signal voltage gain (and therefore slows the sense-amplifier/comparator).

answers.question: If we increase the widths of M5 and M6 in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade?

answer.text:
M5 and M6 are the cross-coupled p-channel devices that, together with M3 and M4, form the regenerative latch.  
During the evaluate phase the small voltage difference that the input pair (M1/M2) has created at the internal nodes X and Y is exponentially amplified by the positive-feedback loop that contains the gm’s of M3-M6.  
The small-signal regeneration time constant can be written approximately as  

  τ ≈ Cnode /(gm3 + gm4 + gm5 + gm6)  

where Cnode is the total capacitance seen at the X (or Y) node.

1. gm5 and gm6 increase roughly in proportion to W/L.  
2. The diffusion, junction and gate-to-node capacitances of M5 and M6 also grow with W, so Cnode becomes larger.  
3. For a given bias current the increase in gm is usually faster than the increase in the effective capacitance, so gm/C improves and τ becomes smaller.  
4. A smaller τ means the latch regenerates more quickly, i.e. the decision delay is reduced.

Therefore, up to a point, widening M5 and M6 makes the latch (and hence the comparator) faster.

Limits and trade-offs  
• Beyond some width the extra parasitic capacitance begins to dominate and the speed benefit saturates or can even reverse.  
• Larger devices load the clock (through S3/S4) and the pre-charge paths, consume more area, and may demand a larger tail current (M7) to keep them in strong inversion.  

So, starting from minimum-sized devices an increase in the widths of M5 and M6 generally improves speed, but there is an optimum size beyond which the added capacitance degrades performance.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
Making the CK / CK̅-driven devices wider does not make the latch faster – it usually makes it slower.

Why  

1. What you gain  
   • Wider devices have a lower on-resistance, so the channel they provide when they are ON is “stronger”.

2. What you pay for  
   • Gate capacitance on the clock nets (Cg ∝ W) increases, so the clock driver has to charge/discharge a larger load every cycle.  
   • Diffusion / junction capacitances at the internal nodes X and Y (Cdj ∝ W) also increase, so every transition at those nodes has a larger capacitive load.  
   • Those extra capacitances are charged or discharged by other transistors, not by the device whose width you just increased; therefore the extra C is not compensated by the higher drive of that device.

3. Net effect  
   In a first-order delay expression τ ≈ C/I, both C and I of the clocked device grow roughly in proportion to W, so for the path that actually goes through that device the RC product hardly improves.  
   All the *additional* capacitances, however, must be driven by other devices whose current did **not** increase. Hence the overall delay of the latch increases, while the clock itself is also slowed and its power rises.

Therefore, after the clocked devices are large enough to keep their on-resistance from dominating the delay, making them wider gives no speed benefit and generally degrades the operating speed of the circuit. The optimum sizing for the CK / CK̅ transistors is normally the minimum (or near-minimum) width that meets noise-margin and leakage requirements.

answers.question: Does the structure in the figure provide quadrature outputs?

answer.text:
Yes – if the clock CK has a 50 % duty-cycle the cell delivers four signals that are spaced by 90 ° (i.e. it provides “quadrature” outputs).

Why:  
• The schematic is a master-slave (C²MOS / dynamic) toggle flip-flop.  
• Because the Q output (node Z, coming from the slave latch) is fed back to the D input of the master (“toggle” configuration), the flip-flop divides the input-clock frequency by two.  
• The master latch (node X) is transparent while CK = 1 and latches when CK goes low; the slave latch (node Y → Z) is transparent while CK = 0 and latches when CK goes high.  
• Therefore node X can change only during the high half-cycle of CK and node Y/Z can change only during the low half-cycle.  
• With a 50 %-duty-cycle clock the time between a transition on X and the next transition on Y (or Z) is exactly half a CK period, which is one quarter of the period of the divided-by-2 signal. One quarter-period corresponds to 90 ° of electrical phase.

Hence  
 X and Z (or X and Y) are 90 ° apart,  
 Z and Z̅ are 180 ° apart,  
and the four nodes {X, X̅, Z, Z̅} give the usual I / Ī / Q / Q̅ set used for quadrature LO generation. (If the clock duty cycle deviates from 50 %, the phase spacing will deviate from the ideal 90 °.)

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the divide-by-two and ideal half-period spacing that gives nominal quadrature, but presents it as exact and omits both key nonidealities: Inv3 delay and unequal latch loading.

• When CK goes low (͞CK high) the “slave” latch on the right (node Y → Z after Inv3) becomes transparent and toggles.  

Thus node X toggles one half-cycle of the input clock earlier than node Z.  
Because the output frequency is one-half of the input frequency, that half-cycle of the input corresponds to one quarter of the output period – i.e. 90°.  

So the two slow-frequency nodes are  
 I-phase : Z (or Y after the restoring inverter)  
 Q-phase : X  

Their complements, available on the opposite sides of the cross-coupled pair, give Ī and Q̄, providing the full set of four 90°-spaced (“quadrature”) outputs. In practice the exact 90° spacing is limited only by the small delay mismatch between the two latches.
