answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
Not really – after a very small point-of-diminishing-return the circuit actually becomes slower when the two clock-controlled devices (the pre-charge device at the top and the evaluation / tail device at the bottom) are made wider.

Reasoning

1. What the clocked devices drive  
   • Their drains/sources are connected only to the two internal dynamic nodes of the latch; the load on those nodes is dominated by the diffusion capacitance of the clocked devices themselves.  
   • When you double the width, the on-resistance falls by ≈2, but the diffusion (and gate-to-clock) capacitances rise by ≈2 as well.  
   →  RC ≈ (1/W) · (kW) ≈ constant, so the time constant seen by the data nodes hardly changes.

2. What they load  
   • The gates of the clocked transistors are driven by the global CK / ĆK lines.  
   • Making them wider increases the gate capacitance that the clock network has to charge and discharge every cycle.  
   →  Clock edges become slower and the win you might have had on the internal nodes is more than lost on the clock path.

3. Net result  
   • Little or no improvement in the internal pre-charge/evaluation time.  
   • Noticeable degradation of the clock slew and therefore of the overall cycle time.  
   • More dynamic power and area.

Hence, beyond the minimum (or a very moderate) size, enlarging the clock-controlled transistors does not speed the latch up; it actually worsens the maximum operating frequency. In practice they are kept close to minimum size and the regenerating (cross-coupled) devices, not the clocked ones, are the transistors that are upsized if higher speed is needed.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It predicts little or no benefit and then slower operation, contrary to the result that wider clocked devices improve speed by lowering series resistance with little data-path loading. It also misses charge sharing as the swing-limiting effect.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
Making the two devices that are driven by CK and  CK̅ “fatter’’ is usually a bad trade-off for delay.

1. Inside the gate  
   – When the device is ON its resistance falls roughly as 1/W.  
   – At the same time its diffusion/overlap capacitance that is connected to the very same internal node rises in direct proportion to W.  
   – Hence the RC product that determines how fast that node can be charged or discharged stays almost constant. So the data path itself does not become faster.

2. Effect on the clock network  
   – The gate capacitance of the larger transistors is also proportional to W, so the clock line has to drive a larger capacitive load.  
   – A slower clock edge means the pre-charge/evaluate phases start later and finish later, increasing the cycle time.

3. Extra side effects  
   – Larger devices inject more charge when they turn off and aggravate charge-sharing and noise problems.  
   – The following stages see a larger diffusion capacitance and therefore switch more slowly.

Because they give essentially no improvement in the internal RC delay while they directly slow down the clock and add parasitics, the overall speed degrades (or at best stays the same) when you increase the widths of the clocked transistors. In practice they are kept at minimum size unless there is a special reason (e.g., leakage, matching) to enlarge them.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer reaches the opposite conclusion: widening the clocked devices improves speed by reducing series resistance while adding little loading to the data path or outputs. It mentions charge sharing, but incorrectly treats it and clock loading as reasons speed degrades.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
What you see is a “broken-ring” made with three CMOS inverters and two single-MOS transmission gates that are driven by complementary phases of the same clock.  
In words, it is nothing more than a 1-bit register (a master-slave latch pair); with the output hard-wired back to the input it automatically becomes a T- (toggle) flip-flop, i.e. a divide-by-2.  

Step-by-step behaviour

1. CK = 1 (“sampling” phase)
   • The left-hand switch is ON, the right-hand switch (CK̅) is OFF.  
   • The ring is cut open after Inv1, so the output of the last inverter (present state Q) is copied to the input of Inv1.  
   • The value appearing on the node after Inv1 (call it X) is therefore X = ¬Q.  
   • Nothing can yet propagate past the open right-hand switch, so the external output Q does not change.

2. CK goes low → 0 (“transfer” phase)
   • The left switch turns OFF, the right switch turns ON, reconnecting the loop but now **after** an extra inversion (Inv1).  
   • X is handed to the second inverter, travels through the remaining two inverters and emerges at the output as Qnew = ¬X = ¬(¬Q) = ¬Q.  
   • Hence the output toggles exactly once per clock period; on every falling edge the stored state is complemented.

Why three inverters?
– An odd number is required so that the closed loop is bistable (only 0 or 1 are stable).  
– Two extra inverters after Inv1 give the loop enough delay so that the two non-overlapping phases (CK / CK̅) never connect two low-impedance drivers together and so that the output duty-cycle is close to 50 %.

Static or dynamic?
The node at the input of Inv1 is a dynamic (capacitive) node when CK = 0, so the cell will eventually lose its state if the clock is stopped for a long time. In normal operation, however, the charge is refreshed every half-cycle, so it behaves like a perfectly good divider.

In summary
• Clock-high: sample the present output into the “master” side.  
• Clock-low : close the ring through the “slave” side, forcing the output to the opposite level.  
• Result: a very compact, low-power divide-by-2 (toggle flip-flop) that needs only three inverters, two switches and one distributed clock phase.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies a dynamic master-slave latch arrangement whose feedback makes it a divide-by-two. The detailed inverter-path claims are secondary under the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
What you are looking at is nothing more exotic than a clocked latch whose output has been hard-wired back to its own input.  
Because the two transmission gates are driven by complementary phases of the clock (CK and  CK̅ ), the latch behaves as a master–slave (level-sensitive) flip-flop; feeding the output back to its input makes it a T- (toggle-) flip-flop, i.e. a divide-by-2 circuit.

Step–by–step operation

Nomenclature  
TG1 … first transmission gate, controlled by CK  
TG2 … second transmission gate, controlled by  CK̅   
M  … node at the output of Inv1 (master node)  
Q  … node at the output of Inv3 (latch output)

1. CK = 1 (high) - “transparent” master  
   • TG1 is ON, TG2 is OFF.  
   • Q is fed straight to the input of Inv1, therefore  
        M = ¬Q.  
   • Q itself is isolated and keeps its previous value (is stored in the slave section).

2. CK = 0 (low) - “transparent” slave  
   • TG1 is OFF, TG2 is ON.  
   • The value that had been generated on node M is now allowed to propagate
     through Inv2 and Inv3, so  
        Qnew = M = ¬Qold.  
   • Thus the content of the latch is inverted once every full clock cycle.

Because one complete inversion of Q takes two opposite levels of CK, the
output toggles at exactly half the clock frequency:

        fQ = fCK / 2      (or TQ = 2 · TCK)

Hence the circuit is a static CMOS divide-by-2 (toggle) flip-flop implemented
with

   – 3 inverters (Inv1-Inv3) providing the required odd number of inversions for
     feedback stability, and  
   – 2 non-overlapping clocked transmission gates that alternately open and
     close the feedback path, forming the familiar master–slave latch structure.

Timing requirements

• The total delay of the three inverters plus the two transmission gates must
  be smaller than one half clock period so that all internal nodes settle before
  the next clock phase.  
• CK and  CK̅  must have a small but finite non-overlap interval to prevent both
  TGs from being ON simultaneously (which would short M to Q) yet must not
  leave both gates OFF for so long that the floating node M loses its charge.

Practical use

Such divide-by-2 cells are the basic building blocks of ripple counters,
prescalers in PLLs, clock generators, etc.  With different wiring (breaking the
feedback and supplying an external “D” input) the same schematic becomes the
well-known gated D latch / master–slave D flip-flop.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the feedback arrangement as a divide-by-two and explains the alternating sample/hold and toggling behavior. However, calling it a static CMOS divider conflicts with the essential dynamic-latch operation, including charge stored on floating nodes.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
The drawing is a small, fully-static C²MOS (Complementary-Clocked MOS) latch pair in which the output of the second latch is fed back to the input of the first through an odd number of inversions.  
Label the nodes as shown below

       CK        CK̅
 Q ──TG1──► A ─I1─► B ─TG2──► C ─I2─► D ─I3─► Q
 │____________________________________________│

TG1 : transmission gate driven by CK  
TG2 : transmission gate driven by CK̅  
I1, I2, I3 : static CMOS inverters

How it works

1. CK = 1 (high)  
   • TG1 is ON, TG2 is OFF → the left (master) latch is transparent, the right
     (slave) latch is closed.  
   • Node A = Q, therefore B = ¬Q (after I1).  
   • Because TG2 is open, the slave keeps its previous value Q.  
   • The complement of the present output has now been prepared at node B.

2. CK = 0 (low)  
   • TG1 is OFF, TG2 is ON → the master latch holds its value (¬Q), the slave
     latch becomes transparent.  
   • Node B is transferred through TG2 to C, and through I2-I3 the same value
     reaches the output: Qnew = I3(I2(C)) = I3(I2(¬Qold)) = ¬Qold.  
   • Thus the output toggles.

Because only one of the two latches is transparent at any given time, no direct
path exists from Q back to itself while it is changing, so the circuit is
well-behaved and completely static: if the clock stops, the state that was last
stored is preserved indefinitely.

What the circuit is

• A master-slave edge-triggered flip-flop realised with transmission gates and
  inverters (a classical C²MOS register).  
• With the (odd-inversion) feedback shown, it becomes a T-flip-flop: the output
  complements itself every time the clock makes a full cycle, i.e. it divides
  the clock frequency by two and produces a 50 % duty-cycle square wave.

Key points

1. TG1 and TG2 are driven by complementary phases of the same clock, so
   overlap-free (non-over-lapping) clocks are not required.  
2. Only three inverters and one transmission gate lie in the critical data
   path of any phase, so the cell can operate at very high speed.  
3. The scheme is purely static: it consumes no power when the clock is idle and
   stores its value without refresh.

Hence, the arrangement in the figure is a static, transmission-gate-based
divide-by-two (toggle) flip-flop built from a pair of complementary-clocked
latches.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly concludes that feedback makes the output divide the clock by two, but it misidentifies the circuit as fully static and claims its state is preserved indefinitely. The figure’s essential implementation is a dynamic-latch divider, where stored charge and leakage matter.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The red gate is not an additional stage in the loop – it is the same kind of inverter as Inv1 but wired in parallel with it:

• Its input is tied to the same node that feeds Inv1.  
• Its output is shorted to the output of Inv1.  

Electrically this is equivalent to making the first stage of the ring oscillator twice as wide.

What changes?

1. Delay of the first stage  
   – Two identical pull-up/pull-down devices in parallel give one-half of the effective on-resistance, so the intrinsic delay of that stage is roughly cut in half.

2. Load seen by the preceding stage  
   – The input capacitance doubles, so the node that drives CK now has to charge/discharge twice the gate-capacitance. That stretches the delay of the preceding stage.

3. Net effect on the oscillation period  
   – In practice the reduction in the first-stage delay is usually larger than the increase in the previous-stage delay, so the loop oscillates a little faster. (How much faster depends on sizing; if the preceding stage is already weak the gain can disappear or even turn into a loss.)

4. Power and area  
   – About twice the silicon area for that stage and roughly twice the dynamic power associated with switching it (because two gate/input caps and two output nodes are being charged and discharged every cycle).

5. Reliability/glitch behaviour  
   – Because both inverters have the same input, their outputs are always intended to be the same logic level. During a transition they may not switch at exactly the same instant, so for a few picoseconds they can fight each other, giving a small increase in short-circuit current, but this is normally harmless.

In short, the red inverter is a straightforward way of strengthening (widening) the first stage. It can increase the ring-oscillator frequency or shorten a critical path at the cost of more load on the previous node, higher power and larger area.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer misidentifies the red inverter as a parallel, output-shorted copy of Inv1. It misses the feedforward path that bypasses part of the first latch, as well as the low-frequency drawback that raises the minimum usable clock frequency.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The red inverter is the so-called keeper (or feedback) inverter that is normally added to a dynamic / domino gate.

What it does  
1. Noise-/leakage hold:  
   • During the pre-charge phase (CK = 0, CK-bar = 1) the dynamic node in front of Inv1 is charged to VDD.  
   • When the clock stays low, the node would otherwise be a high-impedance capacitor and could be disturbed by leakage, charge sharing, α-particle hits, etc.  
   • The keeper senses the high level at the output of Inv1 and feeds a weak pull-up back to the dynamic node, so the node is “latched” high and cannot drift.

2. Turns the domino gate into a pseudo-static gate:  
   Even if the circuit is stopped for an arbitrarily long time in the evaluation phase, the output will not lose its state thanks to the keeper.

How it affects performance

Delay:  
• When the evaluation network wants to discharge the dynamic node (logic 1 → 0 transition) it first has to fight the keeper’s pull-up device.  
• This contention current and the extra gate/drain capacitance of the keeper slow the falling transition of the dynamic node, so the high-to-low delay of the stage increases.  
• Rising transitions (0 → 1) are almost unaffected because the pre-charge PMOS overrides the keeper.

Power:  
• Extra short-circuit (crowbar) current flows for a few hundred picoseconds each time the dynamic node is pulled low because both the keeper PMOS and the evaluation NMOS stack are momentarily ON.  
• Additional dynamic power is consumed to charge / discharge the keeper’s gate capacitance every clock cycle.

Sizing trade-off  
• A strong keeper gives excellent noise immunity but produces large contention and therefore large delay and power.  
• A very weak keeper minimises delay/power but may not be able to hold the node reliably at low clock frequencies or under noise.  
• In practice the keeper is made just strong enough (W/L ≈ 1/4-1/10 of the evaluation pull-down strength).

In short:  
The red inverter greatly improves robustness by keeping the pre-charged node from floating, but it slows down the evaluation transition and adds some static/dynamic power. The designer sizes it to balance speed and noise immunity.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer misidentifies the red inverter as a domino keeper. It misses the feedforward bypass that improves high-speed operation and the unclocked branch’s low-frequency drawback, instead describing an unrelated dynamic-gate mechanism.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The red gate is nothing more than a “keeper” (or feedback) inverter.  
Together with the clock-controlled inverter Inv1 it forms a two-inverter
loop, i.e. a small static latch.  
Its presence changes the circuit from a purely dynamic latch (or
sample-and-hold) into a static one that can keep its logic level for an
unlimited time.

What it gives you  
1. Static data retention – the stored value does not leak away when CK is
   low because the cross-coupled pair regenerates the level.  
2. Full noise margin – the node in front of Inv1 is driven to a legal rail
   voltage instead of being left floating.  
3. Practically zero hold-time requirement – as soon as CK falls, the keeper
   takes over and the data at the latch input may change.

What it costs you  
1. Extra capacitive load – the input capacitance of the red inverter is
   added to the output node of Inv1 and its output capacitance is added to
   the sampling node.  
2. Fight/contending drivers when CK rises – while the input tries to drive
   the sampling node, the red inverter is still driving the previous value
   for a few tens of picoseconds.  The input must overcome this, so
      • D-to-Q (or CK-to-Q) delay increases,  
      • the required set-up time increases.  
3. Some additional dynamic and short-circuit power and a little more area.

In short  

• Without the red inverter – smallest and fastest, but only a dynamic
  latch (cannot stop the clock, poor noise margin, data fades with leakage).  

• With the red inverter – robust, static storage and relaxed hold-time, but
  propagation delay and set-up time are a little worse and power/area are
  slightly higher.

So the red inverter improves reliability and low-frequency operation at the
expense of peak-speed performance.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer misidentifies the red inverter as a keeper/static-latch element and reverses both key effects: it is a feedforward path that improves speed, while its unclocked operation raises the minimum usable clock frequency. Its mention of driver contention is relevant, but does not rescue the central explanation.

answers.question:
In the figure, somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
Yes – the little red inverter is only a “keeper”.  
When the clocked pass device that precedes Inv1 is OFF the node at the
input of Inv1 would otherwise be a high-impedance (dynamic) node and the
charge on it would leak away after a few µs.  
The red inverter, whose output is wired back to that node, forms a weak
positive-feedback loop with Inv1:

    (input of Inv1) ─► Inv1 ─► red-INV ───┘

Because two inversions are present the loop is non-inverting, so whatever
logic level appears at the output of Inv1 is (weakly) forced back onto its
input.  This turns the node into a pseudo-static latch: after the clock
turns the pass device off the value is held indefinitely, limited only by
the sizing of the keeper.

• While CK is high the pass transistor that brings in the new data is
much stronger than the keeper, so the keeper does not disturb normal
operation (only a small contention current flows).

• When CK goes low the pass transistor opens, the node would float, and
the keeper takes over, counteracting leakage and removing any minimum-clock-frequency requirement for that stage.

So the red inverter is not there to add delay or to take part in the logic
function of the ring; its sole job is to maintain the logic level on an
otherwise floating node – exactly what a keeper does.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer misidentifies the red inverter’s connections and calls it a keeper. It is an unclocked feedforward branch that bypasses part of the latch path; it may help at high speed but can overpower the intended latch behavior at low clock rates, raising the minimum usable frequency.

answers.question:
In the figure, somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
The red inverter is not there to make the ring “run” – the three black inverters already give the loop the required odd number of inversions – and it is not just a little “keeper” transistor of the type used in domino logic.  
It is a full-fledged inverter that is cross-coupled with Inv1, so that the two of them form a tiny static latch.

What the latch is used for  
This gated ring oscillator is switched on and off with the two pass transistors driven by CK / CK̅.  
•  CK = 1  → both pass devices conduct and the ring oscillates.  
•  CK = 0  → both pass devices open and the chain is broken: the node that feeds Inv1 (call it N0) and the node at the output of Inv1 (N1) would otherwise be left floating.

When the chain is broken, the cross-coupled pair (Inv1 + red inverter) holds N0 and N1 at the logic values they had the instant CK went low.  
Because these two nodes continue to drive the following inverters, every other node in the ring is also held at a valid static level.  
Therefore the oscillator can be stopped for an arbitrarily long time – leakage cannot discharge any of the nodes – and it will restart in a well-defined phase when CK goes high again.

Why calling it a “keeper” is misleading  
A keeper in dynamic logic is usually a single, very weak transistor that only maintains a pre-charged ‘1’.  
Here we have a complete inverter that stores either ‘0’ or ‘1’; it is normally sized weak enough not to fight the travelling wave when the ring is enabled, but it is much stronger than a classical keeper.

So the correct statement is:

The red inverter, together with Inv1, forms a back-to-back inverter pair that freezes the state of the gated ring oscillator while CK is low, preventing leakage from disturbing the stored value and allowing the oscillator to be stopped for an unlimited time and restarted cleanly.

(It is this freezing function, not the mere presence of a weak keeper, that removes any minimum-frequency requirement.)

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer incorrectly treats the red inverter as cross-coupled with Inv1 and as a keeper. It misses its actual feedforward role and the low-frequency failure that raises the minimum usable clock rate.

answers.question:
In the figure, somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
Not quite.  
What is drawn is not a “keeper” in the usual sense that is used with
dynamic /domino nodes (i.e. a very-weak transistor that leaks just
enough current to compensate the leakage of the floating node while
allowing the logic network to override it easily).  
The red gate is a normal (not deliberately weakened) inverter that is
switched into the loop only when the transmission-gate in front of
Inv1 is open.  
Its purpose is to close a strong, regenerative feedback path so that
Inv1 and the red inverter form an ordinary cross-coupled pair – a
static latch – whenever the clock phase that drives the pass gate is
inactive.

Operation

1. CK = 1 (transparent phase)  
   • The left transmission gate is ON, so the data at the input can flow
     to the node that is the input of Inv1.  
   • The same clock phase turns the feedback path (shown in red) OFF,
     therefore there is no contention; the node can change freely.

2. CK = 0 (hold phase)  
   • The transmission gate opens; the input node is now isolated from
     the external data line.  
   • The feedback path through the red inverter is closed, completing a
     pair of back-to-back inverters (Inv1 + red).  
   • These two inverters actively regenerate and hold the logic level,
     so the stored value is kept indefinitely with true static
     retention.

Because the node is no longer left floating, there is no need for a
minimum clock frequency; the cell has been converted from a dynamic
pass-gate latch to a static transmission-gate latch.  
So while the presence of the red inverter indeed eliminates the
minimum-frequency requirement, calling it a “keeper” is misleading – it
is the feedback element that turns the stage into a static latch rather
than a weak leakage-compensation device.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer mistakes the red inverter for a clock-switched cross-coupled keeper and concludes that no minimum clock frequency is needed. In fact, it is an unclocked feedforward branch that bypasses part of the latch path; it can help at high speed but can overpower the intended behavior at low clock rates.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit shown in the figure for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
For the resistively-shunted common-source LNA the small–signal input resistance and the noise factor can be written very compactly:

1. Input resistance  
   Rin = Rf /( 1 + gm Rf )

2. Noise factor (long-channel MOS, ro  ≫ Rf , neglect gmb)  
   F ≃ 1 + γ /(gm Rs) + Rf /Rs · 1 /(1 + gm Rf )²         (Rs = 50 Ω)

Because the gate is open-circuited, the only independent design variables that remain are gm (set by the bias current and the device width of M1) and the feedback resistor Rf ; M2 can be regarded as an ideal, noiseless current source if it is cascoded properly.

50-Ω broadband matching fixes one relation between gm and Rf:

Rin = 50 Ω  ⇒  50 = Rf /(1 + gm Rf )  ⇒  gm = 1/50 – 1/Rf

or, more conveniently,

gm Rf = A          with        A = Rf /50 – 1                 (1)

so that Rf = 50 (1 + A) and gm = A /[ 50 (1 + A) ].

Insert (1) in the noise expression:

F = 1 + γ + γ/A + 1 /(1 + A)                               (2)

dF/dA = – γ /A² – 1 /(1 + A)²   < 0     for every   A > 0

Equation (2) shows that the excess noise figure is a monotonically decreasing
function of A = gm Rf .  In other words:

• The larger the transconductance gm (hence the larger the dc current you can afford) the lower the noise figure.  
• Rf must be increased at the same time according to (1) so that the real input impedance stays at 50 Ω.  
• As A → ∞ the two additional terms in (2) vanish and the minimum attainable noise factor approaches

        Fmin ≃ 1 + γ      ( ≈ 1.6…1.8   ⇒   NFmin ≈ 2…2.5 dB in CMOS )

Therefore, when 50-Ω matching has to be maintained, there is only one way to optimise the NF:

1. Spend as much bias current as the power budget allows and size M1 as wide as necessary to obtain the largest possible gm.  
2. Choose the feedback resistor from Rf = 50 (1 + gm·50) to keep Rin = 50 Ω.  
3. Make M2 a low-noise cascode (large gds, small γ) so that it adds negligible extra noise.

Once the maximum gm that the power budget allows has been selected, the noise figure is fixed; no further adjustment of Rf, of the over-drive voltage, or of any other linear parameter can lower the NF without breaking the 50-Ω match.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It assumes the infinite-output-resistance approximation, which pins matched gm at 1/Rs and concludes NF cannot fall below 1 + γ. The key result is that finite ro allows gm to exceed 1/Rs while RF is adjusted to keep Rin at 50 Ω, lowering NF below that limit.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit shown in the figure for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
1. Fix the small-signal transconductance.

   When the drain–gate resistor RF is the only path that brings the RF
   source current into the MOSFET gate, a simple small-signal analysis
   (r0 >> RF , Cgs shorted for the signal band) gives

          IIN = (VG – VD)/RF  =  –gm VG         ⇒   Rin = VG / IIN = 1/gm

   Hence the real part of the input impedance is set only by gm.  
   To keep Rin = 50 Ω you must therefore bias M1 at

          gm,opt = 1 / 50 Ω  ≃ 20 mS

   gm is adjusted with W/L and the bias current:

          Id  =  gm · (VGS – VTH)/α        (α ≃ 1 in strong inversion)

2. Make the feedback resistor as large as practicable.

   The two dominant noise contributors are the channel thermal noise of M1
   (id,n² = 4kT γ gm) and the Johnson noise of RF
   (iRF,n² = 4kT / RF).  Re-refering them to the 50-Ω input gives

          (en,MOS)² = (4kT γ gm) / gm² = 4kT γ RS
          (en,RF )² = (4kT / RF) RS²   = 4kT RS / RF · RS

   The overall noise factor becomes

          F  = 1 + γ            (MOS contribution)
                 + RS / RF       (feedback resistor)

   where γ ≃ 2/3 (long channel) … 1 (deep-sub-µ).

   • NF therefore approaches the theoretical minimum  

          Fmin = 1 + γ   (≈ 1.6…2.0, i.e. 1.8–3 dB)

     as soon as RF ≫ RS.  In practice a few kilo-ohms (1–5 kΩ) already
     makes RS/RF < 0.05, i.e. < 0.2 dB extra noise.

   • Increasing RF further no longer changes Rin, so the only real

   • Layout M1 with many short fingers to lower the distributed gate
     resistance RG; its thermal noise appears in series with the signal
     but does not affect the 50 Ω match.

   • Make the cascode device M2 just large enough for gain and voltage
     head-room; its channel noise is divided by the large ro2 and adds
     only a small fraction to F.

   • Choose the “quietest” transistor option the process offers
     (longer channel, thick-oxide if fT margin allows) to minimise γ.

4. There is no benefit in biasing harder than needed for gm = 20 mS;
   gm is fixed by the matching requirement, so extra current only wastes
   power without lowering NF.

Summary of the optimisation steps when Rin must stay at 50 Ω:

1. Set gm of M1 to ≈ 20 mS (Rin = 1/gm).  
2. Use the largest RF that still lets the DC feedback bias work
   (kΩ-range).  
3. Lay out M1 for low gate resistance and use a small, low-noise cascode.

   additional degradation is dominated by RS / RF and by RG, both of
   which you minimise as described above.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit shown in the figure for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
The input is applied to the gate of M1 and the 50 Ω antenna (or test generator) is coupled through C1.  
The only way the antenna “sees” exactly 50 Ω is through the shunt-feedback loop formed by R​F and the intrinsic transconductance of M1.  
With the small-signal model of the cell one obtains    

          Rin = (1 + gds R​F)/(gm + gds)  ≈ 1/gm                ( ro (=1/gds) » 50 Ω )

Hence, as long as we keep ro of M1 reasonably large, the input match is fixed almost exclusively by gm:

          gm ≃ 1/Rin = 1/50 Ω ≃ 20 mS                       (1)

If we try to increase gm any further the input resistance would fall below 50 Ω, so we would have to raise R​F in exactly the amount required by (1) to keep the product in (1) unchanged.  
In other words, the 50 Ω specification ties gm and R​F together; one cannot be changed without readjusting the other.

Noise figure

For the circuit of Fig.-1, neglecting flicker noise and using the usual MOS coefficients
( γ ≃ 2/3 for channel thermal noise and δ ≃ 2 for drain-to-bulk noise), the noise factor can be written to first order as

          F = 1 + γ /(gm Rs) + Rs /R​F + δ gds Rs            (2)

where Rs = 50 Ω.  
Substituting the matching condition gm = 1/Rs into (2) gives

          F = 1 + γ + Rs /R​F + δ gds Rs                    (3)

Observations from (3)  

1. The contribution γ is now a constant ( γ ≃ 0.67 ⇒ 1.6 dB ) once 50 Ω matching is enforced.  
   It cannot be improved unless a device with a smaller γ (longer channel, lower VOV, cooled
   operation, etc.) is used.

2. The term δ gds Rs is normally a few hundredths of a decibel because gds is of the order of tens of µS while Rs = 50 Ω.

3. The only term that can still be influenced by the designer is Rs /R​F.  
   It becomes negligible if R​F is made much larger than 50 Ω (e.g. ≥ 500 Ω).

Design recipe for minimum NF with Rin = 50 Ω

Step-1   Size and bias M1 so that gm ≃ 20 mS (eq.-1).  
          That automatically provides the 50 Ω match.

Step-2   Choose R​F as large as the stability / gain / bandwidth constraints allow.  
          With R​F ≥ 500–1000 Ω the term Rs /R​F falls below 0.05–0.1 dB.

Step-3   Keep M2 (the PMOS load) as small as possible and/or cascode it so that its
          noise and parasitic capacitances do not add appreciably to F and do not
          disturb the wide-band match.

Result

With the above choices the last two terms in (3) are almost zero and the lowest
achievable noise factor is

          Fmin ≈ 1 + γ  →  NFmin ≈ 10·log10(1 + γ) ≈ 2.0–2.3 dB   (γ ≃ 0.6–0.7).

Therefore, once the 50 Ω input resistance is mandatory, the NF of a simple shunt-feedback common-source stage can be pushed only down to about 2 dB by

• providing exactly gm = 1/50 Ω, and  
• making R​F as large as practical so that its own thermal noise is negligible.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
Denote the small-signal voltage of the input node P by vP and the signal current delivered by the photo-diode (or current source) by iIN.  
All MOS transistors are assumed to operate in saturation and are represented by their transconductance gm and output resistance ro.

1. Open-loop gain from node P to the output  
   • Stage-1 (M1) vP → node X  
     iD1 = gm1 vgs1 = gm1 vP  
     vX = −iD1 (RD1 || ro1) = −gm1 (RD1 || ro1) vP ≜ A1 vP , A1 = −gm1R1 , R1 = RD1 || ro1  
   • Stage-2 (M2) node X → node Y (drain of M2)  
     vY = −gm2 (ro2 || ro3) vX = gm1gm2 R1R2 vP , R2 = ro2 || ro3 , A2 = −gm2R2  
   • Stage-3 (M3) node Y → Vout (through RD2)  
     vOUT = −gm3 RD2 vY = −gm1gm2gm3 R1R2RD2 vP  
  
   Hence the open-loop voltage gain seen between P and the output is  

     AOL ≜ vOUT / vP = −gm1gm2gm3 (RD1 || ro1)(ro2 || ro3)RD2       (1)

2. Relation produced by the feedback resistor RF  
   The gate of M1 is an open circuit for small signals, therefore the only path for the input current is through RF (Cin is ignored for the low-frequency resistance calculation):

     iIN = (vP − vOUT)/RF                                          (2)

   Using (1): vOUT = AOL vP  
   Insert in (2) and solve for vP / iIN = Rin

     iIN = (vP − AOL vP)/RF = vP (1 + |AOL|)/RF  
  
     Rin ≜ vP / iIN = RF / (1 + |AOL|)                            (3)

3. Closed-loop input impedance  
   Substituting (1) in (3)

     Rin = RF / [ 1 + gm1gm2gm3 (RD1 || ro1)(ro2 || ro3)RD2 ]     (4)

   Because the loop gain |AOL| is normally very large (|AOL| ≫ 1) in a transimpedance amplifier,

     Rin ≈ 1 / [ gm1gm2gm3 (RD1 || ro1)(ro2 || ro3)RD2 ]          (5)

   To first order, if the two downstream devices are much stronger than M1, the expression is often written in the compact “regulated-cascode” form

     Rin ≈ 1 / [ gm1 (1 + gm2 ro2) ] .                            (6)

4. Interpretation  
   • Without regulation (only M1 in common-source) the input resistance would be extremely high.  
   • The extra gain furnished by M2, M3 and their loads multiplies gm1, pushing Rin down by the large factor (1+|AOL|).  
   • For practical gm’s of a few mS and resistive loads of a few kΩ, Rin is driven to a few ohms or less, creating an excellent “virtual-ground” node for the photo-detector.

Therefore the input impedance of the circuit is

     Rin = RF / [ 1 + gm1gm2gm3 (RD1 || ro1)(ro2 || ro3)RD2 ] ,

and, for the usual high-gain condition, approximately

     Rin ≃ 1 / ( gm1gm2gm3 (RD1 || ro1)(ro2 || ro3)RD2 )  
          ≃ 1 / [ gm1 (1 + gm2 ro2) ] .

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly recognizes that feedback through RF reduces the input impedance, but treats the amplifier as an ideal gain block and uses an incorrect staged gain. It misses the required Miller result, Rin = (RF + RD2)/(1 + A0), including the output resistance.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
Let  

V P  : small–signal voltage at the input node P  
V X  : voltage at node X (drain of M1 – source of M2)  
V Y  : voltage at node Y (drain of M2 – gate of M3)  
V o  : small-signal output voltage (node Vout)  

1.  Small-signal relationships inside the amplifier  

a)  Transistor M1 (common-source)

      i d1 = g m1 V P                           (A)  
      V X = − i d1 ( R D1 ∥ 1 / g m2 )  
          ≈ − ( g m1 / g m2 ) V P              (B)         ( 1∕g m2  «  R D1 )

b)  Transistor M2 (common-gate)

      V Y = g m2 r o2 V X                      (C)  
          ≈ − g m1 r o2 V P                    (D)

c)  Transistor M3 (source follower)

      A 3  = g m3 R L ⁄ ( 1 + g m3 R L ) ≈ 1   (R L  =  R D2  ∥  r o3 )  
      V o  ≃ V Y                               (E)

Hence the open-loop voltage gain of the three-transistor amplifier is

      A OL  = V o / V P  ≈ − g m1 r o2 .       (1)

(With typical values g m1  ≈ 5 mS and r o2  ≈ 40 kΩ, | A OL |  ≈ 200.)

2.  Relation between I in and V P (node equation at P)

At node P the only small-signal elements are the feedback resistor R F and the gate of M1 (open circuit), therefore

      I in  +  ( V P − V o ) / R F  = 0  
⇒    I in  =  ( V o − V P ) / R F .            (2)

3.  Input impedance

From (1) let  A  =  V o / V P .  Substitute in (2):

      I in  =  ( A − 1 ) V P / R F

Therefore the small-signal input impedance is

      R in  ≡  V P / I in  =  R F / ( A − 1 )                (3)

With negative feedback A is large and negative; use its magnitude:

      R in  ≈  R F / ( 1 + | A OL | )  
            ≈  R F / ( 1 + g m1 r o2 )                      (4)

Whenever g m1 r o2  »  1 the first “1” can be dropped, giving the very compact and practical result

      R in  ≃  R F / ( g m1 r o2 ) .                         (5)

Thus the feedback forces the input node to behave like a “virtual ground,” and the input resistance is the feedback resistor divided by the loop-gain g m1 r o2, making it orders of magnitude smaller than R F.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly recognizes that negative feedback reduces the input resistance, but its gain model and resulting formula omit the output resistance in the feedback path. The required exact result is Rin = (RF + RD2)/(1 + A0), with the specified two-stage unloaded gain.

answer.text:
Let  

vP  = small–signal voltage at node P  
iin = small–signal current that the source connected to the amplifier delivers to node P  

Input (small–signal) impedance : Rin = vP / iin.  

The only element that can conduct current away from node P is the feedback resistor RF, because the
gate current of M1 is (to first order) zero.  Hence  

iin + ( vP – vout ) / RF = 0  ⇒  vP = vout  –  iin RF                 (1)

Let A be the open-loop voltage gain of the amplifier block made with M1–M2–M3:

A ≜ ∂vout / ∂vP                                                           (2)

(With the polarities in the figure A is positive; two common-source stages give two sign inversions.)

From (2): vout = A vP.  
Insert this in (1):

vP = A vP – iin RF  ⟹  vP (1 – A) = − iin RF

Therefore  

Rin = vP / iin = RF / (A – 1) ≈ RF / A  (if |A| ≫ 1)                 (3)

Open-loop gain A

Ignoring channel-length modulation (ro → ∞) so that RD1 and RD2 are the only loads,

• First stage (M1, common source): A1 = − gm1 RD1  
• Second stage (M3, common source, PMOS): A2 = − gm3 RD2

A = A1 · A2 = (− gm1 RD1)(− gm3 RD2) = gm1 gm3 RD1 RD2  (4)

Putting (4) in (3):

Rin ≈ RF / ( gm1 gm3 RD1 RD2 )                                            (5)

If the finite output resistances of the transistors and of the current source ISS are taken into account,
replace RD1 and RD2 in (4) by the total resistances seen looking into the drains of M1 and M3,
e.g. RD1‖ro1‖ro2‖roISS , RD2‖ro3 , so that

A ≈ gm1 (RD1‖ro1‖ro2‖roISS) · gm3 (RD2‖ro3)

and  

Rin ≈ RF / A = RF / [ gm1 gm3 (RD1‖ro1‖ro2‖roISS)(RD2‖ro3) ].        (6)

Because the loop-gain term in the denominator can easily be several hundreds,
Rin can be brought down to a few ohms or less, providing the very low input-impedance
required of a transimpedance amplifier.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Step-by-step procedure  

1. Measure the “pushing” factor of the VCO  
   Sweep the supply that feeds the VCO a small amount ( ±ΔV ) and record the change of the oscillation frequency f0 :  

 P ≜ ∂f0 / ∂VDD  [Hz / V]  
   (sometimes quoted in MHz/V).  
   In rad/s units                                  
 K ≜ ∂ω0 / ∂VDD = 2πP  [rad s-1 / V]                (1)

2. Write the transfer function from supply-voltage noise to phase  
   A small supply-voltage disturbance vdd (t) produces an instantaneous frequency
 Δω(t)=K vdd(t).  
   Phase is the integral of frequency, therefore in the frequency domain  

 Φ(j2πf)= K  VDD(j2πf) /(j2πf).                  (2)

   The magnitude-squared transfer function is  

 |Hφvdd(f)|² = K² /(2πf)².                       (3)

3. Multiply the transfer function by the LDO noise spectrum  
   The LDO produces a voltage-noise power spectral density  

 Svdd(f)= Sth(f)  [V²/Hz].  

   Hence the phase-noise spectrum contributed by the LDO is  

 Sφ(f)= |Hφvdd(f)|²  Svdd(f)                    
      = K² Svdd(f) / (2πf)² .                   (4)

4. Express it as single-sideband phase noise (dBc/Hz)  
   By definition, single-sideband phase noise is one half of the double-sideband
   phase spectrum,

 L(f) = ½ Sφ(f) = K² Svdd(f) / (4π² f²)  [rad²/Hz] (linear)   (5)

   or in decibels relative to the carrier  

 L_dB(f) = 10 log10 [ K² Svdd(f) / (4π² f²) ]  [dBc/Hz].      (6)

5. Practical use  
   • Obtain Svdd(f)=Sth(f) from the regulator’s data or simulation.  
   • Find P (or K) from a two-point sweep or a small-signal AC analysis of the VCO.  
   • Insert K and Svdd(f) in (6); the result is the VCO phase-noise spectrum caused
     by the LDO.  
   • If several supply-coupling paths exist (tail current source, varactor bias,
     etc.), evaluate each path’s sensitivity and add the resulting phase-noise
     spectra because noise powers sum.

Thus the VCO phase noise originating from the LDO is obtained simply by
“FM-modulating” the oscillator with the supply-voltage noise and remembering that
phase is the time-integral of frequency, which contributes the familiar 1/f²
shape of equation (5).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly uses supply-pushing sensitivity to convert LDO noise into frequency noise and applies FM-to-phase conversion with a 1/f² dependence. It omits the circuit-specific insight that the supply acts directly on the varactors, making Kpush closely related to KVCO; the factor-of-two convention is not significant.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Think of the LDO as just another noise source that perturbs the quantity to which the oscillator is sensitive – its supply voltage.  
The procedure is identical to the one normally used for “tuning-line” (KVCO) noise:

1. Find the supply-pushing coefficient of the VCO  
   kpush  ≜  ∂fosc / ∂Vout        (Hz / V)                    (1)  
   (or in rad/s per volt, kω = 2πkpush).  
   Do this once in simulation or measurement by changing Vout a few millivolts and
   reading the change in oscillation frequency.

2. The LDO presents a voltage-noise PSD Sth(f)  [V²/Hz] at the VCO supply pin.  
   That noise is therefore translated into frequency noise

        SΔf(f) = kpush² · Sth(f)          [Hz²/Hz]             (2)

   (or SΔω(f)=kω²·Sth(f) in rad²/s²/Hz).

3. Frequency noise is an integrated quantity with respect to phase, so to obtain
   the phase-noise PSD you divide by the square of the offset frequency:

        Sφ(f) = SΔf(f) / f² = kpush² · Sth(f) / f²   [rad²/Hz] (3)

4. Single-side-band (SSB) phase noise L(f) normally quoted for oscillators is

        L(f) = ½ · Sφ(f)  [dBc/Hz]                           (4)

   therefore, in closed form,

        L(f) = 10·log₁₀ [ kpush² · Sth(f) / (2 f²) ]  dBc/Hz  (5)

If the supply line contains additional filtering or on-chip decoupling, include
its transfer function Hs(f) from the LDO output to the VCO core:

        L(f) = 10·log₁₀ [ |Hs(f)|² · kpush² · Sth(f) / (2 f²) ].

Key points:

• A white (flat) LDO-noise spectrum produces a 1/f² phase-noise skirt.  
• The result must be added (in linear units) to the intrinsic phase noise of the
  VCO to get the total output phase noise.  
• kpush is usually tens-to-hundreds of kHz/V for an LC VCO; a lower value or
  stronger supply filtering directly lowers the phase noise contributed by the
  LDO.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly converts LDO voltage noise through the supply-pushing gain and applies the 1/f² FM-to-phase-noise relationship. It omits the circuit-specific insight that supply perturbation acts directly on the varactors, tying Kpush to KVCO; its KVCO reference is only indirect.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
1. Write the small-signal relation between a supply perturbation and the instantaneous oscillation frequency  

     ω(t)=ω0+P ΔVout(t)                   (P = dω/dVout   [rad s-1 V-1])

   P (often called “supply pushing”) can be obtained with a dc sweep or an ac
   transfer-function simulation: change Vout a few millivolts and measure the resulting
   change in oscillation frequency.

2. Convert the regulator noise into frequency noise  

     Sω(f)=P² Sout(f)

   where Sout(f)=Sth(f) (V²/Hz) is the thermal-noise spectrum delivered by the LDO.
   If the VCO core has a finite PSRR, multiply Sth by |PSRR(f)|² first:

     Sout,core(f)=|PSRR(f)|² Sth(f)

3. Frequency noise produces phase noise through one integration (1/j2πf)  

     Hφvdd(j2πf)=P/(j2πf)

     Sφ(f)=|Hφvdd|² Sout,core(f)= P² Sout,core(f)/(2πf)²      (rad²/Hz)

4. Single-side-band phase-noise density (what is usually quoted) is one-half of the
   two-sided phase-noise PSD:

     L(f)=½ Sφ(f)= P² Sout,core(f)/(4π²f²)              (linear)

   or, in the customary dBc/Hz form,

     L(f)[dBc/Hz]=10·log₁₀ [ P² Sout,core(f)/(4π²f²) ].

So, to compute the VCO phase noise produced by the LDO:

• Measure (or simulate) the LDO’s output-noise spectral density Sth(f).  
• Find the oscillator’s supply-pushing coefficient P.  
• If necessary, include the VCO PSRR.  
• Insert the numbers in

     L(f)= P² Sth(f)/(4π²f²)           (for |PSRR|≈1)

This gives the phase-noise contribution (in dBc/Hz) at any offset frequency f
from the carrier that is due solely to the LDO’s thermal noise.

It omits the circuit-specific insight that supply noise acts directly on the varactors, making the pushing sensitivity closely related to KVCO; its phase-noise expression also has a minor factor-of-two inconsistency.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
Adding the capacitor C​T makes the tail node (node P) behave like an rf/low–noise ac-ground.  
Because of this, the noise mechanisms that normally originate in, or are conveyed through, the tail branch are strongly attenuated.

1. Tail-current-source noise is shunted to ground  
   • At frequencies for which |1/ωC​T| ≪ r​tail (the small-signal output resistance of I​SS), the impedance seen looking into the tail node is no longer r​tail but the much smaller 1/ωC​T.  
   • The thermal and 1/f noise current of the tail device therefore flows through C​T to ground instead of being forced through the cross-coupled pair and into the LC tank.  
   • In that offset-frequency range the contribution of the tail branch to phase noise is reduced roughly by the ratio |Z​tail,old| / |Z​tail,new|, i.e.

        ΔL(Δf) ≈ 20 log ( r​tail / (1/ωΔf C​T) )  dB.

2. Less AM-to-PM conversion  
   Fluctuations of the tail node voltage give rise to gm-modulation of M1/M2, which up-converts low-frequency noise to the neighbourhood of the carrier. With the tail node now held almost at ac ground, those fluctuations are suppressed, so the flicker-noise corner is pushed farther away from the carrier.

3. Negative-resistance magnitude is restored  
   A finite tail impedance degenerates the differential pair and reduces its −2/gm negative resistance. By shorting the tail node at the oscillation frequency, C​T removes this degeneration, yielding larger negative resistance and hence better tank excitation with the same bias current, which also helps the phase noise.

Net result

• Close-in (1/f³) corner moves farther out;  
• Mid- and far-offset phase-noise level drops—often by 6–15 dB, depending on how large a capacitor can be placed at the tail node.  

Practical limits

• C​T must be large enough that 1/ω₀C​T ≪ r​tail; beyond that point further increase gives only diminishing returns while slowing start-up and increasing the required bias current.  
• Very-close-in noise (where 1/ωΔf ≫ r​tail) is little affected because C​T no longer looks like a short there.

So, in summary, adding C​T at the tail node improves (reduces) the oscillator’s phase noise, especially at medium and far frequency offsets, by isolating the LC tank from the noisy tail current source and by preventing AM-to-PM conversion through tail-node modulation.

It misses the nonmonotonic effect, including the class-C improvement and at least one degradation mechanism such as flicker-noise upconversion or large-CT instability.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in the figure. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
Placing a capacitor CT from the source (tail) node P to ground makes that node an ac-ground at the oscillation frequency (and its harmonics).  
This has two important consequences for the noise that finally appears as phase jitter on the carrier:

1. Suppression of the tail-device noise  
   • The tail current source is no longer in series with the tank for ac signals; its white and 1/f noise currents flow through CT to ground instead of through the cross-coupled pair.  
   • Because the common-mode voltage on node P is now almost constant, the flicker-noise current of the tail device cannot be up-converted to the carrier by the gm-modulation mechanism.  
   Result: close-in (1/f³, 1/f²) phase noise typically improves by several dB.

2. Smaller amplitude-to-phase conversion  
   • With the tail node ac-grounded, the differential pair draws a nearly constant rf current, so the amplitude of the tank voltage is less sensitive to small current perturbations.  
   • Less AM–PM conversion further lowers the close-in noise skirt.

What does not change (or changes little)  
• The thermal noise generated by the cross-coupled transistors and by the LC tank remains; therefore the far-out (white) phase-noise floor is almost unaffected.  
• If CT is made excessively large, the conduction angle of the pair becomes very narrow, which can slightly increase higher-order harmonics and degrade far-out noise; in practice an optimum CT is chosen that gives the best overall phase-noise improvement.

In short: adding a sufficiently large bypass capacitor at the tail node reduces the up-conversion of the tail current source noise, so the phase noise of the oscillator is lowered—especially close to the carrier (often by 5–15 dB, depending on bias conditions and the value of CT).

 |ZCT| = 1/(ωCT)  ≪  ro,tail .

   • Because that noise current is no longer mixed with the large-signal switching waveform, its up-conversion to offsets around the carrier is strongly suppressed.

2. It restores the ideal, degeneration-free differential pair.  
   • With the sources at ac ground the effective negative resistance is −2/gm (no 1 + gmZtail term).  
   • A larger negative resistance lets the tank swing higher, so the signal power Ps at the tank nodes rises.  Since Leeson’s expression contains the term kT / Ps, a larger Ps directly lowers phase noise.

   • For offsets where ωΔ < 1/(ro,tail CT) the capacitor no longer looks like a short; the tail impedance again becomes large and the current-source flicker noise can be up-converted.

answer.text:
What you have in the figure is simply two identical LC-tank oscillators that are weakly coupled so that their steady-state solutions are 90° apart (quadrature).  
The coupling devices furnish the required in-phase or quadrature currents but they do not add any appreciable phase shift at the oscillation frequency; consequently the frequency is set almost entirely by the resonance of the two LC tanks.

Resonance condition of each tank  
For either of the four tank nodes

  ωL = 1 / (ωCtot)   →  ωosc = 1 / √(L·Ctot)

and

  fosc = ωosc / 2π = 1 / [ 2π √(L·Ctot) ]

where  

• L is the value of either spiral inductor shown, and  
• Ctot is the total capacitance that appears from each node to AC ground
  (varactor capacitance + device parasitics + the small extra capacitance
  contributed by the coupling transistors and wiring).

Because the two tanks are nominally equal and are only weakly loaded by the coupling network, the frequency of the composite quadrature oscillator is practically the same as that of a single tank built with the same L and C.

If numerical values are needed, insert them directly in the expression above.  
Example (just to illustrate):

 L = 2 nH, Ctot = 1 pF → fosc ≈ 1 / [2π √(2 nH·1 pF)] ≈ 3.6 GHz

Hence, to first order

 fosc ≈ 1 / (2π √(L·Ctot)).

(The presence of the second core and the coupling devices only changes Ctot by a few femtofarads, so the frequency shift is usually <1 %. )

The two cores that make up the circuit are nothing more than a pair of identical differential LC oscillators that are (weakly) injection-coupled to obtain the required phase relationship between X1–Y1 and X2–Y2.  
Coupling only adds a small perturbation to the natural resonance of each tank, so to first order the frequency is the resonance of one LC tank:

 ω0 ≈ 1 / √(L Ctot)   fosc ≈ 1 / (2π √(L Ctot))

where  

• L = inductance of the coil connected between each differential node and VDD  
• Ctot = total single-ended capacitance at the node (fixed tank capacitor + varactor + device and coupling parasitics).

If you insert typical on-chip values, e.g.

 L ≈ 3 nH, Ctot ≈ 1.1 pF

you obtain

 fosc ≈ 1 / [2π √(3 nH × 1.1 pF)] ≃ 2.8 GHz.

Thus, aside from a few-percent shift caused by the mutual injection, the oscillation frequency is essentially

 fosc ≈ 1 / (2π √(L Ctot)).

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in the figure.

answer.text:
Each core of the circuit is an ordinary cross-coupled LC‐oscillator.  
Except for a very small extra capacitance that the coupling devices add, the two
cores see exactly the same resonant tank they would have if they were running
alone, so the oscillation frequency is still dictated almost entirely by the
inductor L of each coil and by the total differential capacitance CT that
appears across the tank nodes:

ω0 ≈ 1 / √(L · CT)  
f0 = ω0 / 2π ≈ 1 / (2π √(L · CT))

where  

• L is the inductance of one spiral,  
• CT is the sum of the tuning-varactor capacitance, any fixed metal
  capacitors, the MOS parasitic capacitances (Cgs , Cgd /2, Cdb, etc.) and the
  small capacitance of the coupling transistors.

Because the coupling network mainly provides the required 90-degree phase shift
between the two identical LC cores, it hardly changes CT; therefore the above
expression gives a good estimate of the frequency of the complete circuit.

Example (typical 2.4-GHz IC values)  
If L ≈ 1.5 nH and CT can be tuned from about 0.25 pF to 0.45 pF,

fmin ≈ 1 / (2π√(1.5 nH × 0.45 pF)) ≈ 2.0 GHz  
fmax ≈ 1 / (2π√(1.5 nH × 0.25 pF)) ≈ 2.6 GHz

so the oscillator runs around 2.3 ± 0.3 GHz.  

Thus, to first order,

fosc ≈ 1 / [ 2π √(L · CT) ].
